## UI: Tiled Agent Panel

The extension opens a VS Code Webview panel with one tile per active agent role, one tile per orchestrator-spawned process.

### Panel Layout

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  SwarmForge  [target: my-app]  [7-pack ▾]  [▶ Run] │
├──────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┤
│  coordinator     │  coder                           │
│  ─────────────── │  ──────────────────────────────  │
│  [live output]   │  [live output]                   │
│                  │                                  │
│                  │                                  │
├──────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────┤
│  cleaner      │  architect                       │
│  ─────────────── │  ──────────────────────────────  │
│  [live output]   │  [live output]                   │
│                  │                                  │
│                  │                                  │
└──────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┘
│  Status: running  •  Stage: architect  •  dev/feat-login  │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Two layers: tile-as-view, process-as-substrate

A point worth stating plainly, because there's a tempting wrong turn nearby: **the tiles are TypeScript/webview views; the agent processes the orchestrator spawns are the substrate underneath.** They are not alternatives — they are different layers.

- The **tile** is what you see and interact with: a terminal widget the extension renders and fully controls (styling, layout, the per-tile controls, tracked input).
- The **process** is what runs the agent: an `InteractiveProcess` the orchestrator spawned (shell backend or `vscode.lm` runtime), in its own worktree, with its output stream owned directly by the host. The tile reads that stream and paints it, and forwards your keystrokes back down via `write()`.

Spawning agent processes from TypeScript **is** the intended design — that is what the orchestrator is for. The line not to cross is a different one: do not let **coordination logic** (pipeline sequencing, merge, message routing, convergence) leak into the process layer. The orchestrator is a *process manager* only; coordination belongs in the coordinator role and the message bus. If a step at build time feels like you're building pipeline or routing logic inside the process manager, that's the signal you've drifted across this line.

### Tile Behavior

- Each tile streams stdout of its agent's process in real time (subscribe to the `InteractiveProcess` `onData` stream)
- **Tile border states** (with precedence rules applied):
  - **Dead** (steady red) — agent process terminated abnormally
  - **Needs Human** (blue pulse, 1.5s cycle) — agent awaiting human input (permission prompts, yes/no questions, multiple-choice selections)
  - **Stalled** (steady yellow) — agent idle with no output for >2 minutes
  - **Normal** (grey) — agent idle with recent output
  - **Active** (blue) — agent currently producing output
  - *Precedence: dead > needs-human > stalled > normal. A needs-human border suppresses the stalled color, so you can see when an agent is waiting for you to respond.*
- Tile header shows the role name and (when active) a badge with the backlog item ID and short summary (e.g., "BL-038 · tile header active ticket"); when a role holds multiple parcels, the badge shows the lowest ticket ID plus a "+N" count for the others (e.g., "BL-036 · redo_from tool +1"), so you can see at a glance what each agent is working on
- **Decision-menu LIVE / RESOLVED banner (BL-421).** A rendered decision menu (e.g. an `AskUserQuestion` prompt with numbered options and a highlighted "Recommended" choice) stays visible in a tile's reconstructed transcript long after the pane has moved on, because the retained scrollback (see below) is never purged — so a human could mistake a long-settled decision for one still awaiting an answer. The tile now banners the menu block itself: `⚠ Awaiting your answer` while the pane's current captured frame is still the pending prompt (LIVE), or `✓ Decision already resolved — not actionable` once the frame has moved on but the menu still appears earlier in the transcript (RESOLVED). Liveness is judged only from the current frame, never by pattern-matching the transcript, so a resolved menu that is byte-identical to a live one is still marked RESOLVED. No marker is shown when neither the current frame nor the transcript contains a decision menu.
- Each tile is always a live embedded terminal — you click into any tile and type directly, exactly as you would in a real terminal attached to that agent
- No expand needed; all tiles are simultaneously interactive, one live terminal per role

#### Tile Selection

- Click a tile header to select it; the selected tile expands to fill 2×2 grid cells (double width and height) for easier reading and interaction
- Click the selected tile header again to deselect it and return to equal-sized tiles
- Only one tile can be selected at a time; selecting a new tile automatically deselects the previous one
- Selection persists across webview reloads

#### Tile Scrolling and Autoscroll

Tiles automatically follow the agent's live output ("tail-locked") so you always see the newest transcript line:

- **Autoscroll**: By default, tiles scroll to show the newest output as it streams. The tile anchors to the agent's live content line, positioned just above any pinned TUI footer (the input prompt, status bar, or interrupt indicator)
- **Scrollback history**: Each tile retains a history of earlier output, bounded by `swarmforge.tile.historyLines` (default 500 lines). The extension accumulates this host-side since agents running in tmux's alternate screen have no tmux scrollback to retrieve
- **Manual scroll-up**: Scroll up to read earlier output beyond the visible rows and the tile releases tail-lock — new output no longer forces the view downward. Scroll up to reach the retained history, not just the immediate scrollback
- **Re-engage**: Scroll back down to the live region and tail-lock re-engages, resuming autoscroll to follow new output
- **Footer visibility**: The pinned footer (input box and status line) remains visible while autoscrolling; live content is never hidden behind it

#### Human input is tracked, not a side-channel

Typing directly into a tile is powerful but creates a hazard: a hand-typed instruction ("skip the auth check") lives only in the terminal scrollback — invisible to the pipeline, the Work Tree, the audit trail, and the next agent. That makes human input an *untracked* channel that can silently contradict the tracked message bus.

To close this, direct typing is **mirrored into the message store** as a human-origin event:

- Keystrokes sent to an agent's process are also captured as a `human-input` message (`from: human, to: <role>`, with the text), appended to that agent's message log
- So the instruction becomes part of the same auditable record as agent-to-agent handoffs — it shows in the message view, survives respawn (the agent's auto-pickup sees it), and is visible to anyone reviewing what shaped the run
- A small "✎ human" marker on the tile and in the message view distinguishes human nudges from agent traffic
- This doesn't restrict what you can type — it just ensures nothing you tell an agent is invisible to the rest of the system. The capture is best-effort for raw keystrokes; a dedicated "send instruction" input box per tile (logged cleanly as one message) is the recommended primary path, with raw typing as the fallback

### Resizable Tiles

Tiles are not forced into an equal grid — you can give more screen to the agents you care about.

- Each tile has a **weight** in the layout; drag the divider between tiles to resize, exactly like split editors in VS Code
- Useful for watching one role closely (e.g. make the `specifier` tile large while shrinking `qa`) without losing visibility of the others
- Layout weights persist per workspace, so your preferred arrangement survives restarts
- A tile can be collapsed to a thin status strip (role name + liveness dot + heartbeat age) when you want it present but minimal
- "Reset layout" returns all tiles to equal weight

### Per-Tile Controls

Each tile has a small control row (hover or always-visible header):

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **⟳ Respawn** | Kills that one agent's process and relaunches it in the same worktree, without touching any other agent. The swarm keeps running. |
| **model ▾** | Dropdown of available backends/models (`claude`, `codex`, `copilot`, `grok`, …). Changing it respawns that single agent on the new backend on the fly. |
| **⏸ / ▶** | Pause or resume the individual agent (optional, v1.1) |

Respawn preserves the agent's worktree and branch state — only the running process is replaced. The new process re-reads its role prompt and constitution on launch, so any prompt edits made mid-run take effect on respawn.
- Tiles are **interactive** — the developer can type directly into any agent's session at any time, injecting guidance mid-run without stopping the swarm

### Top Bar Controls

| Control | Behavior |
|---|---|
| **target** | Path or GitHub URL of the target project. Persisted per workspace. |
| **pack selector** | Dropdown: forge analyzes the target and suggests a pack (2 / 4 / 7); user confirms or overrides |
| **▶ Run** | Triggers the swarm run |
| **⏹ Stop** | Signals the coordinator to stand down, then the orchestrator terminates all agent processes (coordinator last) |
| **Start Bridge** | Starts a local read-only HTTP server that projects swarm state via JSON endpoints and a real-time SSE event stream (opt-in; requires a running swarm) |
| **Stop Bridge** | Stops the bridge server |

### Read-Only Bridge (Phase 1)

The bridge is an **opt-in local HTTP server** that exposes the same on-disk swarm state the extension reads, via JSON endpoints and a real-time event stream. Phase 1 is mostly read-only and localhost-only; **BL-790** adds one authenticated control endpoint (`POST /agent-notes`) that queues operator notes into role mailboxes.

**When to use it:** Expose swarm state to a monitoring tool, script, or browser client running on your development machine. Later phases will add remote (off-LAN) access and control endpoints.

**Starting the bridge:**
- Run the VS Code command **SwarmForge: Start Bridge** (`swarmforge.startBridge`)
- The extension generates a one-time bearer token and starts the server on a localhost port (e.g. `http://127.0.0.1:9999`)
- The info message shows both a ready-to-open URL with the token embedded (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/?token=<token>`, for the holistic web UI below) and the raw token for `Authorization: Bearer` API requests

**Stopping the bridge:**
- Run the VS Code command **SwarmForge: Stop Bridge** (`swarmforge.stopBridge`)
- Or terminate the extension; the bridge shuts down automatically

**Security:**
- Every request requires a valid bearer token in the `Authorization` header: `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
- Exception: the root HTML page (below) additionally accepts the token via a `?token=` query parameter, since a plain browser navigation cannot attach a header — scoped narrowly to that one route; every JSON/SSE endpoint stays header-only
- The token is generated per run and held only in the extension host environment — it never appears in the target repo or any commit
- Requests without a valid token receive a 401 Unauthorized response with no state disclosed
- The bridge listens on 127.0.0.1 only; it is not accessible over the network

**Available endpoints (Phase 1):**

| Endpoint | Response | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /` | HTML: the holistic dev-state web UI (see below) | A single-page, self-contained live view of the swarm |
| `GET /pipeline` | JSON: current stage per active parcel | Which role holds each ticket |
| `GET /agents` | JSON: per-agent status + heartbeat | Liveness, stall detection, "needs human" states |
| `GET /backlog` | JSON: active/paused/done items | Backlog folders and ticket metadata |
| `GET /runlog` | JSON: timeline of stage transitions and key events | Run history and audit trail |
| `GET /events` | Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream | Real-time updates when stage or agent state changes |
| `GET /metrics` | JSON: delivery-flow metrics (velocity, burndown, cycle time, forecasts, suite duration trend) | Trend/forecast data for monitoring dashboards or scripts |
| `GET /cost-telemetry` | JSON: per-role token/cost usage by day, cost attributed per ticket, and resource (RSS/CPU) trends | Token spend and resource usage for monitoring dashboards or scripts |
| `GET /cost-rank` | JSON: ranked LLM invocation costs by origin over named horizons (3h, 24h, 7d); query params: `horizon`, `top`, `groupBy` | Cost analysis — which swarm areas/roles consume the most tokens, ranked and grouped by origin |
| `GET /holistic` | JSON: the projection backing the `/` page — swarm assignments, done-by-milestone, recent activity | The web UI's own data source; also usable directly by scripts |
| `GET /stage-dwell` | JSON: per-stage queue-wait/processing dwell (median/p90/max), bottleneck stage, trend vs. prior window | The coordinator's swarm-optimizer instrument; also usable directly by scripts |
| `GET /burn-rate` | JSON: per-role live token burn rate (tokens/hr) | Live "how fast is each agent burning tokens right now" meter, beyond BL-100's daily aggregates |
| `POST /agent-notes` | JSON: queue a `type: note` parcel at priority `00` into a declared role's mailbox | Operator steering from authenticated bridge clients (Bubble Notes UI in BL-793); body `{ "role": "<declared-role>", "message": "<text>" }`; message is one line, max 80 characters total after the `Bubble: ` attribution prefix; refuses undeclared roles, empty/over-budget/multiline messages, and unauthenticated callers; queues via `swarm_handoff.bb` only — never writes mailbox files directly |

`GET /metrics`, `GET /cost-telemetry`, `GET /cost-rank`, `GET /holistic`, `GET /stage-dwell`, and `GET /burn-rate` are all computed fresh on each request rather than folded into the ~1s SSE poll loop the other endpoints share — the underlying git-history walk and handoff-state/transcript reads are too expensive to recompute every tick.

**Holistic dev-state web UI:** Opening the bridge's root URL (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>/?token=<token>`) in any browser — desktop or phone, as long as it can reach the dev machine — serves a single self-contained page (inline CSS/JS, no external fetch or CDN, no localStorage/sessionStorage) showing the backlog board, per-swarm panel, pipeline flow, and recent activity, live-updated over the same `/events` SSE stream the rest of the bridge uses. It is read-only, exactly like every other bridge surface. A ticket's `swarm:` field (defaulting to `primary` when absent, per BL-090) determines whether it's shown as a live-tracked local ticket or labeled remote/last-synced. The page also has a **Metrics section** charting the delivery metrics above — a dependency-free inline SVG bar chart for velocity and for each milestone's burndown, plus text readouts for cycle time and forecasts — fetched once per page load/reconnect from `GET /metrics` (presentation only; no metric computation happens client-side) and re-rendered from the already-fetched data on each live update rather than re-fetching every tick.

**Per-agent burn-rate meter (BL-273):** a **Burn rate** section shows one row per pipeline role with its current tokens/hr — the live counterpart to BL-100's daily aggregates and BL-213's daily sidecar, neither of which is a live rate. `extension/src/metrics/burnRate.ts` sums each role's total tokens (input + output + cache creation + cache read, reusing `transcriptUsage.ts`'s `readTranscriptUsage` feed) whose transcript timestamp falls in a rolling recent window (default 15 minutes) ending at `nowMs`, then extrapolates to an hourly rate; an idle role with no usage in the window reads a real `0`, never omitted. `GET /burn-rate` (token-gated like every other holistic route) serves the per-role payload, and the page fetches it alongside `/holistic` and `/metrics` on load/reconnect (same on-demand posture, not re-fetched every SSE tick). This surface deliberately stays on the LIVE holistic UI, never the static backlog-dashboard PWA — a live rate is machine-local telemetry, not reproducible from git state at a SHA (see the PWA-vs-holistic-UI boundary rule in `local-engineering.prompt`) — and reaching it from a phone still rides the same not-yet-built tunnel/remote-access gap that parks BL-257 slices 3-4 and BL-265 slice 2; BL-273 builds the meter correctly on the live surface, not a workaround.

**Example usage (cURL):**

```bash
# Start the bridge and save the token
TOKEN=$(grep "token:" ~/.swarmforge/current_run.env | cut -d' ' -f2)

# Query pipeline state
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:9999/pipeline

# Subscribe to the event stream
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://127.0.0.1:9999/events
```

**Stateless design:**
- The bridge holds no state; it is a pure projection of `.swarmforge/` and `backlog/` directories
- If the bridge dies or you stop it, the swarm continues unaffected
- Restarting the bridge serves current state again; no data is lost

### Backlog Pane

Below the tiled agent panel, the extension shows a collapsible Backlog section listing all active work items with live traceability:

- Each backlog row shows: ticket ID, title, and the role currently **holding** that parcel (the stage with the active handoff for that ticket)
- The holder column updates live as the parcel moves down the pipeline — tiles and backlog rows always show the same holder (same resolution source)
- For active tickets with no live holder — whether promoted-but-unrouted or whose parcel was already completed and dropped by a stage — the row shows **"queued"** instead of the static assigned_to field. Tile badges also do not appear for holder-less tickets, keeping both surfaces consistent
- Done items show their milestone; todo items show the intended assignee
- This live traceability helps you spot bottlenecks and know at a glance which stage is responsible for each ticket

#### Interactive Backlog Operations

You can interact with active backlog items directly from the panel:

- **Assign an item**: Click the assignee field for any active item and select a team member to assign or reassign it. The assignment is written immediately back to the target repo's backlog YAML file.
- **Mark done**: Click the action button on any active item to move it from the active backlog to the done folder, reflecting completion. The item is moved to `backlog/done/` (or `backlog/done/<milestone>/` if the item specifies a milestone), and the backlog view updates immediately.

These writes are atomic — the extension uses a temporary file + rename mechanism to ensure no partial writes occur if the process is interrupted.

### Metrics Pane

Beside the Backlog pane, the extension shows a collapsible Metrics section that monitors swarm health and performance:

- **Mean ticket time**: How long on average a ticket takes to move from backlog/active/ to backlog/done/. Displayed with the sample count (e.g., "mean 4h 12m over 23 tickets"). Derived from the target repo's backlog git history — no new data collection needed. BL-1074: the end of the interval is the close hop (active→done), not a later re-file under `done/` that only relocates an already-closed ticket.
- **Per-agent busyness**: For each role, the fraction of elapsed run time spent processing handoffs. Computed from `dequeued_at` and `completed_at` headers in `.swarmforge/handoffs/inbox/completed/` handoff files, plus any open interval from an in-process task. Shows 0% for idle agents and agents with no history.
- **Retry count**: Total backward handoffs (messages where the sender sits later in the pipeline than the recipient — e.g., QA rejecting work back to coder). Displayed with per-ticket breakdown for tickets with retries, sorted by worst offenders.
- **Suite duration**: How long the test suite takes to run (averaged over recent runs). Displayed with the latest duration, rolling mean, and sample count. Warns when the latest duration exceeds either the configured threshold (default 120 seconds, configurable via `swarmforge.metrics.suiteWarnSeconds`) or 2x the rolling mean, flagging potential performance creep. Tracks durations from all test runs across the main checkout and every role worktree.
- **Chaser telemetry**: Per-role chase/nudge/dead-letter/respawn totals, plus a recent (7-day) chases+nudges daily rate — e.g. "coder 4 chases/2 nudges (0.86/day)". Answers "how many nudges did a role need this week?" durably, since the daemon's own sidecar counters are discarded once an item completes. Read from `handoffd.bb`'s `chaser-YYYY-MM.jsonl` telemetry log; a role or period with no chaser activity reads as zero, never an error.

The metrics pane folds and unfolds like the Backlog pane and refreshes on the panel's normal cadence — no additional polling loop is introduced.

#### Delivery Metrics (velocity, burndown, cycle time, forecasts)

A second metrics layer, derived purely from git history and the current `backlog/` folder state, computes delivery-flow trends:

- **Velocity**: closed-ticket count over a trailing window, with a trend vs. the prior window (e.g. "12 closed in trailing 7d (+3 vs prior)")
- **Burndown**: remaining-ticket count per milestone, reconstructed so the final point always matches the current backlog state, alongside each milestone's forecast ETA (reusing the same per-milestone forecast below — no parallel ETA model) and an overall "all remaining work" ETA (the latest/max p50 across every open ticket's own forecast). A milestone with no computable forecast shows "no ETA yet" rather than a fabricated date.
- **Cycle time**: median and p85 spec-to-close duration over the recent closed set
- **Forecasts**: p50/p85 completion date per open milestone, projected from trailing throughput and historical cycle-time distribution — dependency-aware, so a ticket's forecast date never precedes its `depends_on` tickets'
- **Suite duration trend**: the existing per-run suite duration (BL-078) expressed as a trend line; reports "no local data" gracefully rather than erroring

Available via the `GET /metrics` bridge endpoint (see Remote Access & Phone App below), the CLI (below), and charted directly in the holistic dev-state web UI's Metrics section (below) — all three are fed by the same computation, so they always report the same numbers.

**Regression flag (BL-252):** the holistic UI's suite-duration readout (`bridge/holisticUiHtml.ts`'s `renderSuiteDurationReadout`) and the daily briefing (`swarmforge/scripts/briefing_email_lib.bb`) both show the latest duration, its trend direction, and — when set — a regression flag, applying the same amber warn treatment used elsewhere in the UI. Both surfaces read the ONE existing BL-078 warn computation in `swarmMetrics.ts` (`latest > warnThresholdMs` OR `latest > 2x` the baseline mean) rather than a second, re-derived threshold, so they can never disagree; with no local duration records, both show a no-data state rather than an error or a fabricated value.

**Suite duration on the static PWA, via committed sidecar (BL-290).** Machine-local suite-duration records can't ride the git-SHA-reproducible `backlog.json` projection directly, so this reuses the same committed-sidecar pattern BL-213/BL-272 already established for cost & health: `emit-cost-health-sidecar.ts` (BL-272's headless CLI) also snapshots the suite-duration trend into the same committed `docs/briefings/<date>.json` carrier — no second commit path. `buildBacklogDashboard` folds that trend into `backlog.json`'s `metrics.suiteDurationTrend` from the latest committed sidecar, exactly like `costHealth`, so a given SHA's `backlog.json` carries whatever was committed at or before it (git-reproducible, never a live read). `pwa/app.js` renders it mirroring `renderSuiteDurationReadout`: latest duration + trend arrow, the same regression mark when warn is set, and a no-data readout with no live/host fetch when there's no local data — the static PWA still reads only `backlog.json`, never a bridge endpoint.

#### Cost & Resource Telemetry

A third telemetry layer tracks token spend and per-role resource usage:

- **Cost telemetry**: per-role token usage (input/output, plus cache-read and cache-creation tokens at their own rates) parsed from the Claude Code transcript files under `~/.claude/projects/`, priced against a versioned per-model USD/MTok table, and rolled up by day. Usage is also attributed per ticket (from the role's handoff holding windows), with an explicit "unattributed" bucket for usage that falls outside every known holding window — never silently dropped.
- **Resource usage**: per-role RSS and CPU trends, sampled periodically and bucketed hourly.

Both are available via the `GET /cost-telemetry` bridge endpoint and the CLI (below). Two scenarios from the ticket's own scope — a rolled-up cost briefing paragraph, and surfacing cost telemetry through the phone/Action bridge — are deferred pending infrastructure (BL-099/BL-097) that doesn't exist yet. **The resource-usage sampler is wired into the real swarm lifecycle (BL-264):** `extension/src/swarm/resourceSamplerActivation.ts`'s `resolvePanePid` composes the existing tmux discovery chain (`readTmuxSocket` → `getPaneBaseIndex` → `resolveAgentPaneTarget` → `getPanePid`, the same chain `PaneTailer` already uses — no second discovery mechanism) to resolve each role's pid fresh on every sampler tick (never cached, so a respawned pane's new pid is picked up automatically), and `buildSampledRoles` maps each discovered role into the `SampledRole` shape `startResourceSampler` expects. `extension.ts` starts the sampler (holding its interval handle in the same module-level-state convention as `currentChaserMonitor`) after every launch-success/reattach call site, and stops it in `stopSwarm`/`stopSwarmCompletely`/`deactivate()` alongside the existing chaser-monitor stop — no leaked interval past teardown. This is wiring only: the sampler module, its telemetry format, and every reader (cost sidecar, bridge, CLI) are unchanged — a live swarm's "Resource usage" line now shows real RSS/CPU samples instead of no-samples-yet.

**Resource sampling also runs headless, so `resourceAnomalies` stops being permanently empty (BL-350, BL-336 finding H1).** BL-264's wiring above only ever starts the sampler from `extension.ts`'s `vscode.*`-activation-gated call site, so a swarm running with no editor attached never recorded a single resource sample — the cost-health sidecar's `resourceAnomalies` field was present in the schema and emitted daily, but always empty, with nothing about the sidecar's own existence signalling the gap. `extension/src/tools/sample-resources.ts` is a headless CLI entrypoint that reuses the same tmux-discovery pid resolution and telemetry writer unchanged (`buildSampledRoles`, `sampleRolesOnce`), shelled from `handoffd.bb`'s existing sweep cadence (`resource-sample-sweep!`, the same posture as `recert-notify-sweep!`/`dead-letter-notify-sweep!` — no new scheduling mechanism invented). A new `shouldSampleThisInterval` check compares against the shared telemetry file's own latest sample, so the headless sweep and an attached editor's host-side sampler never double-count the same interval. This also closes the "quiet day looks identical to a broken sampler" gap: the sidecar now carries a `resourceSamplesObserved` flag, and the briefing's Cost & Health section renders an explicit "none found" anomalies line for a genuinely quiet sampled period, distinct from the silent omission a never-sampled sidecar still produces.

**Resource health also reports host load, not only per-role RSS/CPU (BL-822).** A host thrashing under overall load can degrade every role at once without any single role's own RSS/CPU trend crossing its per-role threshold — the per-role signal above is blind to that shape entirely. `sampleRolesOnce` now also samples `os.loadavg()[0] / os.cpus().length` on the same tick, independently of whether any role's pid resolved (the day a host is on fire but every role pid happens to be unresolvable is exactly the day this signal must not go silent), and records it as a distinct `host_load_sample` event in the same `chaser-*.jsonl` telemetry family `resource_sample` events already use. `computeHostLoadVerdict` marks a day **severe** only when the ratio clears a configurable threshold (`host_load_severe_ratio`, default 4x cores — deliberately above `mutation_cooldown_lib.bb`'s `mutation_busy_load_multiplier` default of 2, since "too busy to start mutation testing" is a lower bar than "this day was resource-abnormal" and the two dials must not drift into contradiction) **and** that ratio has held for a configurable sustained window (`host_load_sustained_minutes`, default 15 minutes) — a single spike or a long ordinary-load stretch alone does not qualify. The cost-health sidecar's `hostLoad` field carries this verdict, additive and optional (never folded into `resourceAnomalies` — a `ResourceAnomaly` always carries `{role, rssBytes}` and the static PWA renders those fields unconditionally, while a host-wide measurement has neither): a severe day's "none found" anomalies rendering is overridden regardless of whether a per-role anomaly is also present, while per-role RSS/CPU detection and `resourceSamplesObserved` (BL-350, above) stay untouched and independent of this signal.

**The per-role sampler was measuring the pane's shell, not the agent — every RSS/CPU figure and every anomaly it ever emitted was shell noise (BL-847).** `resolvePanePid`'s tmux `#{pane_pid}` names the pane's ROOT SHELL, the process tmux itself forked, never whatever that shell went on to exec — so `sampleProcessStats` was running `ps` against a ~100 KB idle shell while the real agent (`claude`, hundreds of MB) went unmeasured, and `cpuPercent` read 0 on every sample of every role. `resolveAgentPid` (`resourceSamplerActivation.ts`) now composes `resolvePanePid` with `selectAgentDescendant` — a BFS over the pane pid's process-tree descendants, nearest generation first, matching a per-role configured agent command name (`DEFAULT_AGENT_COMMAND_NAME = 'claude'`, overridden per role from `swarmRole.agent` so a non-claude role's sampler looks for its own agent, never a hardcoded name) — resolved via one `ps -A` shell-out per tick rather than one call per candidate pid. **BL-1112:** that table is built from `ps … args=` (basename of argv[0]), not `comm=` — Node 24+ on Linux reports thread names such as `MainThread` in `/proc/*/comm`, which made every headless sample report zero roles. When no matching descendant exists, the role records **no sample at all** rather than falling back to the shell pid (invariant 2): a wrong number wearing a right number's clothes is worse than an honest gap, and `resourceSamplesObserved` keeps meaning "we measured the agent." Samples recorded before this fix remain in the telemetry trend as shell measurements, alongside corrected samples going forward — a known, accepted discontinuity, not silently mixed. Orthogonal to BL-822 (which fixes the detector's blind spot to host load) and BL-350 (headless sampling, unaffected): this fixes which process the existing per-role sampler measures. `PaneTailer`'s own use of `getPanePid` for respawn detection is correct and unchanged — the pane's shell pid IS the right identity for "did this pane get respawned."

**The reliability count `daemonRestarts` was a hardcoded zero, not a measurement (BL-904).** Its four sibling reliability fields (`chases`, `nudges`, `respawns`, `failedDeliveries`) all read a real daily series; `daemonRestarts` alone was a literal `{value: 0, trend: computeTrend([])}`, placed among them so it read like one — a day with 248 real daemon restarts (BL-675's freshness watchdog, above) still reported a confident `0` with a trend object attached. `bucketDailyDaemonRestarts` (`costHealthSidecar.ts`) now derives it from `.swarmforge/daemon/freshness-incidents.log`, counting `action=restart` records only — `action=escalate` (a declined restart during cool-off) is a distinct event, not folded in. A missing or unreadable log propagates as `null` through to `trendedDaemonRestarts`, which reports `direction: "unknown"` with an empty series rather than a fabricated zero, so "no data" stays distinguishable from a genuine zero-restart day — the same posture `resourceSamplesObserved` (BL-350, above) already established for the resource sampler. Per-daemon breakdown (which daemon is storming) was reviewed and deliberately deferred: the `daemon` field is still captured per event and available to a future ticket, but a `Record<string, TrendedNumber>` shape would ripple into the briefing renderer and PWA, out of this ticket's scope.

#### Agent CLI

Every role can also run a headless command-line version of the same metrics:

```sh
node extension/out/tools/swarm-metrics.js
```

Runnable from the repo root or from any `.worktrees/<role>/` checkout. Prints a short plain-text summary — mean ticket time, one busyness line per role, retry total, suite duration with warnings, and a chaser telemetry line per role — followed by one line per delivery metric (velocity, burndown, cycle time, forecasts, suite duration trend), then a cost telemetry line and a resource usage line, each one role-summary per role — and exits 0 with placeholder values on a fresh run. The CLI and panel/bridge are fed by the same underlying metrics computation modules, so they always report the same values.

When roles are configured on more than one agent/provider brand (`swarmforge.conf`'s `window` lines), the summary also prints a **"By provider"** line — the same chase/nudge telemetry as the per-role line, grouped by provider brand instead, so you can compare which brand is slower, failing, or idling more without reading per-role detail. Omitted entirely (not printed empty) when every role shares one provider or no provider roster can be derived.

#### Queue status CLI

A second headless, read-only CLI answers "is there actually pending work?" without mixing in the chaser's own operational sidecar files (`.chase.json`, `.nudge`), which used to dominate a raw directory listing and give a false impression of a busy queue:

```sh
node extension/out/tools/queue-status.js [--debug]
```

Runnable from the repo root or any `.worktrees/<role>/` checkout, same project-root resolution as `swarm-metrics.js`. By default, prints one line per role reporting its `inbox/new` and `inbox/in_process` counts SEPARATELY, not flattened into one combined figure (BL-323): a genuinely idle role reads `no work pending`, a role with fresh mail reads `N new pending` (plus an `in_process` suffix if any), and — the case a combined count used to hide — a role whose `new/` is empty but `in_process/` holds an orphaned claim reads `work claimed by nobody`, distinct from true idle. Sidecar files are not even listed by default, not just hidden. Pass `--debug` to additionally list each role's sidecar files, labeled by kind (`chase-sidecar`, `nudge-sidecar`, `other`).

#### Stage-dwell & bottleneck report CLI

A third headless CLI is the coordinator's swarm-optimizer instrument: per-stage queue-wait and processing dwell (median/p90/max, with IQR-based outlier honesty so one wedged parcel can't masquerade as a capacity problem), the bottleneck stage and its multiple over the next slowest stage, and a trend vs. the prior window:

```sh
node extension/out/tools/stage-dwell-report.js [--hours N] [--json]
```

Runnable from the repo root or any `.worktrees/<role>/` checkout, same project-root resolution as `swarm-metrics.js`. Defaults to a 24-hour window; pass `--hours` to change it and `--json` for machine-readable output. Reads every pipeline role's completed handoffs (never the coordinator, which sits outside the forward chain), including batch directories a batch role's `done_with_current_batch.sh` moves completed batches into. Fed by the same computation as the bridge's `GET /stage-dwell` endpoint, so the CLI and bridge always report the same numbers.

#### Routing break-even report CLI (BL-343)

A fourth headless CLI answers the question the dynamic-routing epic (auto-hibernate, routing manifest, quiet-period gate, per-role park/unpark) exists to answer: does parking idle roles actually save money?

```sh
node extension/out/tools/park-cycle-report.js
```

Runnable from the repo root or any `.worktrees/<role>/` checkout, same project-root resolution as `swarm-metrics.js`. Read-only and headless. It pairs every REAL park/unpark event logged by `role_lifecycle_cli.bb` (`.swarmforge/role-lifecycle/park-cycle-log.jsonl` — one line per real park or unpark, an aborted park that never actually removed a role from service is never logged) into complete cycles, then measures each cycle's real cold-start cost and idle-burn saving from the role's own transcript token usage — never an estimate derived from prompt size. For each role with at least one complete cycle it reports the break-even idle duration (the point below which parking that role is a net loss); `routingSavesMoney` is `null`, not `false`, whenever zero real cycles exist yet, so an unmeasured state is never misreported as a measured negative. Until a role has actually been parked and unparked in production, the report is honestly empty — that is expected, not a bug, and is not tuned away.

#### Standing rule violation report CLI (BL-337)

A Babashka CLI answers a direct question about the constitution itself: how often has a standing engineering rule actually been breached since it was written?

```sh
bb swarmforge/scripts/standing_rule_violations_cli.bb <project-root> report
bb swarmforge/scripts/standing_rule_violations_cli.bb <project-root> for-ticket <BL-NNN>
```

`report` scans every top-level rule (a `- ` bullet or `N. ` numbered item, with its wrapped continuation lines) in every `swarmforge/constitution/articles/*.prompt` and `swarmforge/roles/*.prompt` file, and prints each rule's cited `BL-NNN` ticket ids alongside a total citation count across all rules. `for-ticket <BL-NNN>` answers "how many times was this specific ticket cited as a violation" directly. Both derive purely from the committed text of the constitution/role files — no new bookkeeping, no git history walk — so a rule added tomorrow, anywhere in those files, is counted with no code change. A rule's numerically-smallest citation is treated as that rule's own origin (the incident that prompted writing it), never counted as a violation of it; every other citation is a real recorded violation since the rule landed. A `(source: ..., BL-NNN)` citation credits authorship, not a violation, and is excluded. A rule with zero violations is still reported, with a count of zero, never omitted — an all-zero result is a claim to verify, not the assumed answer.

The daily briefing email's `:standing-rule-violations-line` section (`swarmforge/scripts/handoffd.bb`, composed the same way as every other optional briefing line) surfaces the `report` total on every send, e.g. `Standing-rule violations: 38 cited recurrence(s) across 458 rule(s) since they landed (top: "..." x3, "..." x3, "..." x3)`.

#### QA-bounce metric: which role bounces most from QA (BL-454, superseded by BL-635 below)

Attribution for "which agent bounces most from QA?" previously existed only as prose and filenames across the `backlog/evidence/*-bounce-*.md` corpus. This added a structured, durable record and a host-side surface for it.

A go-forward writer appended one JSON-line record (`{ ticket, producing_role, ticket_type, failure_class, commit, at }`) to a gitignored, machine-local log (`.swarmforge/qa_bounces/<YYYY-MM>.jsonl`):

```sh
node extension/out/tools/record-qa-bounce.js --ticket <id> --role <producingRole> \
  --type <ticketType> --class <failureClass> --commit <hex>
```

Every field is validated against a closed set (`producing_role` in `{coder, cleaner, architect, hardender, documenter}`, `ticket_type` in `{feature, bug, defect, chore, docs, enhancement, epic}`, `failure_class` in `{compile, unit, integration, acceptance, behavior, invariant-unencoded, spec-gap}` — widened by BL-688, see below) before anything is written; an unrecognized value is a usage error, never recorded raw.

A one-time backfill seeds the same log from history:

```sh
node extension/out/tools/backfill-qa-bounces.js
```

It scans the git-tracked `backlog/evidence/*-bounce-*.md` corpus, attributing producing role + failure class from each file's own prose/filename and ticket type by joining the backlog YAML — never guessing from the evidence file alone — and skips any file it cannot attribute cleanly (a non-bounce evidence file, e.g. an "already-shipped" record, is never counted). It is idempotent on the record's natural key (ticket + date + class), so re-running it seeds nothing twice.

`record-qa-bounce.js` itself is no longer invoked from any role prompt (QA migrated to the generalised `record-bounce.js` below) but is left untouched and still exercised by its own BL-608 acceptance suite; the log it wrote, and the backfill's seed, remain readable forever as the only pre-2026-07-10 bounce history that exists — see BL-635's read-merge below.

#### Generalised bounce recording by bouncing role + the rework metric (BL-635)

BL-454/BL-608's log measured only QA's half of rework: its writer was invoked from `QA.prompt` alone, so architect send-backs — where repeated bouncing actually concentrates (BL-590: 4 send-backs, BL-606: 3, none recorded anywhere) — were invisible. Reading the QA-only log in isolation concluded "repeated bouncing doesn't happen here" (1 ticket of ~52 in 15 days), the opposite of the truth for architect send-backs.

`record-bounce.js` generalises the recorder so any reviewing stage records its own send-backs, with the bouncing role now REQUIRED (not optional) and written to both durable stores:

```sh
node extension/out/tools/record-bounce.js --ticket <id> --role <producingRole> \
  --type <ticketType> --class <failureClass> --commit <hex> \
  --by <bouncingRole> [--evidence <path>]
```

- `--role` (unchanged meaning): the role whose stage introduced the defect (`producingRole`, the "blamed" role).
- `--by` (new, required): the role performing the bounce — one of `specifier|coder|cleaner|architect|hardender|documenter|QA`. Absent or unrecognized fails the invocation with a usage error and writes nothing to either store — a typo'd bouncer would otherwise silently fragment the split.
- `--evidence` stays optional (BL-608's best-effort ticket-YAML `bounce_history` merge); every prompt invocation passes it in practice.

Every pipeline role that can send work back now calls this CLI under its own `--by` value on a send-back: `swarmforge/roles/architect.prompt`, `QA.prompt`, `cleaner.prompt`, `hardender.prompt`, `documenter.prompt`, and `specifier.prompt` (on a spec-defect bounce). `record-qa-bounce.js` is no longer invoked from any role prompt.

Records write only to the new generalised, go-forward path `.swarmforge/bounces/<YYYY-MM>.jsonl` (`bounceStore.ts`); the legacy `.swarmforge/qa_bounces/` path is never written again, only read. `readBounceRecords` merges both directories on read, so the 53 legacy records (and the backfill's evidence-corpus seed) stay live — a legacy record with no `by` field reads back as **unattributed**, never silently folded into QA or any other role.

The rework signal lands on the briefing's flow-balance line (`extension/src/notify/costHealthSidecar.ts`), split by bouncing role and never pooled — pooling QA and architect bounces into one number is exactly what made the pre-BL-635 log say "rare" when it wasn't:

- `flowBalance.rework.roundsPerClose` — mean bounce rounds per ticket closed in the trailing window, one trended number per bouncing role (`{ specced N/day, closed N/day, rework <role> N.N rounds/close, ... }` on the rendered line, with a trend arrow).
- `flowBalance.rework.bouncesPerDay` — the daily count, split by role, supporting the headline mean.
- `flowBalance.rework.maxRounds` — a `{ ticket, rounds, by }` indicator naming the single worst-bounced ticket, so a 4-send-back ticket like BL-590 stays distinguishable from four separately-once-bounced tickets (an average alone would hide that shape).

A declared recording epoch (`REWORK_ATTRIBUTION_EPOCH_ISO = '2026-07-25'` in `reworkRounds.ts`) marks where by-attributed history actually starts: every day before it renders **unavailable**, never a fabricated zero — a flat "architect: 0" line before this shipped would read as "no send-backs happened" when the truth is "nothing was ever recorded." Legacy unattributed records are exempt from the epoch (they carry real dates, just no `by`) and remain counted under `unattributed`. The metric sources exclusively from this durable log or a ticket's own `bounce_history` — never commit subjects or briefing prose, which the ticket's own investigation showed to be doubly contaminated (title matches like `BL-115-bounce-watcher-resilience`, and one bounce's fix propagating through 5-6 merge commits each repeating "bounce fix" in its subject).

`computeQaBounceTally`, the daily briefing's `:qa-bounce-line` optional section (`briefing_email_lib.bb`, key unchanged, copy updated), and the holistic-UI surface all still apply the same posture as BL-454: this is machine-local, host-side data only, never ridden on the static backlog PWA / `backlog.json` projection. The bounce-line copy now reports who bounced as well as whose work bounced, with legacy by-less records shown as unattributed rather than framed as QA's.

#### Recordable failure-class vocabulary widened to `invariant-unencoded`/`spec-gap` (BL-688)

BL-654 (above) named `invariant-unencoded` as the architect's bounce class for a missing/vacuous invariant property test, and Article 4.4 separately names `spec-gap` for a specification-level finding — but `KNOWN_FAILURE_CLASSES` (`qaBounce.ts`) still only recognized the original five (`compile, unit, integration, acceptance, behavior`), so every bounce recorded under either new class hit the closed-set usage error and was silently dropped: not misclassified, simply never written to `.swarmforge/bounces/<YYYY-MM>.jsonl` or the ticket's `bounce_history`. Measured 2026-07-27: all 5 recorded architect bounces that month read `"failureClass":"behavior"`, none `invariant-unencoded`, and whether that reflects a true `behavior` bounce or a dropped `invariant-unencoded` one is unrecoverable from the log — which is itself the defect, since bounce rate underpins the Article 3.5 circuit breaker.

`KNOWN_FAILURE_CLASSES` now lists seven values: `compile, unit, integration, acceptance, behavior, invariant-unencoded, spec-gap`. The widening is additive only — every pre-existing record, tally, and USAGE ordering for the five original classes is unchanged — and the vocabulary stays closed and case-sensitive: `Behavior`, `flaky`, or any other value outside the seven is still a usage error that writes nothing. Both `record-bounce.js` and the legacy `record-qa-bounce.js` share the same validator (`isKnownFailureClass`) and so both accept the two new classes; `qa-sibling-check.js --class` (sibling-deferral recording, above) accepts them too — a deferral can now cite either new class as its blocker's failure class, with no change to suppression semantics.

#### One bounce record can carry its whole defect inventory + a defects-per-bounce metric (BL-689)

Article 4.4 requires one bounce per review pass carrying EVERY defect that
pass found, but `record-bounce.js` recorded exactly one
`(producingRole, failureClass)` pair per call — a four-defect sweep and a
first-failure stop looked identical in the durable log, so the regression
the amendment exists to prevent was unmeasurable.

`record-bounce.js` gains two optional flags. One call still stays one
bounce event:

```sh
node extension/out/tools/record-bounce.js --ticket <id> --role <producingRole> \
  --type <ticketType> --class <failureClass> --commit <hex> --by <bouncingRole> \
  [--items '<json>'] [--blocked <n>]
```

- `--items <json>` — a non-empty JSON array of `{id, class, blamed, pointer}`
  objects: the item label (`D1`), its failure class (the BL-688-widened
  seven-value set), the role blamed for it
  (`coder|cleaner|architect|hardender|documenter`), and a remediation
  pointer (file/function/scenario id).
- `--blocked <n>` (default 0) — how many checks the pass could not run
  because an earlier item blocked them, so a legitimately short inventory
  (a compile failure blocking eight gates) stays distinguishable from a
  first-failure stop.
- The existing `--role`/`--class` still describe the item being ROUTED on
  (the earliest blamed role's most severe item) — Article 4.3 routing and
  every pre-existing tally are unaffected.

Degrade posture is deliberate (engineering.prompt Guardrails: an optional
JSON flag must catch its own parse errors): unparseable JSON, a non-array, an
empty array, or an invalid item each fall back to writing the core
single-item record exactly as if `--items` were absent, print their own
degrade reason (`unparseable` | `empty` | `invalid-item`), and exit **zero**
— a reviewer who mistypes the inventory JSON never loses the bounce record
itself. A call with no inventory at all writes the byte-identical record it
wrote before this ticket; `BounceRecord`'s new `items`/`blocked` fields are
optional and every existing reader/tally that doesn't know about them is
unaffected.

`qa-bounce-line.js` — the briefing's only live reader of the bounce log —
gains a `defectsPerBounce` figure: total inventory items across recorded
bounces divided by bounce count, where a record with no inventory counts as
**one** defect (so the pre-existing records and every future minimal call
stay comparable in the mean rather than being excluded from it).

Depends on and reuses BL-688's widened failure-class vocabulary for
per-item classes; `bounceStore.ts`'s shape/value guards already pass unknown
fields through untouched, so no store change was needed to round-trip the
new fields.

#### A ticket's own `bounce_history` dedup key widened to match the store's (BL-876)

The durable store's own idempotency key, `bounceNaturalKey` (`qaBounce.ts`), is `ticket + date + class + commit + by` — fine enough that two same-day same-class bounces from different roles, or the same role after a rework citing a new commit, are recorded as distinct events (BL-590: four architect send-backs in one day). A ticket's own `bounce_history:` block, merged in by `updateTicketBounceHistory` (`bounceHistory.ts`), used a coarser key — `date + class` only — so a second same-day same-class bounce landed correctly in the JSONL store but silently no-op'd as `duplicate` against the ticket's own file, and `bounce_count` under-reported. Since the BL-819 lifecycle ledger (above) reads the ticket's `bounce_history`, not the JSONL, the loss was unrecoverable downstream: BL-819 itself closed with `bounce_count: 1`, missing the QA bounce (`8ac82a0e`, 2026-08-07) its own JSONL record proves happened, because the architect's same-day `behavior` bounce claimed the coarse key first.

`entryNaturalKey` now matches the store's key minus the implicit ticket: `date + class + commit + by`. A true CLI re-run (identical `commit` and `by`) still collapses to one entry — the fix widens what counts as distinct, it does not disable dedup. Both `record-bounce.js` and the legacy `record-qa-bounce.js` reach this through the same merge path, so the fix covers both CLIs with no flag change to either. BL-819's own closed-ticket record was hand-repaired in the same parcel (`bounce_count: 1` → `2`, QA's entry added, sourced only from the JSONL and its already-committed evidence file) — a corrected key does not retroactively repair a record already written.

#### Rework observatory CLI (BL-430, epic BL-429 slice 1 — OBSERVE)

A read-only CLI computes the swarm's first self-observed health signal: how much of the pipeline's work is rework. It composes ingredients the pipeline already records — backward-handoff bounces, each ticket's own `mutation_cost`, QA bounce evidence committed to `main` — into one rolling rework rate, without moving any knob or changing promotion behaviour.

```sh
node extension/out/tools/rework-observatory.js
```

Runnable from the repo root or any `.worktrees/<role>/` checkout, same project-root resolution as `swarm-metrics.js`. It reports the QA-bounce/rework rate over a trailing 14-day window against a trailing 14-day baseline, attributed to the role and ticket-class where rework concentrates most, and persists the signal (versioned, additive schema) for the diagnosis slice (BL-431) to read. An empty window reports `NO_SAMPLE` rather than a divide-by-zero or a fabricated rate; a baseline period with no completed tickets independently reports a null baseline without blocking the main window's own rate. Bounce evidence is read from the `main` ref (BL-340), never a role's own worktree checkout, since evidence files committed by QA are absent from any parcel's ancestry.

This is the concrete signal source for Article 3.5's health-based intake throttling circuit breaker: "QA-bounce rate ... rising meaningfully above their trend baseline" is exactly what this CLI's `reworkRate` vs `baselineRate` comparison measures.

#### Suboptimality diagnosis + escalation (BL-431, epic BL-429 slice 2 — DIAGNOSE + ESCALATE)

BL-430 only persists a raw rework signal; on its own that is data, not a diagnosis. `reworkDiagnosis.ts` reads that signal and, only when the current rework rate is more than 2x the trailing baseline (the same relative-creep idiom `computeSuiteDuration`/BL-078 already uses for "meaningfully above" — a fixed absolute threshold is wrong because baselines drift), emits a ranked suboptimality verdict: the rework rate and baseline, the likely cause (the role and/or ticket-class where rework concentrates, from BL-430's own attribution — falling back to "no single role or ticket-class dominates" when neither is identifiable), and a recommended action. A rate at or below 2x baseline, or no sample/baseline yet, produces no verdict at all — no false alarms on a healthy or not-yet-measurable pipeline.

The recommended action is classified against an allowlist (`classifyRemediationDisposition`): only `"lower the intake throttle"` — the coordinator's Article 3.5 intake-throttle knob, the one the ACT slice (BL-432) is authorized to move automatically — is `auto-tunable`. Every other recommendation, including any future remediation type nobody has classified yet, defaults to `escalate-only`: named in the verdict for a human to act on, never auto-applied. This split is the epic's safety contract (BL-429).

The verdict reaches the human through the existing daily briefing, not a new channel. A headless CLI shells out to read BL-430's persisted signal and print one line when (and only when) a verdict exists:

```sh
node extension/out/tools/suboptimality-verdict-line.js
```

`briefing_email_lib.bb`'s `:suboptimality-verdict-line` optional section (`swarmforge/scripts/handoffd.bb`) wires this CLI into the daily briefing the same way every other optional section works — a blank block (no verdict) leaves the briefing untouched rather than appending a fabricated "all clear" line.

#### Auto-tuned intake throttle (BL-432, epic BL-429 slice 3 — ACT, the mandatory wiring slice)

BL-430 (observe) and BL-431 (diagnose) can both land fully green while the coordinator still promotes at full depth into a pipeline BL-431 has just diagnosed as thrashing — observe + diagnose with no act is a report, not a loop. This slice closes it, automating the ONE knob Article 3.5's circuit breaker already sanctioned by rule but that nothing previously moved in code: the coordinator's `active_backlog_max_depth`.

`reworkDiagnosis.ts` classifies an `auto-tunable` verdict into a two-level `ThrottleSeverity`: `degraded` once the rework rate crosses 2x baseline (BL-431's own trigger), escalating to `severe` if it keeps climbing to 4x baseline. `emit-throttle-recommendation.ts` (`node extension/out/tools/emit-throttle-recommendation.js <target-repo-path>`) maps that severity to a recommended cap — `1` for degraded, `0` for severe, `null` (no recommendation) once the diagnosis clears or the verdict is escalate-only — and persists it to `.swarmforge/coordinator/throttle-recommendation.json`, appending a line to `.swarmforge/coordinator/throttle-changes.jsonl` only when the recommended cap actually changes (a steady-state refresh writes no log spam).

The coordinator's promotion path no longer reads `active_backlog_max_depth` from `swarmforge.conf` directly. It now resolves the **effective** cap via:

```sh
bb swarmforge/scripts/effective_backlog_depth_cli.bb <project-root>
```

where `<project-root>` may be the master checkout or any linked worktree of it (BL-966, below). It refreshes the throttle recommendation fresh on every call (never trusts a periodic sweep that might be stale between coordinator wake-ups), then prints `min(configured cap, recommended cap)` — `backlog_depth_lib.bb`'s `effective-max-depth`. The recommendation only ever *lowers* the effective cap, never raises it above the human-configured value; a configured cap of `-1` (no ceiling) is not run through a bare `min` (a negative sentinel would otherwise always "win") — it resolves straight to the recommendation instead, so an unlimited cap can still be temporarily throttled during a severe diagnosis. When the diagnosis clears, the recommendation lifts and the effective cap returns to the configured value on the very next call — the swarm is never permanently stuck throttled. A failed refresh (CLI not yet compiled, `node` missing) degrades to a logged skip and falls through to whatever recommendation is already on disk, the same shell-and-degrade posture `handoffd.bb`'s other `emit-*.js` callers already use.

This slice moves only this one knob — it does not self-generate tickets, respawn a role, reroute work, or touch code; those stay BL-431's escalate-only recommendations for a human, exactly the epic's safety contract (BL-429).

#### Promotion gates: one chokepoint for every promote/route decision (BL-663)

Three different promotion gates were bypassed in 48 hours, each caught only because a human happened to be watching, none by machinery: `human_approval` and `severity` were never read by the promotion path at all; an Article 3.2.4 expedite-lane violation (a feature promoted over an approved defect/high sitting in `paused/`); and a promotion silently flipping a ticket's `assigned_to: specifier` to `coder`, skipping the spec stage the ticket's own acceptance required. The pattern recurred a fourth time on 2026-08-01, five days after the ticket was filed, confirming it as live and unattended-recurring rather than historical — and the swarm now runs unattended overnight shifts, so a skipped gate is a night lost to the wrong work, not a caught mistake.

`promotion_gates_lib.bb` (pure decisions) and `promotion_gates_cli.bb` (its one shell-callable entry point) are now the single chokepoint every promotion path calls, never a locally-reimplemented check:

- **`human_approval`** — any present value other than the literal `approved` (pending, amending, rejected, or unrecognized) refuses promotion; an absent field passes (not applicable). Absence never buys expedite priority either (below).
- **Article 3.2.4 expedite lane** — a `defect` ticket with `severity: critical` or `high` sorts ahead of every non-expedited candidate regardless of priority number; missing `severity:` fails closed (never expedited, never guessed). Legacy `type: bug` is retired (BL-1095): the predicate no longer matches it, and mint-time hygiene refuses it (`RETIRED-TICKET-TYPE`) so a later `bug` ticket cannot silently lose the lane.
- **Assignee / spec-stage routing** — `assigned_to: specifier` is never rewritten and always routes to the specifier; every other value routes to coder, and is corrected to `coder` only when it does not already read `coder` (so an already-correct ticket triggers no write).
- **`active_backlog_max_depth`**, **orthogonality** (two active tickets sharing an `epic:` are treated as the same in-flight scope), and the **hold marker** (a ticket parked in `backlog/hold/` is never a promotion candidate, including by direct `BL-id` name) — pre-existing behavior, now folded through the same chokepoint so a future auto-picker cannot grow a second, divergent copy.

Both `promote_and_route_next.sh` — its auto-pick path (`select`) and its by-name path (`evaluate`), previously the weaker of the two since it skipped even the buildability check — and `route_backlog_to_coder.sh`'s independent `assigned_to` rewrite site (routing invoked on its own, outside a promotion, carried its own copy of the same bug) now call `promotion_gates_cli.bb` for every decision. A refusal names the failing gate and reason (e.g. `REFUSE|human_approval|human_approval is pending, not approved`) rather than reading as an unattributed "no candidate," which is what kept all four incidents invisible to machinery. The literal string `promotion_gates` is required to appear at both call sites — a gate library that is built but never wired in refuses the ticket's own acceptance check by design.

A fully compliant ticket (approved, correctly laned, already correctly assigned) promotes and routes exactly as before this change — the gate layer only ever refuses or leaves a decision unchanged, it never alters a compliant promotion's outcome.

**The promotion path never asked whether the depth cap is unlimited: a configured `-1` silently resolved to `5` (BL-853).** With the pack conf declaring `active_backlog_max_depth -1` and five tickets already active, every promotion through the sanctioned path refused with "active count 5 >= cap 5 — no open slot" — a coincidental collision (the resolved fallback happened to equal the active count), not an intentional cap, and the one time a human caught it the workaround was to un-promote in-flight work by hand to free a slot for an expedited defect. Four faults in one resolution chain, all fixed together: (1) `promote_and_route_next.sh`'s cap validation was unsigned-only (`^[0-9]+$`), so the documented `-1` sentinel was rejected as malformed before it could even reach the fallback; (2) the fallback called `backlog_depth_cli.bb` with the project **root**, but that CLI documents (and `swarmforge.sh` already correctly passes) a **config file path** — `slurp` on a directory threw, and the library silently degraded to its own `default-max-depth`; (3) if both readers failed, the shell declared its own second, tighter default (`CAP=5`) rather than deferring to the library's; (4) even a correctly-resolved `-1` still refused at any active count, because `promotion_gates_lib.bb`'s `depth-refusal` was a bare `(>= active-count max-depth)` with no no-limit branch. The fix: `promote_and_route_next.sh` now accepts a signed integer at every step and declares no depth default of its own (a new `backlog_depth_conf_path_cli.bb` resolves the correct conf path for the fallback, replacing the root-as-conf-path bug), and `depth-refusal` consults the shared `backlog-depth-lib/no-limit?` predicate before comparing — the same sentinel `swarm_handoff.bb`'s `depth-exceeded?` warning and `ready_for_next.bb`'s auto-promote gate already honoured correctly. A finite cap (including the `1`/`0` values Article 3.5's circuit breaker throttles to) refuses exactly as before — only the no-limit sentinel's own path changed. Landing this alone moves the blocker rather than removing it: with the depth gate no longer refusing, the separate *orthogonality* gate (two active tickets sharing an `epic:`) becomes the sole blocker on a large share of paused tickets — a distinct fix, [BL-854](../../backlog/done/M8/BL-854-orthogonality-advises-instead-of-blocking-on-the-epic-tag.yaml), below.

**The orthogonality gate advises on epic overlap instead of refusing on it (BL-854).** `epic:` is the gate's only scope proxy — no ticket field declares real file/module scope — and the buckets it groups by are large: measured against `backlog/paused/` (204 tickets), 76 share `epic: swarm-reliability` alone, so a single active defect in that epic refused 112 of the 204 (55%) on this gate. The coordinator was already overriding it by hand every time, comparing the tickets' actual declared file paths and finding zero real overlap (`3fbe05e9`) — the automated layer could raise the question but had no data to answer it. `promotion_gates_lib.bb`'s `orthogonality-refusal` is now `orthogonality-advisory`: it returns alongside `{:ok true}` rather than in place of it, so `evaluate`'s stdout contract (`ALLOW` / `REFUSE|<gate>|<reason>`, same exit codes) is byte-identical for every existing caller. When a paused candidate shares an epic with one or more active tickets, `promotion_gates_cli.bb` additionally writes `ADVISORY|orthogonality|epic <epic> is also active on <BL-id>[, <BL-id>...]` to **stderr**, naming every overlapping active ticket (not just the epic) so the coordinator can check real file overlap without re-deriving which ticket to compare against. `select` mode's Article 3.2.4 ranking is unchanged by construction — an advisory drops nothing from the candidate set. `promote_and_route_next.sh` prints the winning candidate's advisory once, for the ticket it actually promotes; a non-blocking verdict nobody sees would read as a clean promotion and bury the signal it exists to raise. The file-overlap judgement itself stays exactly where the constitution's Concurrent Work Orthogonality rule already puts it — with the coordinator; this fix only stops the automated proxy from refusing on an answer it never had. `human_approval`, the depth cap, the hold marker, and Article 3.2.4 ranking are all unchanged (BL-854's own invariants). Out of scope: a declared file-scope ticket field to replace the epic proxy entirely — rejected for now because no ticket carries one today and a wrong backfilled scope would reproduce this same false positive less visibly; the advisory is where that field would hang if it is built later.

**The chain never read `depends_on`, so a dependent ticket could reach the coder before the work it depends on had landed (BL-957).** `depends_on:` was honoured only on the TypeScript side (`makeTopPrioritySafety.ts`, `bridgeServer.ts`), whose own comment deferred the completion question to "the coordinator's promotion gate" — a gate that had never been built; the field was read nowhere in `swarmforge/scripts/` at all. The coordinator spent four commits on 2026-08-19 fighting its absence, the auto-picker re-promoting the same blocked BL-955 immediately after each hand revert because nothing in the promotion path had changed. It was never a one-off: measured against the live backlog that day, **20 otherwise-promotable candidates carried at least one dependency not in `backlog/done/`** — half of the 48 candidates declaring any dependency at all — including BL-603 and BL-604 with nine unlanded dependencies each. `promotion_gates_lib.bb` gains a `depends_on` link in `evaluate`'s fixed chain, placed **after `human_approval` and before `depth`** so a ticket-property refusal beats a transient global one and the coordinator gets the actionable reason; both invocation modes inherit it from the one BL-663 chokepoint (`cmd-select` drops a refused candidate from the ranking rather than crashing the selection, `cmd-evaluate` prints `REFUSE|depends_on|<reason>` and exits 2), which is why the "every route, including one added later" invariant is cheap to hold here and expensive anywhere else. The gate **fails closed in both directions**: a dependency counts as satisfied ONLY in `backlog/done/`, so an ACTIVE dependency still refuses (the standard the coordinator had already applied by hand during the incident), and an id resolving to no ticket anywhere refuses rather than promotes — the same posture Article 3.2.4 takes on a missing `severity:`. The refusal names every unsatisfied id and no satisfied one (`depends_on not yet landed in backlog/done/: BL-620`), so the next action needs no re-derivation by hand. The gate carries its **own reader** rather than reusing `read-field`, which returns nil for a blank value by documented design (`field: >`/`field: |` must read as absent) and would therefore have failed OPEN on block-style lists — exactly the tickets the gate exists to catch, two of which sit in `paused/` today. `read-depends-on` extracts every `BL-<n>`/`GH-<n>` token from the field's value and its indented continuation lines, stripping inline comments, which reads all four live forms (`[]` 118 tickets, flow list 47, block list 2, bare scalar with trailing prose 1) without parsing the prose; a present-but-unparseable value is flagged and refused, never silently read as dependency-free. Resolving a dependency uses `done-ids`, which recurses `backlog/done/` over flat files AND `<Mx>/` subfolders (the close-into-`done/<Mx>` convention), taking the filename's leading ticket token and falling back to the `id:` field. No existing gate is weakened or reordered, and a ticket with `depends_on: []` promotes exactly as before. Out of scope: auto-promoting the dependency instead of refusing (the coordinator decides what to promote; this gate only refuses), and transitive cycle detection across `depends_on` — `makeTopPrioritySafety.ts` already handles cycles for the make-top primitive, and nothing in the promotion path traverses. The sibling open-slot nudge that consults this chain when a slot frees is BL-963, a separate slice; BL-626 (unmaterialized `.feature` pointer) and BL-634 (slice-size envelope) stay independent too.

**The same repository answered two different caps depending on which checkout asked (BL-966).** `effective_backlog_depth_cli.bb` documents a `<project-root>` argument, and every role following that usage from its own worktree got a confidently wrong governance constant: measured 2026-08-20, the master checkout returned **7** (swarm-identity present, `launch_pack full-forge` → `packs/full-forge.conf`) while `.worktrees/coder` returned **3** — the tracked default — with no warning, nothing on stderr, and exit 0 in both cases. The cause is that `.swarmforge/` is master-checkout runtime state which no linked worktree carries, so `conf-file-path` read swarm-identity at the caller's own root, found none, and fell through silently. This is the BL-897 mirrored-constant shape moved across checkouts, and it was the third depth-cap confusion in two days (BL-961's hold cited `2` read from the wrong pack's conf; the all-roles broadcast said `7`; the architect measured `3`). `backlog_depth_lib.bb` now resolves identity at the repository's MASTER checkout regardless of who asks: `resolve-identity-root` runs `git rev-parse --git-common-dir` against the given root and takes its parent — the one place `.swarmforge/` lives — memoized per root (the mapping is stable for a process lifetime and this lib is loaded by `handoffd.bb` inside its poll cycle), with the subprocess wait routed through BL-967's shared bounded `sh!` chokepoint rather than an unbounded one. `conf-file-path` reads identity there and resolves the persisted conf path relative to that same root. Degradation is deliberate and total: a non-git root — the standard test-harness shape, a plain temp dir — resolves to itself unchanged, and so does any git failure, so the fix never requires fixtures to be git repositories (the ticket's third invariant). What remains is the genuine no-identity case, a repository that was never launched: it still gets the tracked default conf's value on stdout with exit 0, but the fall-through is now announced on stderr (`backlog_depth_lib: no swarm-identity for <root> - falling back to the tracked default conf <path>`) — a cap that does not derive from a resolvable swarm-identity is never returned silently again, while every existing scripted caller keeps parsing stdout exactly as before. The CLI's own usage text now states what the argument accepts: the master checkout or any linked worktree of it. The one harness case that asserted empty stderr on the fall-through path (`test_effective_backlog_depth_cli.sh`'s live-wiring case) was adjusted in the same parcel, which is the only caller-visible behavior change. `backlog_depth_conf_path_cli.bb` shares the lib and therefore moves with it, keeping the two CLIs in agreement by construction. Out of scope and unchanged *at BL-966 land*: `promote_and_route_next.sh`'s own `2>/dev/null || true` stderr swallow (noted as shared fragility — it runs from master, so promotion was always correct, and its caller contract is untouched), the throttle-recommendation and pause-marker layers of the effective cap (**completed by BL-1106**: both now use the same `resolve-identity-root`), and how OTHER `swarm_identity_lib` consumers (ancillary provider routing, babysitter topology) resolve identity — the same fallback family, separate slices.
