## Inter-Agent Communication

Agents communicate through persisted YAML messages with explicit status tracking. This solves a real failure mode: agents fall asleep, and the sender needs to know whether a handoff was picked up — and chase it if not.

### Message store

One YAML file per message, kept with the swarm state — **not** committed to the target:

```
.swarmforge/messages/
  0001-architect-to-coder.yaml
  0002-coder-to-reviewer.yaml
  ...
```

(Lives alongside SwarmForge's existing `logs/agent_messages.log`, but structured and status-bearing.)

### Message schema

```yaml
id: 0002
from: coder
to: reviewer
subject: "feat-user-login: slice 3 ready for review"
body: |
  Implemented the login form validation.
  Branch: .worktrees/coder
  Files touched: src/auth/login.ts, src/auth/login.test.ts
status: sent          # sent | received | done
created_at: 2026-06-25T14:02:11Z
received_at: null
done_at: null
chase_count: 0
last_chased_at: null
```

### Status lifecycle

```
sent ──────► received ──────► done
  │             │
  │ (receiver   │ (receiver finishes
  │  acks /     │  the handed-off work
  │  reads it)  │  and marks done)
  │
  └─► sender polls: if still "sent" past timeout → chase
```

| Status | Set by | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `sent` | sender | Handoff written, receiver not yet acknowledged |
| `received` | receiver | Receiver has picked up the message and started |
| `done` | receiver | Handed-off work is complete |

### Chasing sleeping agents

Agents tend to go idle. The sender (or a lightweight monitor in the extension) watches its outgoing messages:

- If a message stays `sent` past a configurable timeout, the sender **chases**: re-notifies the receiver (the orchestrator writes a nudge to the receiver's inbox / re-prompts it), increments `chase_count`, updates `last_chased_at`
- Escalation: after N chases with no `received`, surface a warning on the receiver's tile (red border + "not responding") so the human can intervene — e.g., respawn that agent
- The monitor can also flag messages stuck in `received` (picked up but never completed) past a longer timeout

### UI surfacing

- Each tile shows a small badge: inbound message counts by status (e.g., `2 sent · 1 received`)
- A messages view (panel tab) lists every message with status, age, and chase count — so the human sees the whole conversation and spots stalls at a glance
- Stuck messages (`sent` and overdue) are highlighted

### Implementation notes

- Reading/writing messages is exposed to agents as helper commands on their PATH (part of the forge's reusable tool layer, `extension/src/tools/`): e.g. `send-handoff`, `ack-handoff`, `complete-handoff`
- The chase monitor runs in the extension host, polling the message store on an interval — no dependency added to the target

### Reliability (making it rock-solid)

The naive "edit a YAML field in place" approach has the classic distributed-messaging failure modes: partial writes, lost updates, duplicate processing, out-of-order delivery, and chasing dead agents. The hardened design:

**Atomic writes.** Never edit a message file in place. Write to a temp file and `rename()` it into place — `rename` is atomic on POSIX, so a reader never sees a half-written message. This alone eliminates the corrupt-parse class of bugs.

**Append-only event log, not mutable status.** Model each message as an immutable sequence of events rather than a record whose `status` field gets overwritten:

```yaml
# .swarmforge/messages/0002.log  (append-only, one event per line)
{id: 0002, seq: 1, from: coder, to: reviewer, event: created, at: 2026-06-25T14:02:11Z, schema: 1}
{id: 0002, seq: 2, by: reviewer, event: received, at: 2026-06-25T14:03:40Z}
{id: 0002, seq: 3, by: reviewer, event: done, at: 2026-06-25T14:09:02Z}
```

Current status = the last event. History is free, "who changed what when" is auditable, and the same-field write race disappears because nobody mutates — they only append.

**Stable id + idempotent receivers.** Every message has a stable `id`. Receivers record the ids they've handled, so a re-delivered message (e.g. from a chase) is a no-op, not duplicate work.

**Work-in-progress lease (not just delivery idempotency).** Delivery idempotency stops a message being *picked up* twice, but not a message being *worked* twice — the dangerous case is: a receiver is mid-work (status `received`), the watchdog respawns it for being slow, and the fresh process auto-picks-up the same message and starts again, while the old in-flight work may be orphaned mid-merge. Fix: a `received` event carries a **lease** — the claiming process's identity (`claimed_by: <role>@<pid/epoch>`). On (re)spawn, auto-pickup only resumes a `received` message if the lease is *stale* (its owning process is gone per the watchdog) or absent; a live lease means "someone is already on this," so the new process leaves it alone. Combined with the heartbeat-gated chase below, this guarantees exactly one live worker per message: the watchdog kills the old process *before* respawn, which invalidates the lease, so the fresh process can safely reclaim — no overlap, no orphan.

**Monotonic sequence numbers.** A per-sender `seq` lets a receiver detect gaps and reject out-of-order application (a `done` can't be processed before its `received`).

**Outbox as durable retry queue.** The sender writes to its outbox and treats a message as *unconfirmed* until the receiver appends an explicit `received` ack event. On respawn, an agent replays its unacked outbox — combined with receiver-side auto-pickup, no handoff is lost across a crash.

**Explicit dead-letter state.** After `maxChases` with no ack, the message transitions to `dead-letter` (a terminal event) and escalates to the human (red tile) — rather than chasing forever or rotting silently.

**Automatic recovery before escalation (implemented: `handoffRecovery.ts`).** A dead-lettered or stalled parcel is not immediately handed to the human: it is first re-delivered to its current live holder, with bounded retries, and only escalates to the needs-human tile state once retries are exhausted. Recovery never re-delivers into a busy recipient's in-flight work (the BL-109 busy-recipient bug), and redelivery resets the parcel's stale mtime and chase-count sidecar so the daemon's own chase clock doesn't immediately dead-letter it again on the next sweep (the chase-then-recover race). **Recovery owner:** the same extension-host watchdog timer that already drives `chaserMonitor`'s sweep, not any single pipeline agent — an agent process can exit and tear the swarm down around it (see Heartbeat & Watchdog above and BL-107), so recovery is owned by the supervised extension-host timer rather than becoming a new single point of failure.

**Schema version on every message.** `schema: 1` on the `created` event means a mid-project format change won't break in-flight messages.

**Heartbeat-gated chasing.** The chase monitor consults watchdog heartbeat state before chasing: if the receiver is *dead* (not just slow), escalate to **respawn first**, then let auto-pickup replay the pending message — don't shout at a corpse. This wires the comms layer and the watchdog together so recovery is one coordinated path, not two competing ones.

**Garbage collection.** Completed (`done`) message logs older than a run are archived/compacted so the message store doesn't grow unbounded across long sessions.

---

## Heartbeat & Watchdog

The extension host runs a watchdog that tracks the liveness of every agent independently of message status. Message chasing tells you a *handoff* stalled; the heartbeat tells you an *agent* stalled — even one with no pending messages.

### Heartbeat

The heartbeat signals *productive activity*, not mere process liveness. It's emitted by decorating the agent's tool calls: every tool invocation is wrapped so it emits a heartbeat on entry and on exit.

- Each tool call (file read/write, test run, lint, handoff send/ack, commit, etc.) fires a heartbeat through the wrapper
- The heartbeat writes a timestamp — plus the tool name and phase — to `.swarmforge/heartbeats/<role>`:

  ```yaml
  role: coder
  last_beat: 2026-06-25T14:07:33Z
  last_tool: write_file
  phase: exit            # entry | exit
  in_flight: false       # true between a tool's entry and exit
  beat_count: 412
  ```

- Because the signal is bound to tool calls, an agent that is genuinely working keeps beating, while a wedged agent — looping internally but making no tool calls — goes silent and trips the watchdog. This closes the "alive but unproductive" gap that a timer-based heartbeat can't catch.
- A long-running single tool (e.g. a slow test suite) is covered by `in_flight: true` set on entry: the watchdog treats an in-flight tool as alive even past the stale timeout, with a separate (longer) `inFlightTimeout` to catch a truly hung tool.

**Where the decorator lives:** the heartbeat wrapper is part of the forge's reusable tool layer (`extension/src/tools/`), so every tool the swarm uses is automatically instrumented. Agents don't opt in — they get heartbeats for free by using the standard tooling. No instrumentation leaks into the target.

### Watchdog (extension host)

A single monitor loop in the extension host, polling on an interval:

| Check | Trigger | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **Heartbeat stale** | No heartbeat from a role past `staleTimeout` and no tool in flight | Mark tile amber ("idle"), attempt a nudge (orchestrator re-prompts / writes to the agent's inbox) |
| **Tool hung** | A tool in flight (`in_flight: true`) past `inFlightTimeout` | Mark amber → red; surface the stuck tool name on the tile |
| **Heartbeat dead** | Still stale past `deadTimeout` after nudges | Mark tile red ("not responding"); optionally auto-respawn if enabled |
| **Process gone** | Backend PID for a role no longer exists | Mark red; auto-respawn if `autoRespawn` is on |
| **Message stuck** | (from comms layer) message overdue in `sent`/`received` | Chase, then escalate to tile warning |

### Auto-respawn (optional, configurable)

- When `autoRespawn` is enabled, a dead agent is respawned automatically in its existing worktree
- On relaunch the agent auto-picks-up its pending messages (see above), so recovery is seamless — including a parcel the prior (killed) process had already claimed into its own `inbox/in_process/` but never finished: every respawn path (auto-respawn, a manual restart, the chase daemon's own respawn, or a fresh swarm launch) converges on one generated launch script that checks the role's `in_process/` queue first and explicitly instructs the fresh agent to resume it, rather than relying on the agent to notice unprompted (BL-323 — a real ~4-hour stall where an orphaned `in_process` claim survived two relaunches before a human manually nudged it by name)
- A per-role respawn cap (e.g., 3 within a window) prevents crash-loops — once exceeded, the watchdog stops and leaves the tile red for human intervention

### UI surfacing

- Tile border encodes liveness: green (alive), amber (idle/stale), red (dead/not responding)
- A heartbeat indicator (last-seen age) shown per tile
- The status bar shows aggregate health: e.g. `4 agents · 3 alive · 1 idle`

### Configuration

Heartbeat and watchdog timeouts are configured in the main settings block (see Extension Settings) — `intervalSeconds`, `staleTimeoutSeconds`, `deadTimeoutSeconds`, `inFlightTimeoutSeconds`, `autoRespawn`, and `maxRespawnsPerRole`.

### Why the extension host owns it

Agents are unreliable pollers — that's the whole problem. A single watchdog in the extension host (not in the agents) is the dependable observer: it sees heartbeats, PIDs, and message status together, and it's the one component guaranteed to stay awake.

### Per-role idle context clearing

**Last Updated:** August 29, 2026 (BL-1238: the agent-side NO_TASK idle-clear
respawn — `ready_for_next_task.bb` for task-mode roles, `ready_for_next_batch.bb`'s
own copy for batch-mode roles (cleaner, hardener) — now honours the SAME
fullness threshold as the extension-host path below instead of respawning
unconditionally on every idle boundary. Before this fix the agent side paid
a full boot-prefix reload at every NO_TASK regardless of how much of the
window was actually free — exactly the cost the fullness gate exists to
avoid. Reuses BL-141's `resolveContextFullness` contract (telemetry wins
when present, else a line-count proxy, else `:unavailable`) and the same
`swarmforge.contextClear.fullnessThresholdPercent` setting, so the two
paths cannot disagree about whether a role is full; an unavailable reading
never clears (fail-closed, per the locked human decision). No telemetry
source exists on the agent side today, so the proxy reading always decides
in practice.)

To prevent context window exhaustion during long swarm runs, individual roles can be configured to clear their session context at idle boundaries. This is useful for roles that don't need cross-parcel context (e.g., hardener, documenter) to reduce token accumulation:

- **Per-role opt-in flag:** configured via an optional token on the `window` line in `swarmforge.conf` (e.g., `window hardener claude hardender idle-clear`). Absent means OFF; default for every role is disabled.
- **Trigger:** clearing occurs only after a role completes its current task/batch AND its queue returns NO_TASK (i.e., at the idle boundary, never mid-task or mid-batch) AND the role's context window reaches a minimum fullness threshold. The window fullness is measured by the backend's telemetry if available (exact token usage), or a deterministic proxy metric (pane history line count) otherwise. This prevents unnecessary clearing of roles that go idle with mostly-empty windows — saving context resets for moments when they matter cost-wise.
- **Fullness threshold:** `swarmforge.contextClear.fullnessThresholdPercent` (default 75%). Set to 0 to skip the fullness check and clear as soon as drained-idle boundaries are reached. When the backend does not report real context usage, the fullness indicator shows "proxy" in the Context Clear output channel so you know the gate ran on line-count estimation rather than exact tokens.
- **Action:** the launcher sends `/clear` + Enter, causing the role's session to reset. The fresh session receives the full role re-bootstrap (constitution, pipeline, role prompt) exactly as if it had just been respawned.
- **State preservation:** only session context is cleared; durable inbox/outbox state, in-process audit trails, and handoffs are completely unaffected
- **Safety:** clearing never interrupts in-flight work, pending human input, or graceful bounces. Roles with the flag disabled (most roles, including specifier and coordinator) continue as before with accumulating context.
- **Cost tradeoff:** enabled roles lose in-session short-term coherence between parcels, trading that for reduced token cost. Roles that need cross-parcel recall should keep the flag disabled.
- **Agent-side parity (BL-1238):** the extension host isn't the only clearer — a role's own `ready_for_next_task.bb`/`ready_for_next_batch.bb` re-exec at a `NO_TASK` idle boundary honours the identical opt-in flag and fullness threshold, so the two triggers cannot disagree about whether a role is full.

This is safe because the protocol is already context-free between parcels — every handoff body says "re-read your role and constitution," and durable state (backlog, handoffs, messages) lives on disk.

### Cooldown-aware wake scheduling (rate-limit backoff)

When an agent reports hitting a rate limit and provides a reset time (e.g., "tokens available again at 2pm"), the swarm automatically avoids waking that agent during the cooldown window and resumes normal operation once the cooldown expires. Detection and enforcement are split across two components that share one state file, `.swarmforge/rate-limit-cooldown.json`:

- **Detection (extension host):** the same pane tailer that already watches for session URLs (`swarmPanel.ts`'s `setupTailer`) scans for a usage/rate-limit line naming a reset time and records the cooldown to the shared file via `cooldownScheduler`'s `parseResetTime`/`recordCooldown`
- **Suppression + resume (handoff daemon):** `handoffd.bb`'s live chase sweep (`chase_sweep_lib.bb`) reads that same file each cycle — a cooling-down role is skipped entirely (no chase/nudge/wake); once past the reset time it is woken exactly once and marked woken, so it does not re-trigger the next cycle
- **Automatic resume:** once the cooldown timestamp passes, normal chase and wake behavior resumes automatically
- **Resilience:** cooldown state persists on disk — an extension reload or daemon restart before cooldown expires does not lose the suppression window
- **Isolation:** cooldown affects only the role that hit the limit; other agents continue normal chase/wake behavior uninterrupted

This prevents the "retry storm" where a rate-limited agent gets nudged repeatedly while unable to act, saving tokens and clearing the notification noise during the windowed recovery period.

### Mutation-run progress (long hardening passes)

A Stryker mutation pass can run for hours with no visible signal beyond an
opaque spinner. A durable, structured progress file closes that gap
independently of the heartbeat mechanism above:

- Every mutation run writes `.swarmforge/mutation-progress/<role>.json`,
  refreshed as mutants are tested and finalized (`status: "done"`) when the
  run completes: `{file, tested, total, percent, survived, timedOut,
  elapsed_s, eta_s, updated_at, status}`.
- The file is plain JSON — readable with `cat` at any time, with no
  dependency on the extension or webview being healthy.
- `updated_at` staying fresh distinguishes a progressing run from a hung
  one, the same distinction the heartbeat makes for agents in general.
- Written via a Stryker reporter plugin (`mutation-progress`, alongside the
  built-in `clear-text`/`progress` reporters in
  `extension/stryker.config.json`) that taps Stryker's own reporter
  lifecycle rather than re-implementing its progress/ETA math.

### Bounded test-run memory footprint (BL-422)

A plain `vitest run` used to size its worker pool to the host CPU count with
no per-worker heap limit. One run ballooned four workers to ~13GB on a 15GB
host and drove the kernel OOM-killer into a death-spiral that killed swarm
agents twice in one day plus a half-launch — the test suite itself, not a
runaway agent, was the OOM source.

- `extension/vitest.config.mjs` now sets `pool: 'forks'` with
  `poolOptions.forks.maxForks`/`execArgv` (a `--max-old-space-size` per
  worker), so a run's worst-case footprint is a fixed, small number instead
  of scaling with host CPU count.
- The cap numbers (`MAX_WORKERS`, `PER_WORKER_HEAP_MB`,
  `SAFE_HOST_RAM_FRACTION`) and the pure `computeWorkerMemoryBudget`
  predicate live in `extension/src/tools/vitest-worker-memory-budget.ts` — a
  shared module value the config and its unit test both read, mirroring
  `check-suite-file-budget.ts`'s pattern, rather than a number buried only
  inside the config where nothing can assert on it.
- Stryker's own vitest-runner hardcodes `pool: 'threads'` + `maxThreads: 1`
  (the worker-thread rule below) and overrides these caps entirely, so
  mutation runs are unaffected by this cap.
- **Widened within the same RAM budget (BL-445).** Profiling traced the
  recorded whole-suite wall-clock (10-13s, over the operator's 10s target)
  to this cap serializing 292 test files onto just 2 forked workers on a
  20-core host. `MAX_WORKERS`/`PER_WORKER_HEAP_MB` moved from `2`/`2048` to
  `6`/`1280` — worst-case footprint stays inside the unchanged
  `SAFE_HOST_RAM_FRACTION` ceiling (7680MB on the 15360MB reference host);
  only the worker-pool shape changed, not `test_count` or coverage.
- **Per-file isolation disabled, the real pole (BL-445, QA bounce fix).**
  The widened worker cap above still left the suite at 16.8-24.9s — QA
  bounced it. Further profiling found the actual cost wasn't test-execution
  parallelism at all: Vitest's default per-file isolation resets the module
  registry/environment before each of the 290+ files regardless of worker
  count, dominating the reporter's own `prepare`/`collect` phases (~35s
  combined on a ~25s run). `poolOptions.forks.isolate: false` in
  `extension/vitest.config.mjs` cuts that combined cost to under 1s, with
  no change to `MAX_WORKERS`/`PER_WORKER_HEAP_MB` — the RAM budget above is
  untouched. Safe because the suite already restores every stub/global it
  touches (see the fake-cwd/HOME rule) rather than relying on Vitest's
  per-file reset, and the two module-level test caches that keep
  deliberate cross-test state already ship explicit reset-for-test
  exports. Stryker's own vitest-runner hardcodes `pool: 'threads'` and
  reads `poolOptions.threads` instead, so mutation runs are unaffected.
  `mermaidRender.test.js` separately memoized one canonical fixture render
  for its two read-only assertions (well-formed PNG, render width),
  keeping the determinism test's own independent second render — same
  assertions, half the redundant real elkjs-layout + resvg work.
- **A second, CPU-axis ceiling (BL-935).** Everything above is a MEMORY
  budget: `resolveWorkerPoolSize` derives the fork count from
  `os.totalmem()` and nothing else, so it has no signal for how many cores
  are already busy. Under a live full-forge pack — 8 concurrent Claude
  sessions plus handoffd and the front-desk bridge on a 2-physical-core
  macOS host — it still returns 3, and two overlapping `vitest run`
  invocations put ~6 forks on a box already running at 8-150x its core
  count. `resolveVitestForkCeiling` adds a second, independent ceiling
  beside the memory one, resolved from `SWARMFORGE_PACK`, `os.platform()`
  and an optional `SWARMFORGE_VITEST_MAX_FORKS`, in this order:
  1. an explicit **positive integer** `SWARMFORGE_VITEST_MAX_FORKS`
     replaces the pack rule (an override that cannot override is not an
     override);
  2. otherwise a `full-forge` pack on `darwin` resolves to **1 fork**;
  3. otherwise the existing memory-derived count, unchanged.

  A non-positive or non-numeric override (`0`, `-1`, `1.5`, empty,
  whitespace-only, any text) is **ignored** and falls through to rule 2 —
  never floored, never coerced. The ceiling is then handed to
  `resolveWorkerPoolSize` as its own `ceiling` argument, so the RAM budget
  remains an absolute upper bound and the pool keeps its floor of 1: this
  can only ever LOWER the fork count, never raise it (`…MAX_FORKS=9` on
  the 8192MB host still resolves to 3). A human running the suite outside a
  pack has no `SWARMFORGE_PACK` at all, so a quiet laptop keeps the full
  budget. **How the variable reaches an agent shell is inherited, not
  wired**, and the distinction decides whether this ceiling engages at all:
  no launcher in this repo exports `SWARMFORGE_PACK=full-forge`. The five
  alternative-provider wrappers (`start-swarm-{gpt,mistral,qwen,anthropic,
  gemini}.sh`) each export a `*-mono-router` value; the default
  `start-swarm.sh` only READS the variable (`resolve_launch_pack`) and
  passes the result to `swarmforge/scripts/swarmforge.sh` as `--pack`,
  which consumes it as a **config-file selector** (`swarmforge/packs/
  NAME.conf`) and keeps `PACK` a plain unexported local. The env var the
  resolver reads and the `--pack` config selector are two different
  mechanisms sharing one name. So the ceiling engages only when the shell
  that launched the swarm already carried `SWARMFORGE_PACK=full-forge`,
  which the pane processes then inherit. Measured on this host 2026-08-19,
  both halves: a role shell reports `SWARMFORGE_PACK=full-forge` and its
  `vitest.config.mjs` resolves 1 fork (3 with the variable cleared), while
  the PER-SESSION `tmux show-environment -t <session>` table answers
  `unknown variable` for all 8 sessions. That is a wrong probe, not a
  missing variable: the value rides the tmux SERVER's global environment,
  which every pane inherits and which only `tmux show-environment -g`
  reads. Confirm the cap is live with `-g` or with the pane's own `env`,
  never with the per-session table. Making that inheritance explicit
  at launch — so the ceiling does not depend on how the swarm happened to
  be started — was BL-961's job, not this ticket's, and BL-961 has since
  landed it: every generated `.swarmforge/launch/<role>.sh` now exports the
  pack the launcher loaded, so this paragraph describes the pre-BL-961
  inheritance path (see the next bullet). Both lanes compose the ceiling and the memory
  budget through **one** shared `resolveVitestWorkerPool`, rather than the
  identical eight lines each config used to carry: neither lane can size
  its pool by a route the other does not share, by construction. The module
  stays pure — pack, platform, override and host RAM are all passed in by
  the caller, so nothing reads `process.env` or `os` inside it. Stryker is
  unaffected for the same reason as the caps above.

- **The launcher now WIRES that variable instead of inheriting it
  (BL-961).** The paragraph above describes the state before this ticket:
  `SWARMFORGE_PACK` reached a role shell only because the shell that
  invoked `./swarm` happened to carry it, so the CPU-axis ceiling engaged
  by launch-context luck. Nothing was broken on this host — the cap was
  measurably live (`maxForks` 1 with the variable set, 3 with it cleared)
  — but the next `./swarm` from a clean shell would have dropped it back
  to 3 silently, with no error: fragility, not inertness. The launcher now
  states the pack explicitly. `write_role_launch_script` in
  `swarmforge/scripts/swarmforge.sh` derives `launch_pack_name` as
  `basename "$CONFIG_FILE" .conf` — the conf file the launcher ACTUALLY
  loaded, the same derivation `ancillary_provider_lib.sh` already uses for
  its swarm-identity fallback — and writes
  `export SWARMFORGE_PACK='<pack>'` into the generated
  `.swarmforge/launch/<role>.sh` heredoc, beside the existing
  `SWARMFORGE_ROLE` export. Two consequences are the point of the ticket.
  (1) The env var and the `--pack` config selector can no longer name
  different packs for one launch: both resolve from the single
  `CONFIG_FILE`, so the exported value is identical in every role's script
  and equals that file's basename. (2) The export lives in the generated
  FILE, not in a `tmux set-environment` call or the initial tmux command,
  so a single-role respawn — which re-runs `.swarmforge/launch/<role>.sh`
  directly — still carries it. A default `swarmforge.conf` launch exports
  `swarmforge`; a `--pack full-forge` launch exports `full-forge`. No
  consumer keys on the default name, and a human running the suite outside
  a swarm still has no `SWARMFORGE_PACK` at all and keeps the full budget.
  Rollout note: this changes what future launch scripts SAY, so
  already-running panes pick the export up at the next `./swarm` relaunch
  or single-role respawn — a live shell missing the value before then is
  the expected rollout condition, not a regression. Probing a live shell
  is not evidence about this fix in either direction (the tmux server's
  global environment can already supply the value); only grepping a
  freshly generated `.swarmforge/launch/<role>.sh` is. No extension
  command, setting, or UI changes — launcher wiring for a signal the
  extension's own test tooling consumes.

### Whole-suite duration budget verdict (BL-445)

`extension/src/tools/check-suite-duration-budget.ts` is the whole-suite
sibling of `check-suite-file-budget.ts`'s per-file guard: it classifies one
recorded run's `duration_ms` against the operator's 10-second target
(`SUITE_DURATION_BUDGET_MS`, `>=` counts as over-budget) and prints a
`within-budget`/`over-budget` verdict naming the measured duration, wired
in-process into `recordTestDuration.js` right after the duration is
measured. It surfaces an over-budget run rather than hard-failing the
build — the recorded duration jitters under swarm load, and a hard fail at
the 10000ms boundary would flake on that jitter; the per-file 7s guard
remains the hard gate. This is the durable ratchet against the target
creeping back unnoticed; the existing suite-duration trend
(`swarmMetrics.ts`) still only reports relative "slower than before".

### Unit suite green + per-file duration profile (BL-792)

Slice A of the `unit-suite-speed` epic (BL-791). Every recorded `npm test` run
in `extension/` since 2026-07-07 had `result: fail` (169.5s/438 files, workers
terminated mid-run) — a duration that measured crash-recovery noise, not test
work, so optimizing against it would have optimized the wrong thing. This
slice's whole scope is making the run green and publishing what that green run
actually measures; any speed cut is deliberately left to slice B.

- `extension/src/tools/build-test-duration-profile.ts` reads the same Vitest
  JSON report `check-suite-file-budget.ts` already parses (via its shared
  `extractFileDurations`) plus the newest row of `.test-durations.jsonl`
  (BL-078), and writes a per-file duration table, slowest first, to a
  committed markdown file — `docs/reference/BL-792-test-duration-profile.md`
  for this baseline run. `assertRecordPassed`/`assertTestCountNotShrunk`
  enforce the ticket's own invariants in code: a non-`pass` record throws
  rather than becoming a baseline, and a `test_count` drop from the previous
  recorded run throws rather than silently shipping.
- When the recorded run is over the human-given 13s `OPERATIONAL_CEILING_MS`
  (distinct from — never a substitute for — `SUITE_DURATION_BUDGET_MS`'s
  coded 10s ratchet), the report also names "poles": the smallest
  slowest-first set of files whose cumulative duration reaches at least half
  the total measured file time. That named set is slice B's entire input.
  CLI: `node build-test-duration-profile.js <vitest-json-report-path>
  <test-durations-jsonl-path> <output-md-path>`.
- The baseline run recorded 440 test files at 316.3s, over the ceiling; the
  profile names the 20 slowest files as the poles slice B must cut, each with
  its own measured duration.
- **CRAP follow-up (same ticket, hardener pass).** `main()` originally
  inlined argv parsing, file reads, and orchestration behind a subprocess-only
  path with 0% in-process coverage (CRAP 23.52). Split into `parseArgs`
  (pure) and `runBuildProfile` (the real read/assert/build/write
  orchestration, no CLI wiring), wired through `makeArgsGuardedMain` — the
  same thin-wrapper split this codebase's other CLIs already use
  (`co-change-report.ts`) — so an in-process test exercises every branch a
  subprocess invocation would. No behavior or CLI usage change; max CRAP
  4.00.

### Mutation-run worker RSS profiling (BL-427, measure-first)

`extension/stryker.config.json`'s `"concurrency": 4` is a fixed, RAM-blind
number — the mutation-run equivalent of the gap BL-422 closed for the unit
suite, but BL-422 explicitly does not touch mutation runs (previous
section). This ticket measures rather than wires an adaptive default; a
named follow-up will size concurrency from live free RAM.

- `node extension/out/tools/profile-mutation-workers.js [--interval-ms N]
  [--reserve-mb N] -- <command> [args...]` wraps an already-configured
  mutation command, samples its child worker processes' RSS at a fixed
  interval (default 5000ms) until it exits, and prints each worker's peak
  RSS plus a concurrency recommendation sized from current free RAM
  (default reserve: 2048MB).
- The sampler walks the wrapped command's FULL descendant process tree
  (`collectDescendantPids`, a BFS over children/grandchildren/...), not just
  its direct children — this project invokes Stryker through `npm exec` /
  `npx`, which interpose a shell between the spawned process and the real
  worker processes underneath it, so a direct-children-only sampler measures
  the wrapper shell instead of the workers it wraps (QA bounce, BL-427).
- `extension/src/metrics/mutationWorkerRss.ts` holds the two pure pieces:
  `computePeakRssPerWorker` reduces raw RSS samples to each worker's peak
  (max, never last/average) over its lifetime, and
  `recommendMutationConcurrency({freeRamBytes, peakRssPerWorkerBytes,
  coreCount, reserveBytes})` recommends
  `clamp(floor((freeRamBytes - reserveBytes) / peakRssPerWorkerBytes), 1,
  coreCount)` — floored at 1 (never zero workers), capped at the core count
  (RAM headroom can't buy more parallelism than the host has cores).
- Actually changing `stryker.config.json`'s concurrency to this
  recommendation is a named follow-up ticket, not this one — until it
  lands, the mutation run still uses the fixed `4` and this module is a
  correct-but-dark measurement tool run on demand.

### Mutation gate zero-kill health verdict (BL-446)

A mutation run reporting zero killed mutants reads identically to a clean
pass — "no survivors" — whether every mutant was genuinely killed or
Stryker's own kill mechanism produced nothing at all. That ambiguity let a
transient stale-incremental-cache read look like a healthy hardener gate.

- `extension/src/mutation/mutationGateHealth.ts` classifies a completed
  run's `killed`/`survived` counts into `healthy` (any mutant killed),
  `zero-kill-suspect` (zero killed, but mutants existed to kill), or
  `no-mutants` (nothing in scope) — a pure, root-cause-agnostic predicate
  that guards against any future recurrence of this failure mode, not just
  the one incident that prompted it.
- Wired into `MutationProgressReporter.onMutationTestReportReady()`
  (`extension/src/mutation/mutationProgressReporter.ts`): a non-healthy
  verdict is printed to stderr at run completion, visible in a live
  `stryker run` regardless of TTY, alongside the existing progress
  reporting.
- `mutationProgress.ts`'s run state/record now also tracks `killed`
  alongside the existing `survived`/`timedOut` counters, since the health
  verdict needs it.
- This incident's actual root cause was a stale `stryker-incremental.json`
  read, not a broken kill mechanism — a fresh, cache-cleared run killed
  mutants normally. The health verdict is the durable ratchet regardless of
  cause: a genuine future zero-kill run can no longer be silently read as a
  clean gate pass.

### Mutation gate entrypoint-boilerplate survivors (BL-447)

Distinct from BL-446 above (that was the gate reading ZERO kills as clean;
this is the opposite failure mode, surfacing once kills work again): every
`tools/*.ts` CLI ends with the shared `if (require.main === module) {
runCliMain(main); }` guard (~52 call sites) and tsc emits a
`Object.defineProperty(exports, "__esModule", ...)` header at the top of
every compiled file — and neither line can ever be killed by any test. An
in-process `main()` test never executes the guard line itself (it calls
`main()` directly), so it reads as `NoCoverage`; a subprocess smoke test
spawns a fresh `node` process that never carries Stryker's in-memory
`activeMutant`/coverage globals, so it can't register a kill for anything it
runs, guard included. A module that follows every existing thin-wrapper/
in-process-`main()` rule perfectly (`check-suite-duration-budget.ts`) still
showed 9/42 unkillable survivors purely from this fixed residue.

- `extension/src/mutation/entrypointBoilerplateIgnorer.ts`'s
  `classifyMutantLocation` is a pure, coverage-blind predicate: it decides
  `excluded`/`kept` from STRUCTURAL LOCATION alone (never from whether a
  mutant has coverage or survived), so an untested mutant in real exported
  logic structurally cannot be classified as boilerplate — only the named
  shapes are ever excluded. `isRequireMainGuardNode`/
  `isEsModuleBoilerplateNode` recognize the guard's `require.main ===
  module` `IfStatement` and tsc's `__esModule` `Object.defineProperty`
  call by AST shape. A third shape, tsc's import-helper preamble
  (`__importStar`/`__importDefault`/`__createBinding`/`__setModuleDefault`,
  the `var __NAME = (this && this.__NAME) || (…)` init tsc emits at the
  head of every compiled `import * as x` file), was added by BL-498:
  ~20-45 behaviorally-equivalent survivors per such file (123 `src` files
  use that import convention) inflated the gate on every run until this
  was excluded. Matched the same anti-vacuous way as the other two — a
  closed set of the exact tsc helper names AND the exact init shape, never
  name-alone or a broad head-of-file exclusion — so a project variable that
  happens to share a helper's name but not its initializer stays `kept`.
- Wired into `extension/src/mutation/stryker-plugin.ts` as
  `EntrypointBoilerplateIgnorer`, a `PluginKind.Ignore` plugin alongside the
  existing Reporter. The first wiring attempt registered the plugin via
  `appendPlugins` alone and shipped silently inert — Stryker only invokes an
  Ignore-kind plugin whose name also appears in the separate `ignorers`
  config array, so without `"ignorers": ["entrypoint-boilerplate"]` in
  `extension/stryker.config.json` the plugin ran zero times and every
  boilerplate mutant still reported Survived. Fixed by adding that config
  entry plus a regression test pinning the registered plugin name against
  the config's activation list, so the two can't drift apart silently again.
- A fresh, cache-cleared Stryker run scoped to
  `check-suite-duration-budget.js` confirms the fix is surgical: the
  `require.main` guard and `__esModule` boilerplate mutants are now reported
  Ignored, and the file's 25 real-logic mutants are still fully mutated and
  killed — the exclusion did not leak into tested-or-not real code. No
  human-facing command or setting; this is internal mutation-gate tooling
  that only changes what the hardener's own gate reports.

## Swarm Availability Ledger (BL-823)

Two of the intervals during which the swarm cannot process work have never
had a durable record: a control/cooldown pause (`.swarmforge/operator/control-pause.json`
is a *current-state* marker — resume overwrites it, leaving no history) and a
stop-to-start gap (`kill_pipeline_swarm.sh` / `stop-swarm.sh` write nothing at
all). This ledger records both, append-only, so a future consumer can tell a
genuine flow stall apart from a span when the swarm simply wasn't running.

**This ticket only records and exposes intervals — it never subtracts them
from anything, and it changes no alarm.** The Flow Watchdog above still
measures parcel age in wall-clock time unchanged; wiring the ledger into that
math is BL-650's job, and BL-650 `depends_on: [BL-823]`.

### Storage

`.swarmforge/telemetry/availability-<YYYY-MM>.jsonl` — append-only, one JSON
object per line, monthly files (the same convention `llm_cost_ledger_lib.bb`
already uses for `llm-cost-<YYYY-MM>.jsonl`):

```json
{"ts":"2026-08-06T19:00:03Z","event":"pause-start","class":"control-pause","source":"telegram-front-desk-bot:pause"}
```

- `event` — `pause-start` \| `pause-end` \| `stop` \| `start`
- `class` — `control-pause` (covers both a human/Telegram pause and a
  cooldown-window pause — BL-650 treats them as one class) or `swarm-stop`
- `source` — names the emitting call site, for audit

### Writers

Every pause/stop/start transition already funnels through one of two
existing choke points; the ledger appends inside those, adding no new call
sites to hunt down:

- **TS** — `extension/src/metrics/availabilityLedgerStore.ts`'s
  `appendAvailabilityRecord`, called from both pause twins on every
  transition: `writeControlPauseState` (`telegram-front-desk-bot.ts` — used
  by a human `/pause`/`/resume`, the BL-617 cooldown window, and the
  auto-resume sweep) and `writeOperatorPauseState`
  (`telegramCursorOperatorExec.ts`).
- **Shell** — `swarmforge/scripts/availability_ledger_lib.sh`'s
  `availability_record`, called from `kill_pipeline_swarm.sh` (a `stop`) and
  `start-swarm.sh` (a `start`).

**A ledger write failure never blocks, fails, or alters the transition it
observes** — both writers swallow their own errors.

### The ungraceful-stop close

A `kill -9`, host reboot, or daemon crash writes no `stop` record — the
class of gap the 2026-08-05 handoffd outage belongs to. To avoid that
interval staying open forever, `start-swarm.sh` calls
`availability_close_ungraceful_stop` before recording its own `start`: if the
ledger's last record isn't already a `stop`, it reads the daemon's last tick
from `.swarmforge/daemon/handoffd.heartbeat` (an existing single-value file,
already written every cycle) and appends a synthetic `stop` at that
timestamp, sourced `heartbeat-inferred`. No heartbeat file (or one no newer
than the last `start`) emits nothing — that span is left to fall back to
wall clock, the same safe default BL-650 already uses everywhere else.

### The reader

`swarmforge/scripts/availability_ledger_lib.bb`'s `fold` turns records into
`{:start-ms :end-ms :class :provenance}` intervals — `provenance` is
`"proven"` (both ends are real records), `"inferred"` (closed via the
heartbeat), or `"open"` (no closing record yet; `:end-ms` is `nil`, never a
guessed timestamp). It spans month-file boundaries and skips blank,
malformed, or unparseable-timestamp lines rather than crashing the fold or
inventing a record. This is BL-823's only reader — `fold`'s caller is
BL-650's `evaluate-effective-age`, in the Flow Watchdog section below.

### See Also

- **BL-617** — Nightly Cooldown Window: its `writeControlPauseState` writer
  now also appends to this ledger on every pause/resume.
- **BL-650** — the flow watchdog's active-time clock: `evaluate-effective-age`
  subtracts these ledger intervals, plus provider-outage intervals (BL-840),
  from a waiting parcel's effective age. See "Effective Age and Provider-Outage
  Evidence (BL-650/BL-840)" below.

## Human-Loop Reliability Ledger (BL-595)

The Telegram front desk previously emitted **no** reliability trend for the
human↔swarm channel — the blind spot that hid silently failing approval taps
(BL-582) until a human noticed a stuck button. BL-595 adds four series on one
append-only ledger so falling tap success or rising 409 counts become visible
as leading indicators. **This ticket only measures** — fixing tap or steer
failures remains BL-582 / BL-566.

### Storage

`.swarmforge/telemetry/human-loop-<YYYY-MM>.jsonl` — append-only, one JSON
object per line, monthly files (same posture as the availability ledger and
`context-events.jsonl`). Covered by the top-level `.swarmforge/` gitignore.

Outcome records (series 1–3):

```json
{"at":"2026-08-25T16:40:00.000Z","series":"approval-tap","outcome":"recorded"}
{"at":"2026-08-25T16:40:01.000Z","series":"approval-tap","outcome":"silently-dropped","reason":"not-principal"}
{"at":"2026-08-25T16:40:02.000Z","series":"steering-delivery","outcome":"delivered"}
{"at":"2026-08-25T16:40:03.000Z","series":"poll-health","outcome":"conflict-409"}
```

Duration records (series 4):

```json
{"at":"2026-08-25T16:40:04.000Z","series":"tick-duration","durationMs":42}
```

### Series

| Series | Outcomes / value | Emit sites |
|--------|------------------|------------|
| `approval-tap` | `recorded` / `silently-dropped` / `repaint-failed`; drops carry `reason` (`not-my-chat` / `not-principal` / `unrecognized-data`) | `telegramFrontDeskBotCore.ts` — record / drop / repaint paths |
| `steering-delivery` | `delivered` / `no-pane` / `undelivered` / `menu-blocked` (BL-566 / BL-568 `SteerDeliveryResult`) | steer redirect + ask-answer delivery |
| `poll-health` | `degraded` / `conflict-409` | `applyPollCycleResult` when a degraded warning fires |
| `tick-duration` | wall-clock `durationMs` per concierge tick | `runOneConciergeTick` after `runConciergeTick` |

Every outcome string is one the emitting code **already computed** — no
aggregator invents a classification.

### Emit posture (measuring must not worsen what it measures)

`humanLoopReliabilityStore.ts` appends **fire-and-forget async** (chained
promises; production callers never `await`). Write failures are swallowed so
an unwritable or non-directory ledger path never fails, blocks, or slows the
tap, steer, poll, or tick being recorded. A naive synchronous append on every
concierge tick is explicitly the wrong shape for series 4 (that tick already
does large sync `readFileSync`/`JSON.parse` work on the same event loop as
`getUpdates`).

Production wires `PollAdapters.humanLoopRoot` (and the concierge tick root)
to the project path; fixtures may omit it and emit nothing.

### Aggregation

`humanLoopReliability.ts` folds an **in-memory** record list into
`trend.ts` series points — file-free aggregation:

- Outcome series → per-window **success rate** (`recorded` / `delivered` count
  as success).
- Tick-duration → per-window **mean** `durationMs`.

  this ledger trends the outcomes).

## Self-Heal Events Trend (BL-597)

The swarm heals itself constantly — stale-build recompiles, supervisor
respawns, `kill_all_swarm`, mono-router rotation respawns, claim-heal —
but historically counted none of it; a recovery that fixed a live outage
stayed invisible until grepped by hand. BL-597 structures each existing
prose log moment as a durable event and trends **per-type counts** over
time. **Measurement only** — recovery behaviour is unchanged; a failed
telemetry append must not block or alter whether self-heal runs.

### Storage

`.swarmforge/telemetry/self-heal-<YYYY-MM>.jsonl` — append-only, one JSON
object per line, monthly files. Explicitly listed in `.gitignore` (and
covered by the top-level `.swarmforge/` ignore). Clojure sites call
`self-heal-telemetry-lib/append-self-heal-event!` (failures swallowed);
tests may use `selfHealTelemetryStore.ts` / `self_heal_telemetry_cli.bb`.

Record shape:

```json
{"type":"stale-build-recompile","subject":"front-desk-supervisor","reason":"recompiling before respawn","at":"2026-08-27T09:00:00.000Z"}
```

### Event types and emit sites

| Type | Subject (typical) | Emit at existing log site |
|------|-------------------|---------------------------|
| `stale-build-recompile` | `front-desk-supervisor` | `front_desk_supervisor.bb` `ensure-current-build!` (with `stale-build-detected`) |
| `supervisor-respawn` | `front-desk-supervisor` | `front_desk_supervisor.bb` `log-event!` `:started` |
| `kill-all-swarm` | `lifecycle` | `kill_pipeline_swarm.sh` after SUCCESS (via CLI) |
| `rotation-respawn` | `mono-router-resident` | `handoff_lib.bb` mono-router persona swap |
| `claim-heal` | `handoffd` | `handoffd.bb` resume orphaned `in_process` |

Each record is emitted **at the existing prose log site** for that recovery
action — no parallel detection path.

### Aggregation

`selfHealTelemetry.ts` `aggregateSelfHealCounts` folds an **in-memory**
event list into per-type `trend.ts` / `computeTrend` series (current /
prior / delta / direction) — file-free aggregation.

### See Also

- **BL-594** — swarm-behaviour-trends epic.
- **BL-595** — human-loop reliability ledger (sibling monthly JSONL /
  `computeTrend` posture).
- **BL-096** — shared `computeTrend` / `TrendResult` framework.

## Context-Compaction Cadence (BL-601)

Compaction frequency is a proxy for which roles are under context pressure,
but the pane spinner strings (`auto-compact NN%`, `Compacting`) change between
CLI versions and must never be the primary signal. BL-601 derives compaction
records only from structured GH-22 context-events with `compaction: true`
(BL-665 producer), pairs each with the token level at that instant
(`input_tokens` → `tokens-at-compaction`), and trends **compactions/hour** plus
the **token-at-compaction distribution** per role. **Measurement only** —
this ticket never tunes compaction thresholds or alters agent behaviour.
Pairs naturally with BL-596 (a persona that compacts constantly is also a
rotation-cost signal).

### Storage

`.swarmforge/telemetry/compaction-<YYYY-MM>.jsonl` — append-only, one JSON
object per line, monthly files (same posture as the human-loop and
availability ledgers). Covered by the top-level `.swarmforge/` gitignore.
`compactionTelemetryStore.ts` appends fire-and-forget; write failures are
swallowed so an unwritable ledger never fails the emitting path.

Derived record shape (from a `compaction:true` context event):

```json
{"role":"coder","model":"claude-sonnet-5","tokensAtCompaction":180000,"timestamp":"2026-08-27T06:00:00Z","timestampMs":1756274400000}
```

### Signal rules

| Input | Result |
|-------|--------|
| Context-event with `compaction: true` | One compaction record (`role`, `model`, `tokensAtCompaction` = `inputTokens`, `timestamp`) |
| Context-event with `compaction: false` / missing | No record |
| Pane spinner text alone | No record |

### Aggregation

`compactionCadence.ts` folds an **in-memory** record list — file-free:

- Per detectable role, per daily window: `compactionsPerHour` and
  min / median / max token-at-compaction.
- `trendForCompactionCadencePerHour` / the window series feed `computeTrend`
  for current / prior / delta / direction.
- Roles **not** in the caller's `detectableRoles` allow-list return
  `applicable: false` with an empty series (NA) — never a fabricated zero,
  even when unrelated records exist for other roles.

### Dependency direction (acyclic)

`compactionCadence` imports `computeTrend` from `./trend`. Callers that need
`trendForCompactionCadencePerHour` load it from `out/metrics/compactionCadence`.
`trend.ts` must **not** re-export anything from `./compactionCadence` — that
back-edge was the standing architect bounce (cycle) this rematch closed.

### See Also

- **BL-665** / **GH-22** — structured `context-events.jsonl` producer
  (`contextTelemetryProducer.ts` + handoffd sweep; `compaction:true` is the
  primary detection signal). How-to:
  `docs/how-to/BL-665-context-telemetry-producer-wiring.md`.
- **BL-596** — rotation-cost trend (cross-read with high compaction cadence).
- **BL-595** — human-loop reliability ledger (sibling monthly JSONL /
  `computeTrend` posture).

## Human-Decision Latency (BL-600)

Some tickets wait on the swarm; some wait on the human. BL-600 pairs each
ApprovalRequested ask with its verdict and trends **ask→verdict latency**
per gate (`approve` / `amend`) so approval-queue wait is visible separately
from swarm velocity. **Measurement only** — never nudges, blocks, or alters
asks or human verdict recording.

### Derivation

`humanDecisionLatency.ts` is pure over paired timestamps:

| Input | Output |
|-------|--------|
| Ask + verdict (`verdictAtMs >= askAtMs`) | Decided `latencyMs` for that gate |
| Ask still pending | `openAgeMs` only — never folded into decided median/outliers |

Ask times come from existing stores (`approvalAskPostedAtMs` /
`telegram-approval-ask-messages.json` pairing). Aggregation reuses
`stageDwell.splitOutliers` for median + outlier honesty, then feeds
`computeTrend` (current / prior / delta / direction).

### Dependency direction (acyclic)

`humanDecisionLatency` imports `computeTrend` from `./trend` and
`splitOutliers` from `./stageDwell`. `trend.ts` must **not** re-export
decision-latency helpers — that back-edge was the standing acyclic bounce
this rematch closed.

### See Also

- **BL-594** — swarm-behaviour-trends epic.
- **BL-591** — ETA already treats blocked-on-human as non-velocity; this
  quantifies the human side.
- **BL-595** — human-loop reliability ledger (sibling `computeTrend` posture).
- **BL-096** — shared `computeTrend` / `TrendResult` framework.

## Handoff Latency (BL-602)

On mono-router, a handoff to a dormant role waits until the resident next
rotates into that role — so queue wait looks identical to “never sent”
without a metric. BL-602 pairs each parcel’s existing `enqueued_at` (send)
with `dequeued_at` (ready_for_next claim) and trends **enqueue→dequeue
latency** per recipient role. **Measurement only** — never changes
dispatch, rotation, or claim behaviour. Pairs with BL-596 stranding.

### Derivation

`handoffLatency.ts` is pure over header timestamp pairs:

| Input | Output |
|-------|--------|
| `enqueued_at` + `dequeued_at` (`dequeued >= enqueued`) | Processed `latencyMs` for that recipient |
| `enqueued_at` only (still in `new/` / claimed without stamp) | `openWaitMs` only — never folded into processed median/outliers |

Gather reads **master and worktree** role mailboxes (`new/`, `in_process/`,
`completed/`) — master-only would false-negative worktree seats.
Aggregation reuses `stageDwell.splitOutliers` for median + outlier honesty,
then feeds `computeTrend` (current / prior / delta / direction).

### Dependency direction (acyclic)

`handoffLatency` imports `computeTrend` from `./trend` and `splitOutliers`
from `./stageDwell`. `trend.ts` must **not** re-export handoff-latency
helpers — keep the metrics graph acyclic (same posture as BL-600 / BL-601).

### See Also

- **BL-594** — swarm-behaviour-trends epic.
- **BL-596** — rotation-cost / stranding (cross-read with handoff wait spikes).
- **BL-577** — flow watchdog (stall alarms vs this latency distribution).
- **BL-595** — human-loop reliability ledger (sibling `computeTrend` posture).
- **BL-096** — shared `computeTrend` / `TrendResult` framework.

## Behaviour-Trends Board (BL-603)

The BL-594 series (BL-595–BL-602 plus the global-tokens BL-605) are
producers; BL-603 is their surface. A Trends board on the LIVE holistic
console (the same token-authed bridge surface as the epic-reorder and
spec-tree screens, BL-572/BL-592) publishes all nine — never the static
backlog-dashboard PWA, which carries only git-SHA-derivable data and has
no bridge connectivity (Architecture rule 5). Consumer slice only: no
instrumentation added, read-only, no write path.

### Data flow

`GET /trends?token=...` (`bridgeServer.ts`) computes
`buildTrendsBoardState` (`bridgeState.ts`) fresh on every poll from the
series registry (`extension/src/metrics/trendsBoardRegistry.ts`), each
entry computed through the shared `computeTrend` framework
(`trend.ts`). `renderTrendsBoard` (`holisticUiHtml.ts`) maps over
whatever the payload carries into the console's `trendsBoard` section.
Registering a series is the only edit needed to publish it — neither the
payload builder nor the renderer holds a per-series list.

### The honesty rule

A series with nothing to plot reads **"no data yet"** and draws nothing —
never a zero, a flat line, or an interpolated point. This covers two
causes deliberately indistinguishable on screen: a producer that has not
landed a source reader (`human-decision-latency` at BL-603 mint), and one
that landed but recorded nothing for a stretch (`self-heal-events`, dark
between 2026-08-27 and 2026-08-29 after a merge, `2e37477ec`, silently
dropped the five production emit sites BL-597 shipped — restored by
BL-1273). Drawing a flat line at zero during a gap like that would read as
"the swarm never self-heals" — the exact false green BL-597 was built to
prevent.

## Flow Watchdog (BL-577)

The flow watchdog detects when a parcel stalls in any mailbox without progressing through the pipeline. Unlike the agent heartbeat (which monitors *liveness*) or message chasing (which monitors *delivery*), the flow watchdog monitors *flow* — whether work is moving through the handoff system.

### What it detects

Every parcel in any `.swarmforge/handoffs/` mailbox (both `new/` and `in_process/` directories, across all roles) must progress within a threshold. A parcel over the threshold — measured from its `enqueued_at` or `created_at` timestamp (never mtime) — triggers a flow-stall alarm regardless of:

- Role dormancy (even an idle role with no session can be rotated)
- Parcel type (git_handoff, note, broadcast)
- What any liveness signal says (a role can be "alive" per the agent heartbeat but still holding a stalled parcel)

The watchdog is **root-cause-agnostic**: it catches the class of flow stalls including causes not yet met, complementing focused fixes like BL-576 (aged-note actionability) that target specific root causes.

### Alarm channels

Flow watchdog alarms are **unsuppressable by design** — they go to Telegram (the operator's standing Operator topic) with a prescribed action verb, not to email where they could be muted by role dormancy. The alarm carries:

- **Parcel identity:** id, type, from → to
- **Age:** humanized elapsed time since enqueued
- **Location:** role name, `new/` or `in_process/`
- **Action verb:** what to do
  - `rotate` — the holding role has no live session; rotate it to process the parcel
  - `investigate` — the role is live but stalled in `in_process/`; check the pane for unexpected waits or loops
  - `expedite` — the role is live but the parcel sat in `new/` too long; nudge or wake it
- **Threshold (BL-827):** which resolved warn/escalate value fired and where it came from — appended as `Threshold <humanized> via <key>.`, `<key>` being the matched `from->to|type` / `*->to|type` spec or `global`. Since the fired threshold is now variable per route rather than one fixed pair, an alarm that omitted it could not be judged at 3am; the suffix is only ever absent when neither value was computed (a pre-BL-827 caller path).

### Configuration

Configure the flow watchdog in `swarmforge.conf`:

```
config flow_watchdog_warn_ms 900000           # global fallback warn at 15 minutes (default)
config flow_watchdog_escalate_ms 3600000      # global fallback escalate at 1 hour (default)
config flow_watchdog_calibration_ceiling_factor 4      # BL-827: calibrated warn may exceed the global warn by at most this factor (default)
config provider_outage_observe_min_interval_ms 60000   # BL-840: throttle for provider-outage evidence writes (default)
```

These are the **global fallback thresholds**. `provider_outage_observe_min_interval_ms`
is a separate knob governing how often a standing provider-outage banner is
recorded as evidence (see "Effective Age and Provider-Outage Evidence
(BL-650/BL-840)" below) — it does not affect warn/escalate thresholds
themselves. Per-spec thresholds are resolved outside `decide-tier` from a calibrated percentile table (`.swarmforge/daemon/flow-watchdog-thresholds.json`), keyed by the alarm's own `(from→to, type)` identity:

- **Warn tier (≈ p67):** fires when age exceeds the 67th percentile of historical mailbox residence for that spec — roughly the slowest third of cases
- **Escalate tier (≈ p97):** fires when age exceeds the 97th percentile — roughly the slowest 3%
- **Fallback chain:** exact `from->to|type` → `*->to|type` → the global conf pair above (when a key lacks ≥8 samples). A coarser `*->*|type` row mixing unrelated routes under one type would mis-calibrate dormant pipeline roles; as of BL-827 it is neither written nor consulted at any point in the chain — a value that would only ever have been dead data.
- **60s is a reject gate, not a floor (BL-835):** a route whose raw warn percentile falls below 60s has not earned a calibrated threshold — no exact/to-type entry is written for that key, and resolution falls through the chain above instead. Earlier behavior clamped a sub-60s raw percentile *up to* 60000ms and wrote it as if calibrated, which false-alarmed WARN on parcels sitting a healthy ~1 minute on fast hops (e.g. `QA→coordinator`); the gate rejects those keys outright rather than inventing a number the history never showed.
- **Calibration ceiling, reject not clamp (BL-827):** a calibrated warn percentile derives from whatever a route has actually been doing, so a hop that has been chronically slow for two weeks would otherwise teach the table that slow is normal and the alarm would quietly stop firing on it. `flow_watchdog_calibration_ceiling_factor` (default 4) bounds this: a raw warn percentile above `global warn × factor` is REJECTED — the key falls through to the global pair, which then fires — never clamped down to the ceiling. Same reject-not-clamp posture as the 60s floor above, and it composes with it: a key must clear the 60s floor AND stay under the ceiling to calibrate at all.
- **No suppression:** once a parcel reaches its resolved warn-tier age, one alarm fires; once it reaches escalate-tier age, one escalation fires. The same parcel never re-alarms between tiers, and dormancy of the holding role is never a reason to silence the alarm. Spec dependence changes which numbers are fed into `decide-tier`, never whether the alarm may speak.
- **Escalate is always strictly greater than warn (BL-827):** every resolved pair — calibrated or the global fallback itself — is sanitized so escalate is at least warn + 1ms, closing the case of a misconfigured `flow_watchdog_escalate_ms` sitting at or below `flow_watchdog_warn_ms`.

Malformed or absent config values fall back to the defaults above — the watchdog never disables itself. The percentile table is refreshed at most every 6 hours from each role's `completed/` and `abandoned/` audits.

### Durable state and dedup

The watchdog maintains `.swarmforge/daemon/flow-watchdog-state.json` keyed by parcel id:

```json
{
  "00_20260724T162845Z_000798_from_QA_to_documenter": {
    "tier": "warn",
    "alarmed_at": "2026-07-24T17:00:00Z",
    "snoozed": false
  }
}
```

**Dedup/pacing:** one alarm per parcel per tier — a parcel progresses (picked up, claimed, or reappears in another role's inbox) and its entry clears; no future re-alarms for that parcel even if it stalls again elsewhere.

**Snooze (read-only in this ticket):** if `snoozed: true`, the watchdog honors that state and does not alarm until the snooze is cleared by human action (a future slice wiring the snooze writer).

**Ambulance mode's sync deliver path, busy-resident rotate gate, and engage target are closed to the first live-run gaps (BL-691).** BL-655 wired the hold into daemon poll delivery and dequeue, but `swarm_handoff.bb`'s synchronous `handoff_inject_lib/deliver-parcel!` never consulted `ambulance-lib/parcel-held?` — a non-patient parcel could land in `inbox/new/` with a sync `HANDOFF DELIVERED` while the hold was engaged. That path now uses the same predicate; held parcels stay byte-identical in the sender outbox until release. Mono-router chase may rotate a busy resident to the role whose `inbox/new/` holds patient mail (`:ignore-busy?` when patient mail waits) — ambulance exists so the patient interrupts; cooldown / once-per-sweep budget unchanged. CLI and Telegram `engage` refuse any patient not in `backlog/active/`, naming the folder and instructing promote-before-engage (never auto-promote), closing the silent deadlock of engaging a `paused/` ticket. How-to: `docs/how-to/BL-691-ambulance-mode-workflow-gaps-from-bl688-live-run.md` (updates BL-655).

**Ambulance hold composes into the same snooze channel (BL-679):** a parcel held by an engaged [ambulance mode](../how-to/BL-655-ambulance-mode-the-hold.md) is muted through this exact mechanism — `evaluate-parcel-tier` (the caller that assembles `decide-tier`'s input map) ORs the parcel's ambulance-held state in alongside any pre-existing human-ack snooze, so `decide-tier` itself gains no new branch and the design guarantee above (five allowed input keys) is untouched. The ambulance ticket's own parcels are never held, so they are never muted by this path.

### Where it runs

The flow watchdog is a pure decision core (`swarmforge/scripts/flow_watchdog_lib.bb`, unit-tested) driven from the handoff daemon's (`handoffd.bb`) existing sweep loop. It:

1. Enumerates all roles from `roles.tsv`
2. Scans each role's `:new` and `:in_process` mailbox directories
3. For each parcel, extracts age and decides: `:none` | `:warn` | `:escalate`
4. Emits alarms to `.swarmforge/operator/telegram-reply-outbox.jsonl` and logs the state

**Design guarantee:** the decision core's input carries no `role`, `type`, or `dormancy` field — only age and tier state — so the no-suppression contract is structurally enforced and unit-tested: a test asserts that the allowed input keys exclude any that could trigger role/type/dormancy-based exemptions.

### What the watchdog doesn't cover (blind spots)

1. **Handoffd daemon itself is dead AND its supervisor is broken** — the watchdog runs inside handoffd, so a dead daemon detects nothing. A dead handoffd_supervisor breaks the daemon-death alarm chain; this ticket adds no new supervision layer for the supervisor itself.

2. **Telegram bridge or front desk is parked** — alarms are durably queued in the outbox (`.swarmforge/operator/telegram-reply-outbox.jsonl`) but undelivered until the bridge recovers. The daily briefing stays the backstop narrative layer for undelivered alarms.

3. **Work never enqueued as a parcel** — a dispatch gap (work that exists but never became a handoff in any mailbox). The dispatch-gap sweep (BL-222) owns that detection. An active ticket whose `assigned_to` is absent/blank/`none`/`unassigned` is *not* a dispatch-gap candidate — BL-1093 routes those to the unassigned-active coordinator nudge so they are not auto-routed as `to: none`.

4. **QA landed on origin/main but never notified the coordinator** — the ticket stays in `backlog/active/` with a *complete* dispatch trail, so dispatch-gap and unassigned-active both stay silent. The `landed-but-open` sweep (BL-1104) owns that detection: subject-anchored QA approval on the main ref, no Close, one nudge to QA to resend the coordinator notify (observe only).

### Operator workflow

1. Receive a flow-watchdog alarm in your Operator Telegram topic
2. Note the action verb and the holding role
3. **Rotate:** if the role is dormant, rotate it to `ready_for_next.sh` to process the parcel
4. **Investigate:** if the role is live but in `in_process/`, check the pane — it may be awaiting a question, blocked on a menu, or in a rare internal loop
5. **Expedite:** if the role is live but the parcel is in `new/`, nudge or wake it (the chase daemon already does this, but an explicit nudge helps)
6. Once the parcel is claimed and progresses, the watchdog's state entry clears and no further alarms fire for that parcel

### Effective Age and Provider-Outage Evidence (BL-650/BL-840)

`flow_watchdog_lib.bb`'s `evaluate-effective-age` is the active-time clock
the sweep feeds into `decide-tier` instead of raw wall-clock age. It
subtracts two independent interval classes from a waiting parcel's span:
BL-823's availability-ledger intervals (`control-pause`, `swarm-stop`) and
BL-650's own `provider-outage-intervals` (gap-grouped at
`default-provider-outage-max-gap-ms`, 10 minutes). Both classes were built
and hardened at the pure-function level by BL-650/BL-823; BL-840 is what
supplies the second class with a real, production evidence source —
`flow-watchdog-sweep!` previously called `evaluate-effective-age` with no
`:provider-outage-evidence-for` adapter at all, so it silently defaulted to
`(constantly [])` and no parcel had ever had a millisecond of provider outage
subtracted, live false-alarm source and all.

**The evidence source rides an observation the daemon already makes.**
`observe-standing-role-auth!` already captures ~20 lines of every live
role's pane scrollback on every chase sweep for BL-536's auth-class
observer; BL-840 feeds the SAME snapshot (no second tmux capture) to
`observe-pane-provider-outage!`, which records a line whenever the text
classifies `:unavailable` per `classify-provider-error`
(`agent_runtime_lib.bb`, cross-language twin
`extension/src/swarm/providerErrorTaxonomy.ts` — the two are asserted for
parity and must stay in parity). The `:unavailable` pattern was extended to
recognize `529` / `overloaded_error` as part of this ticket: the incident
text that prompted the human's original outage-subtraction ruling
(`"API Error: 529 {...\"type\":\"overloaded_error\"}"`) classified `:unknown`
before this fix, so wiring the adapter alone would not have caught it.

**Storage** — `provider_outage_evidence_lib.bb` mirrors
`availability_ledger_lib.bb`'s shape exactly: one lib, sole writer and sole
reader of `.swarmforge/telemetry/provider-outage-<YYYY-MM>.jsonl`. Each line
records the observation timestamp, the provider, the observing role, and the
observed text.

**Throttled write** — at most one line per role per
`provider_outage_observe_min_interval_ms` (`swarmforge.conf`, default
`60000`; a positive-integer knob, any other value degrading to the
default). 60s sits well inside the 10-minute gap-grouping window, so a
standing multi-hour outage banner still reconstructs as one contiguous
interval rather than one line per sweep.

**Attribution is by provider, not by pane.** An outage observed on one
role's pane is applied to every role configured with that same provider
(the existing BL-208 role→provider lookup), never only to the role whose
pane produced the observation — the load-bearing case under mono-router,
where only the resident has a standing pane and every dormant role's
parcel would otherwise go unsubtracted.

**Fail closed.** A missing, empty, or unparseable evidence file — or any
error reading it — subtracts nothing; wall-clock effective age is the safe
fallback, and the sweep completes without error. This is subtraction only:
there is no alarm-suppression path, and an outage never mutes what the
watchdog would otherwise say.

- **BL-839** — Master-Checkout Drift Alarm: a different sweep in the same `handoffd.bb` cadence, reusing this same Telegram Operator outbox, but alarming on a different question (does the master checkout's own working tree still match `main`, not parcel age) — see [the runbook](../how-to/BL-839-master-checkout-drift-alarm.md)
- **BL-891** — Master-Main Reconcile Sweep: another sweep in the same cadence, mirroring BL-356's push-sweep in the opposite direction — merges `origin/main` forward into the master checkout's local `main` ref, surfacing a `note` to the coordinator (not this Telegram alarm channel) only when a dirty or untracked path actually overlaps a path the incoming merge would change (BL-919 narrowed this from a blanket any-dirt gate) — see [the runbook](../how-to/BL-891-master-main-reconcile-sweep.md)

## Portable Agent Memory Transfer (BL-1177)

First slice of epic BL-1176 (`agent-memory-transfer`). When a **same-role
model swap** replaces the outgoing agent, continuity must survive without
shipping a vendor-opaque session blob as the only artifact. BL-1177 defines a
**schema-versioned portable payload** and a pure **capture / inject API** in
`extension/src/tools/agentMemoryTransfer.ts`.

### Payload schema (v1)

| Field | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `kind: 'portable-agent-memory-payload'` | Discriminator — never a vendor blob alone |
| `schemaVersion` | Currently `1` (`AGENT_MEMORY_PAYLOAD_SCHEMA_VERSION`) |
| `role` | Normalized recipient role (must match inject target) |
| `continuitySummary` | Transcript / session summary for the incoming seat |
| `openParcelContext.openParcelIds` | Sorted, de-duplicated open parcel ids |
| `handoffPack` (optional) | Structured handoff continuity bag |
| `toolStatePointers` (optional) | Named tool-state references |

### Capture

`capture(outgoingState)` wraps pure `aggregateCapturePayload` over named
inputs (`transcriptSummary`, `openParcelIds`, optional `handoffPack` /
`toolStatePointers`). Unit-testable without a live agent — no filesystem or
vendor session read in this slice.

### Inject (fail-closed)

`inject(role, rawPayload)` validates with `validatePortablePayload`, checks
role match, and returns either:

- `{ ok: true, openParcelContext, continuitySummary, pretendedContinuity: false }`, or
- `{ ok: false, signal, pretendedContinuity: false }` for missing, malformed,
  or role-mismatched payloads.

**Never** silently pretends continuity on bad input.

### Hot-swap wiring (BL-1178)

`switchRoleModel` (`backendSwitch.ts`) builds outgoing capture state from open
handoff parcels, calls `attemptSameRoleModelSwitch`, and only respawns when
inject succeeds. Trial start/end reuse `runTrialBoundaryMemoryTransfer` with
the same fail-closed contract. How-to:
`docs/how-to/BL-1178-wire-agent-memory-into-hot-swap-and-trial.md`.

### BoB starting cast (BL-1181)

Model Steward cherry-picks a starting lineup: `bob_starting_cast_lib.bb`
exports one top certified `(provider, model)` per role (mixed vendors allowed).
Apply goes through ModelFactory assignment overlay or pack model apply —
`assertKnownApplyPath` rejects any third route. When apply changes a role's
model, `applyBobCast` runs capture/inject (BL-1177) before writing the overlay.
How-to: `docs/how-to/BL-1181-bob-starting-cast-cherry-pick-apply.md`.

### Out of scope (BL-1177 API slice)

- Cross-vendor adapters — **BL-1179**
- Cross-role memory merge

### See Also

- **BL-1176** — agent-memory-transfer epic
- **BL-235** — per-role model dropdown + respawn (consumer path for BL-1178)
- **BL-669** — outage-driven seat failover via Model Steward (different continuity problem)

## Per-Agent Lifecycle Control

A core capability: managing individual agents without disrupting the swarm.

### Respawn a single agent

- Kills only that agent's backend process; its worktree and branch are left intact
- Relaunches the configured backend in the same worktree
- The rest of the swarm continues uninterrupted
- Useful when one agent is stuck, looping, or has drifted

**Auto-pickup on launch:** when an agent (re)spawns, it scans the message store for messages addressed to it still in `sent` or `received` and resumes them automatically — so a respawned receiver picks up its pending handoffs without waiting to be chased again.

Respawn replaces the *process* itself — the orchestrator kills the old backend PID and re-issues the launch for that role in the same worktree.

### Change an agent's model on the fly (BL-235, M5 — Claude-backed roles only)

**Landed slice:** a per-tile model dropdown, shown only for Claude-backed roles, lets you pick a different model for that one role. The extension rewrites that role's `.swarmforge/launch/<role>.claude-settings.json` `model` field in place (every other field untouched) and respawns just that role's pane via the existing single-agent respawn — no other agent is affected, `swarmforge.conf` and the launch script itself are never touched, and the swap is gone on the next fresh swarm launch (the settings file is regenerated then). Because role prompts and the constitution are re-read at launch, the respawned agent picks up the new model and resumes its in-process work normally. The dropdown's model catalog is the same versioned list `pricingTable.ts` uses for cost estimation — one list, not a second copy that could drift.

**Pricing table correctness and roster coverage (BL-627).** `extension/src/metrics/pricingTable.ts` is the single Anthropic list-price table (`PRICING_TABLE_VERSION` bumped on every rate change). BL-627 corrected wrong Opus/Fable/Haiku rates, added `claude-opus-5`, and exported `checkPricingCoverage` / `collectReferencedClaudeModels`: every bare `claude-*` id referenced by `swarmforge.conf`, `swarmforge/packs/*.conf`, and `.swarmforge/launch/*.claude-settings.json` must have a table entry or the check fails naming the offender — never silent zero attribution for a model in service. Provider-prefixed OpenRouter/Mistral/etc. ids are outside this table's charter. No cron or pricing scraper (operator rejected that shape): rate accuracy stays a human/agent verification against the published page. `claude-sonnet-5` keeps published list $3/$15; its introductory $2/$10 through 2026-08-31 is deliberately not modeled (time-bounded rates stay out of this data table).

**Deferred (not yet built):** switching a role to a *different backend* (e.g. Claude → Codex, or to an in-process `vscode.lm` runtime) — see the note below and Agent Backends. That needs a TypeScript launch-command builder porting `swarmforge.sh`'s per-agent-CLI case-statement (five different CLIs' exact flags, including a documented past secrets-handling incident), which does not exist yet; a same-agent model switch needed none of that porting, so it shipped first as the safe narrow slice.

> **Doc-accuracy note:** the "Agent Backends" section below describes a `vscode.lm` in-process runtime and a backend-agnostic `InteractiveProcess` abstraction as already-built. As of BL-235, that TypeScript-side abstraction and runtime do not exist in `extension/src` — `vscode.lm` appears nowhere in the codebase outside this aspirational prose. Only Claude-backed model switching (above) is real today; treat the rest of "Agent Backends" as the target design, not shipped behavior, until a future ticket lands it.

## Email Notifications for Needs-Human Events

When an agent needs human input (a question, permission prompt, or approval gate), the extension can email you with the agent's request, including a link back to the swarm session. This is useful when you step away from the editor — you get notified remotely and can jump back to answer.

### Configuration

Email notifications are **off by default**. To enable:

1. Set `swarmforge.notify.email.to` to your email address
2. Set `RESEND_API_KEY` environment variable (or VS Code secret `swarmforge.resendApiKey`) with a valid [Resend](https://resend.com) API key
   - Resend is a lightweight transactional email service; free tier covers typical usage
   - The onboarding sender (`onboarding@resend.dev`) delivers only to account owners — use a verified domain address for production

Optional tuning:

- `swarmforge.notify.email.from` — sender address (default: `onboarding@resend.dev`)
- `swarmforge.notify.email.graceSeconds` — how long (seconds) a needs-human state must persist before the first email (default: 60)
- `swarmforge.notify.email.cooldownSeconds` — minimum time between emails for the same role (default: 600)

### When notifications fire

An email is sent when:
- An agent's needs-human state first persists for `graceSeconds` without being answered
- OR the agent remains needs-human for another `cooldownSeconds` after the previous email

A genuinely **stuck/wedged agent** (no progress despite chasing — see Heartbeat & Watchdog) is alerted independently of whether the tiled agent panel is open: this notifier runs on its own extension-host interval, not the panel's poll loop, so closing the panel while the swarm keeps running does not silence stuck-agent alerts. A **question or permission prompt** (the agent is waiting on live pane content) still requires the panel to have been open to be captured, since the panel's pane tailer is the only reader of that content. In the rare case where a role is a captured question AND later escalates to stuck in the same window, you may receive two separate emails instead of one merged one — a redundant alert, never a missed one.

### What the email contains

- **The agent's role** — which role is asking
- **The question or permission snippet** — the exact text the agent is waiting on (if captured)
- **A session link** — a direct link back to the swarm panel in VS Code, pre-opened
- **The run name/item** — which work item triggered the notification

This lets you read the request on your phone and decide whether to jump back to your desk to respond, or continue what you're doing.
