## `project.prompt` and `engineering.prompt` — Contracts

These, plus the onboarding scope contract below (BL-262), are the only files the swarm reads from the target. `project.prompt`/`engineering.prompt` are intentionally simple plain text; the onboarding contract below is structured YAML plus a generated legible view, so the target still has no forge-schema dependency on anything but that one small shape.

### `project.prompt` (target repo)
```
# Project
<what this project does and why>

# Goals for this swarm run
<what you want built or fixed — updated before each run>

# Constraints
<anything the swarm must not touch or break>
```

### `engineering.prompt` (target repo)
```
# Tech Stack
<languages, frameworks, runtimes>

# Conventions
<naming, folder structure, testing approach>

# Architecture rules
<patterns to follow, anti-patterns to avoid>
```

The `Initialize Target` command scaffolds these with sensible defaults so the developer only fills in the blanks.

### The onboarding scope contract (BL-262, slice 1) — survey, propose, agree, fail-closed gate

A separate, higher-level contract sits above these two files and above the per-ticket acceptance contract (`docs/tutorials/Onboarding-New-Project.md`'s section 3): the overall mandate for what the swarm will and will not do on a target, which the swarm surveys and proposes and the operator must agree before any ticket for that target dispatches. `proposeContractFromSurvey` (`extension/src/onboarding/contractSurvey.ts`) is a pure function mapping already-gathered `RepoSurveyFacts` (languages, layout, README, seed vision, initial backlog — the survey itself is swarm/agent behavior, not this function's job) into a `ProposedContract` (scope, out-of-scope, boundaries, initial-backlog summary, `agreement: proposed`). `node extension/out/tools/propose-onboarding-contract.js <target-repo-path> <survey-facts-json-path>` runs it and scaffolds + commits the hybrid artifact into the target via `initializeTargetContract` (`extension/src/config/targetBootstrap.ts`, generalized from the same idempotent plan/write/commit seam `initializeTargetRepo` already uses): `.swarmforge/contract.yaml` is the structured source, `CONTRACT.md` a generated legible view rendered from the same source so the two can never diverge (`extension/src/onboarding/contractView.ts`). The operator flips `agreement` to `agreed` once satisfied (or back to `pending` to re-open scope and re-hold the gate). Before every promotion of a paused ticket into `backlog/active/`, the coordinator runs `node extension/out/tools/onboarding-contract-gate.js <target-repo-path>` (`swarmforge/roles/coordinator.prompt`'s Onboarding Contract Gate section); `evaluateBuildStartGate` (`extension/src/onboarding/buildStartGate.ts`) is fail-closed — only `agreed` allows dispatch, and missing/malformed/`proposed`/`pending` all hold with a reason, never a default-allow (BL-099 missing-data posture), so a target with no contract yet simply reads as `missing` until surveyed and proposed. This does not replace or duplicate per-ticket `human_approval` — it gates whether any ticket can start, not what each ticket contains. Slice 1 (this) ships survey → propose → single agree/hold.

**The iterative negotiate loop (BL-344).** A single-round proposal is a take-it-or-edit-it-yourself, not a negotiation, so `negotiate-onboarding-contract.js` adds the request-changes → revise → re-propose loop on top of slice 1's own artifact and gate, unchanged: `node extension/out/tools/negotiate-onboarding-contract.js <target-repo-path> object "<objection text>"` revises the committed contract IN RESPONSE to the operator's own words (`reviseContractFromObjection`, `extension/src/onboarding/contractNegotiation.ts` — keyword-driven: "remove/exclude X" moves a matching scope entry to out-of-scope, "add/include X" adds a new scope entry carrying the operator's own text, anything else is recorded as a new boundary, so the objection is always reflected somewhere, never silently dropped), commits the revision, and appends a durable round record (`{round, objection, changedFields}`) to `.swarmforge/onboarding-negotiation.jsonl`. `node extension/out/tools/negotiate-onboarding-contract.js <target-repo-path> approve` flips `agreement` to `agreed` and commits — the first programmatic way to agree; previously the only path was the hand-edit described above. The loop is bounded at `DEFAULT_MAX_NEGOTIATION_ROUNDS` (5): an objection attempted after the budget is exhausted is refused and ends the negotiation without approving anything, while approval remains valid at any point up to and including immediately after the last round in budget (state is reconstructed fresh from the contract's own `agreement` field, the round log, and an explicit terminal marker on each separate invocation, since rounds can be hours apart). The build-start gate is unchanged — a revision is still just `agreement: proposed`, so it holds through every round exactly as in the single-round case.

**Generated target prompts (BL-269, child slice of the BL-262 family).** The same survey that proposes the contract also proposes real content for the two files immediately above — `proposePromptsFromSurvey` (`extension/src/onboarding/promptProposal.ts`) maps the identical `RepoSurveyFacts` into a `ProposedPrompts` (`project.prompt`/`engineering.prompt` text, mirroring those files' own section headers, populated from the seed vision/initial backlog and the surveyed languages/layout/README rather than `Initialize Target`'s generic angle-bracket placeholder). These two files ride the SAME agreement marker as the contract — one agreement, whole artifact set: `initializeTargetPrompts` (`extension/src/config/targetBootstrap.ts`) checks the contract's `evaluateBuildStartGate` decision and withholds both files (writes nothing, `withheld: true`) while it's `hold` (proposed/pending/missing/malformed), releasing them for commit only once `allow` (agreed). `node extension/out/tools/propose-onboarding-prompts.js <target-repo-path> <survey-facts-json-path>` is safe to re-run at any point in the negotiation — a no-op until agreement, the actual write+commit once agreed.

**Verbosity is negotiated into the contract, not fixed (BL-382).** The human's own ask: some users want precise/long agent messages, others concise. Rather than a global config knob, verbosity rides the same negotiated contract as scope/boundaries — `ProposedContract` gains an optional `verbosity` field restricted to a closed enum, `VERBOSITY_LEVELS = ['concise', 'normal', 'detailed']` (`extension/src/onboarding/contractTypes.ts`), following the same posture as `CONTRACT_AGREEMENT_STATES` immediately above it in that file — never free text, which would be unvalidatable and would splice arbitrary content straight into a generated prompt. `proposePromptsFromSurvey` takes an optional raw verbosity term and resolves it via `resolveVerbosity` — a `KNOWN_VALUES` lookup, never a passthrough or a binary `===` with an else-branch (the shared-cell mutation hazard the engineering article's Gherkin rule calls out) — appending an explicit `Be <verbosity> in your responses and explanations.` instruction to both generated `project.prompt` and `engineering.prompt`. An offered value outside the enum is refused outright. A contract that never mentions verbosity at all — every contract negotiated before this term existed, including this repo's own agreed `CONTRACT.md` — resolves to `DEFAULT_VERBOSITY` (`normal`) rather than crashing or leaving a blank instruction. The real CLI, `propose-onboarding-prompts.js`, reads the target's `.swarmforge/contract.yaml` (`parseContractYaml`, `extension/src/onboarding/contractView.ts`, which now carries a present `verbosity` through the parse rather than dropping it) and passes the negotiated term into `proposePromptsFromSurvey`, so an agreed verbosity actually reaches the generated `project.prompt`/`engineering.prompt` end to end, not just in the pure functions' own unit tests. Related, not duplicated: BL-383 (sequenced after this one) reads the same contract field to drive the Telegram front desk's own human-facing reply verbosity — the other half of the same human ask, where the human actually feels the preference. **QA bounce, same ticket:** `initializeTargetPrompts` reused the existence-only idempotency `writeAndCommitBootstrapPlan` gives every other bootstrap artifact, so once a target's `project.prompt`/`engineering.prompt` had been generated once, a later change of mind on verbosity (object → revise → re-approve → re-run) never reached the already-materialized files — the re-run silently skipped them. It now writes unconditionally once the contract is agreed, the same posture as BL-344's `updateTargetContract`, relying on `writeFilesAndCommit`'s own `git diff --cached --quiet` no-op check (decided before ever invoking `git commit`, since git's "nothing to commit" message text varies when the target repo has any other untracked path) so an unchanged regeneration still produces no spurious commit.

**Onboarding provisions the target's own Telegram bot and group (BL-380).** So the contract negotiation loop above can eventually move to Telegram (BL-381), each onboarded target gets its own bot and forum group — never a shared one: `getUpdates` long-polling is scoped to the bot token, and its update offset is per-token and global across chats, so two targets sharing a token would 409 on concurrent polls and silently steal each other's updates. `provisionTelegramChannel` (`extension/src/onboarding/telegramChannelProvisioning.ts`) is the pure decision core wired by a thin CLI, `node extension/out/tools/provision-onboarding-telegram-channel.js <target-repo-path> <bot-token> <bot-username> <host-secrets-file-path>` (`extension/src/tools/provision-onboarding-telegram-channel.ts`), reusing `telegramClient.ts`'s existing `createForumTopic` rather than a second Telegram client. The Bot API has no create-bot or create-group/enable-topics method, so one irreducible manual step per target remains — BotFather, group creation, enabling Topics, adding the bot as admin — which the command reduces to printed steps plus a `t.me/<bot>?startgroup=true` deep link; the human is never asked to type a chat id, because a brand-new per-target bot has seen no chat before onboarding, so `decideChannelDetection` treats the first chat its own `getUpdates` reports as the target's group and opens a "Contract negotiation" topic there. `createNegotiationTopic` is only ever called once detection reports ready, so a half-finished setup (bot exists, group not yet Topics-enabled or the bot not yet added) reports not-ready rather than opening a topic against an unready chat — safe to re-run. Storage splits by sensitivity, mirroring the existing local-engineering secrets rule: the bot token is host-side only (`telegramChannelSecretStore.ts`, one entry per target repo path, `isPathInside` — shared with `recruiter/secretStore.ts` via the new `util/pathContainment.ts` — structurally refusing a secrets path inside the target's own working tree), while the non-secret chat id and negotiation topic id are persisted into the target's own `.swarmforge/operator/telegram-channel.json` (`telegramChannelStore.ts`). **QA bounce, same ticket:** the first cut's `getUpdates` adapter discarded `GetUpdatesResult`'s own `success`/`error` and handed `provisionTelegramChannel` only the bare updates array, so a bad or revoked bot token, a network error, or a rate limit read as the exact same `{ready: false}` as the legitimate "the human hasn't finished the manual setup step yet" case — indistinguishable to whoever is running onboarding, who would then re-check a group/Topics/admin setup they'd already done correctly, indefinitely. `getUpdates` now returns the same `GetUpdatesResult` shape `telegramClient.ts` already produces, and a fetch failure returns `{ready: false, error: ...}` — present only on a genuine failure, absent on the legitimate not-ready-yet case — mirroring how the sibling `createNegotiationTopic` adapter in the same module already surfaces its own failure.

**The contract negotiation runs over Telegram, not only files/CLI (BL-381).** The epic's wiring ticket: BL-380 above provisions the channel and topic, BL-344's `negotiate-onboarding-contract.ts` (`runObject`/`runApprove`) already runs the rounds and durable log — this ticket is what actually calls them from a live Telegram poll instead of leaving both pure modules dark. `negotiationTelegramRouting.ts` is the pure per-update decision: reuses `telegramFrontDeskBotCore`'s own `isFromMyChat`/`isFromPrincipal` guards (the BL-379 authorized-sender check) and adds only the negotiation-topic-id check and the objection-vs-agreement classification on top — `isAgreementText` matches the reply against a closed pattern, never a bare substring, so "I agree with most of this but remove the PWA work" is routed as an objection, never misread as approval (see BL-442 below for the pattern's exact shape and a fixed misclassification). `negotiationTelegramRelay.ts` is the adapter-injected relay core (unit tested against fake adapters); the thin, untested-boundary CLI is `node extension/out/tools/relay-onboarding-negotiation-telegram.js <target-repo-path> <host-secrets-file-path> post-proposal|poll`. `post-proposal` posts the current `contract.yaml` into the negotiation topic via `formatContractForTelegram` (a plainer, Telegram-safe rendering of the same field order as `contractView.ts`'s `CONTRACT.md`, never a second contract vocabulary) and is idempotent via a marker file, exactly like BL-380's own provisioning step. `poll` requires `TELEGRAM_PRINCIPAL_USER_ID` (`post-proposal` does not), reads one `getUpdates` batch, routes each update through `negotiationTelegramRouting.ts`, and for an objection calls the real `runObject` (posting the revision back into the topic) or for an agreement calls the real `runApprove` (which is what flips the contract to `agreed` and releases `buildStartGate.ts` — the "real writer" the ticket's own notes insist on, never an assumed sibling slice). Every round still lands in the same `.swarmforge/onboarding-negotiation.jsonl` the CLI form writes, so scenario 04's restart-survival holds regardless of which form carried a given round; the relay's own poll cursor is a second, narrower piece of restart state it alone owns (`.swarmforge/operator/negotiation-relay-offset.json`), so a restarted relay never re-applies an already-handled reply as a duplicate round. A `postToTopic` delivery failure logs and moves on rather than throwing — the round is already durably written by then, so a failed notification can only delay the human seeing the revision, never lose or duplicate a round.

**QA/architect bounce, same ticket: `poll` needed a live, unattended trigger.** A one-shot `poll` action was reachable only by a human running the CLI by hand — QA bounced the ticket because nothing in the live swarm ever called it, so an objection or agreement in the topic could sit unseen indefinitely. A new `poll-loop` action runs `poll` forever (paced by Telegram's own long-poll, writing a heartbeat each cycle), supervised per target by `negotiation_relay_supervisor.bb` + `launch_negotiation_relay.sh` — spawn/crash-detect/bounded-restart/heartbeat-stall/give-up-escalation, reusing `front_desk_supervisor.bb`'s own pure state machine (`front_desk_supervisor_lib.bb`) wholesale rather than a second implementation. The architect then bounced it again: the launcher existed but still needed a human to run it as a third manual step after `post-proposal`. `post-proposal` now spawns the supervisor automatically (detached, via an injectable `LaunchRelaySupervisorFn`, mirroring `swarmLauncher.ts`'s own `SwarmSpawnFn`/`defaultSwarmSpawn` DI shape) the moment the proposal is posted — the first moment a human could reply — closing the loop with no further manual step; a target repo under the system temp dir never triggers a real spawn regardless (`isTestFixtureRoot`, mirroring `daemon_alarm_lib.bb`'s own `test-fixture-root?`), and `poll`/`poll-loop` both stay directly runnable for manual recovery.

**The front desk's own replies follow the agreed verbosity too, not just the generated agent prompts (BL-383).** BL-382 feeds the negotiated verbosity into the agents' generated `project.prompt`/`engineering.prompt` — useful, but not what the human actually reads; the messages he reads are the front-desk Operator's own replies on Telegram, a different codebase (Babashka, not TypeScript), so this is its own slice reading the same field BL-382 defines (`depends_on: [BL-382]`, never a second vocabulary). `operator_lib.bb`'s `front-desk-reply-prompt` (the pure function that composes the front-desk Operator's whole self-contained prompt, BL-334's `--tools ""` boundary) now takes an additional `:verbosity` key and prepends a `Be <verbosity> in your responses and explanations.` directive — the exact same wording `promptProposal.ts`'s own instruction uses, so the negotiated term reads as one property felt in two places, not two independently-invented ones. `resolve-front-desk-verbosity` re-implements BL-382's closed three-value set (`concise`/`normal`/`detailed`, defaulting to `normal`) as its own small literal — a Babashka script can't import a TypeScript constant, and a three-value set isn't worth a cross-language sharing mechanism — but is written to never accept a raw value BL-382's own `resolveVerbosity` would reject; an absent or unrecognized term both resolve to the same default. `compose-front-desk-reply-prompt` is the one seam that reads a target's raw `.swarmforge/contract.yaml` text and builds the full prompt from it; `operator_runtime.bb`'s real front-desk launch path calls this same seam, and so does this feature's own acceptance steps, so the acceptance run proves the live composition rather than a re-derivation that could silently drift from it. The contract file is re-read fresh on every front-desk wake — never cached — which is what makes a re-negotiated verbosity take effect on the very next reply with no swarm restart: the front-desk Operator is already disposable and re-prompted per event (BL-334), so this restart-free property falls out of the existing design rather than needing new machinery, but is pinned by its own scenario precisely because a build that read the value once at launch and cached it would otherwise pass every other scenario while silently breaking that property.

**The Onboarder: a standing conversational agent guiding a human through onboarding, starting with prerequisites (BL-590, slice 1 of 3).** Sections above ship a full onboarding toolchain (survey/propose/negotiate/provision-channel/relay/gate) but no orchestrator and no persona — a human ran each CLI by hand, in order. This slice is the first of three that close that gap: a standing "Onboarding" topic (`ONBOARDING_SUBJECT_ID`, `decideEnsureOnboardingTopicAction`, `extension/src/tools/telegramTopicDecisions.ts`) in the PRIMARY swarm's own group, ensured-or-reused exactly like every other standing topic (Backlog, Control, Babysitter) and **never per-target** — one topic reused across every onboarding, since per-target identity lives in the onboarder's own state, not the topic. Inbound routing (`decideOnboardingReplyAction`, `telegramFrontDeskBotCore.ts`) is attempted last of all the topic side-channels and never reaches the front-desk SUP path. The onboarder does **not** run a second Telegram poller — unlike the per-target negotiation relay (BL-381), its message handling runs in-process inside the front-desk bot's own single poller (`attemptOnboardingTopicDelivery`); `onboarder_supervisor.bb` + `launch_onboarder.sh` (registered in `start_ancillary_services.sh`/`stop_ancillary_services.sh`, mirroring `negotiation_relay_supervisor.bb`'s spawn/crash-detect/bounded-restart shape) supervise only an outbound topic-*reconcile* loop, which is not subject to the one-poller-per-token restriction because it only calls outbound Bot API methods. The prerequisites state machine (`extension/src/onboarding/onboarderState.ts`, pure and clock-injected) covers `needs-target → checking-prerequisites → prerequisites-ready`: posting a repo URL opens (or, via `findInFlightStateForTarget`, resumes) a per-target state, keyed by `normalizeTargetRepoUrl` so scheme/`.git`/trailing-slash aliases of the same target collapse onto the same in-flight onboarding rather than silently overwriting verified progress with a fresh one (an architect-bounced defect, fixed). Five guide-and-verify steps — `toolchain`, `github-access`, `fork-clone`, `target-repo`, `bot-token` — each carry the exact command for the target host and name the verification the human must paste back (`PREREQUISITE_STEPS`); a step advances only on a passing `verifyPrerequisiteStep` match against required/failure markers, never on a bare completion claim (`isBareDoneClaim`, whole-message-anchored so a real verification paste is never swept in). The `bot-token` step explicitly instructs a NEW, dedicated token and forbids reusing the primary's (the BL-622 one-token-one-poller invariant, enforced here at guidance level). `pause`/`proceed` controls (`classifyControl`) hold and resume the flow; state persists per target (`onboarderStateStore.ts`, atomic write, one file per target keyed by a normalized-URL slug + digest) so an onboarder restart resumes at the same step with prior verifications intact. Declared invariant (BL-633): every durable write is idempotent under redelivery of the same Telegram update — proven by a coder-authored property test (architect bounce, non-vacuous generator reach) after four of the slice's six architect send-backs circled exactly this property without it ever being stated. **Scope, stated plainly:** this slice ends at `prerequisites-ready` and announces that the survey phase comes next; slice 2 (BL-624, immediately below) is what actually runs survey/propose/negotiate/gate from there. Neither slice claims to launch a swarm on the target host, which the human still does by hand per the human ruling above (slice 3, BL-625, immediately below, is the prompts/launch handoff — the state machine's terminal slice).

**The Onboarder, slice 2: survey through an agreed, gated contract on the onboarder's own clone (BL-624, slice 2 of 3).** Picks up exactly where slice 1 leaves off — `prerequisites-ready` — and drives the do-for-you phase to `contract-agreed`, all inside the same Onboarding topic and the same per-target state slice 1 already persists, through a small control vocabulary this slice adds: `proceed` (start the survey, or later agree the contract), `show-me` (post the current proposed contract, no state change) and `change-this <objection>` (a real negotiation object round). `contractPhaseRelay.ts` is the pure decision (`decideContractPhaseAction`) plus its adapter-injected execution (`runContractPhaseAction`), mirroring `negotiationTelegramRelay.ts`'s own split; `onboarderContractPhaseRouter.ts` is the thin seam that tries slice 1's existing, unmodified `handleOnboardingMessage` first and only falls through to this slice's own phases (`prerequisites-ready`/`contract-proposed`/`negotiating`; `contract-agreed` is terminal here, BL-625's territory) when nothing checking-prerequisites is active. No CLI is reimplemented: `proceed` from `prerequisites-ready` clones the target with this box's own GitHub access, runs the existing survey and `propose-onboarding-contract.js`'s own `proposeContractFromSurvey`, and posts the result; `change-this`/a later `proceed` route through the exact SAME `negotiate-onboarding-contract.ts` `runObject`/`runApprove` the CLI and Telegram-relay forms already call (via a shared `negotiationOutcomeAdapters.ts` wrapper, cleaner-deduped out of the CLI's own translation code — never a second negotiation engine, the BL-381 invariant). Agreement cascades straight into the existing fail-closed `onboarding-contract-gate.js` (`proveGateAndPush`); only once the gate allows does it commit and push the agreed contract back to the target repo and post the commit reference into the topic — `commitAndPush` has exactly one call site, reached only after the gate's own `allow`, so declared invariant 2 ("nothing is pushed before the human has agreed") holds structurally, not just by convention. Any clone/survey/propose failure leaves the state exactly at `prerequisites-ready` with a visible reason and a `Fix the issue and post "proceed" to retry.` instruction — never a silent stall or a half-advanced phase. Real adapters live in `contractPhaseRealAdapters.ts`, the one file in this slice that ever shells to git/`claude`/node (unit tests fake `ContractPhaseAdapters` entirely); it derives its clone directory under `.swarmforge/onboarding-clones/<slug>` the same way `onboarderStateStore.ts` derives its own per-target state path. **Architect bounce, same ticket:** the first cut's survey step shelled to `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions` with `cwd` set to the real target clone — the established `--dangerously-skip-permissions` precedent (`claudeCliExecutor.ts`) is safe only because its `cwd` is always a disposable scratch fixture, a condition that never held here against a live, human-supplied, potentially adversarial target repo sitting on real push credentials. Fixed by scoping the survey agent instead: `surveyCliArgs()` now passes `--allowedTools Read,Glob,Grep`, dropping the blanket permission skip outright; swept for the same defect class elsewhere and found nowhere else it applies. Declared invariant 1 (redelivery idempotency) is re-proven at this slice's own new phases by `onboarderContractPhaseRedeliveryIdempotent.property.test.js` against the real, unmodified redelivery guard.

**The Onboarder, slice 3: prompts, launch handoff, done, topic reuse across targets (BL-625, slice 3 of 3 — closes the state machine).** Picks up at `contract-agreed` and drives the remaining three phases. `proceed` runs the existing BL-269 `propose-onboarding-prompts.js` building blocks via a new `proposePrompts` adapter, committing and pushing the proposed project/engineering prompts through the same `commitAndPush` adapter contract-agreed already uses, and advances to `prompts-proposed` — the real adapter persists the survey's raw facts at survey time and reads them back here rather than re-running the multi-minute `claude` CLI survey on every `proceed`, so the prompts derive from the SAME survey that produced the agreed contract's own scope. A further `proceed` at `prompts-proposed` posts the exact `./swarm <path> --pack mono-router` launch command (the path derived from the persisted `targetRepoUrl`, never hardcoded) and states plainly that the human runs it on the target host, advancing to `ready-to-launch`; any other text there — including "is it running?" — restates the same disclaimer plus the command, because the onboarder never claims to launch or observe a swarm it cannot reach. A final `proceed` at `ready-to-launch` marks the target `done` with a completion summary naming it. The single Onboarding topic is then reused for the next target's own repo URL rather than closed, matching slice 1's standing-topic design. Declared invariant 2 (new this slice): a plain reply that cannot be attributed to exactly one in-flight target among two or more concurrent ones (any state from `checking-prerequisites` through `ready-to-launch`) is refused rather than silently applied to whichever target was last touched — `pickUnambiguousInFlightState` in `onboarderContractPhaseRouter.ts`, proven by a coder-authored property test with a "most recently touched" mutant demonstrating non-vacuity. Declared invariant 1 (redelivery idempotency) is extended through these three new phases by the same property test slice 2 introduced. This closes the state machine slice 1 opened: `contract-agreed → prompts-proposed → ready-to-launch → done` (the ticket's own "gate-open" waypoint is conceptual — proving prompts committed before advancing — not a distinct persisted phase), with the topic-reuse loop back to `needs-target` for the next onboarding.

**The onboarder supervisor's `"not-started"` restart branch spawned without reaping siblings, leaving one orphan reconcile poll-loop per abnormal supervisor death, unbounded (BL-928).** `stop-all!` kills only pids it recorded in `onboarder-supervisor.status.json`, and `stop_onboarder()` then `rm -f`s that file — a supervisor that dies without running its own `finally` (SIGKILL, crash, a host kill) leaves its child (`node extension/out/tools/onboarder-reconcile.js <root> poll-loop`) reparented to PID 1 with no record anywhere, and `check-one!`'s bare `"not-started"` spawn — the one branch BL-403/BL-411 deliberately left without a `kill-pid!` — never looked for it. Measured live, 2026-08-18: two such orphans (~19h, ~11h old) alongside the current healthy pair. Harmless to the one-poller-per-token contract, since these poll-loops only call outbound Bot API methods and never a second `getUpdates` poller, but each leftover shares `onboarder-heartbeat.json` with every other writer — so the stall detector's `poll-heartbeat-stale?` can be answered by a process the running supervisor does not supervise, masking a genuinely stalled child — and each fires its own duplicate outbound topic-ensure call per reconcile interval. `onboarder_supervisor.bb` now sweeps once at startup, before the first tick spawns its own child, never per-tick: a sibling can only come into existence when a supervisor has already died, so scanning the host process table every 2s would put live-process hunting on the hot path the BL-367 failure class forbids. The decision sits beside `front_desk_supervisor_lib.bb`'s existing pure-decision shape: a new `onboarder-reconcile-poll-loop-holder?` mirrors `bridge-entrypoint-holder?`'s own two-part cmdline check (the reconcile entrypoint AND `poll-loop` AND THIS swarm repo root must all appear, not just one, so a poll-loop naming a different root — including a tmp fixture root — is never mistaken for ours), and `decide-onboarder-orphan-reap` filters `process_table_lib/list-processes!`'s result (never a hand-rolled scan) through that predicate and then through `process_table_lib/parent-orphaned?` (BL-879) — a process whose parent is alive, including the running supervisor's own child, is never a candidate by construction. `list-processes!`'s BL-849 nil-vs-empty-vector distinction survives end to end: an unreadable process table reaps nothing and logs that it could not enumerate, never conflated with a genuinely empty candidate set. Human decisions locked at mint time: no ad-hoc kill of the two live leftovers (they clear on the next supervisor start), no janitor class widened to hunt host-repo daemons (the BL-367/BL-879 decapitation boundary the existing agent-reaper deliberately respects), and the sweep fixes the START path only — `stop_onboarder()` itself is untouched; leftovers clearing at stop time would be a second ticket.

## Named Runs

Every swarm run is named after the backlog item it delivers. This makes the full history of swarm work traceable and meaningful.

- The developer names the run when triggering it (or the extension pulls the item name from a backlog file if one exists in the target)
- The run name becomes the swarm dev branch and PR source: `dev/<item-slug>`
- The PR title and body reference the item name
- The extension maintains a local run history log (stored in the forge, not the target):

```
runs.log (forge-local)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2026-06-20  feat-user-login        7-pack  PR#42  merged
2026-06-21  fix-payment-timeout    2-pack  PR#43  open
2026-06-25  feat-export-csv        7-pack  PR#44  open
```

The `View Last PR` command uses this log to know which PR to open. A future `SwarmForge: Run History` panel can surface the full log.

**A swarm launched from the shell is now recorded too (BL-352).** Before this, `runs.jsonl` (the same log the bridge's `GET /runlog` above serves) only ever gained an entry through the VS Code launch/stop/openPR/setRunMode commands — but the real swarm, including this project's own self-hosting swarm, is launched via `./swarm`/`swarmforge.sh` directly, so the actual runs never appeared and `/runlog` read stale or empty. `swarmforge.sh`'s own launch path and `kill_all_swarm.sh`'s own stop path now record into the exact same log via a new shared CLI (`record-run.js start|stop <target-path>`), reusing `runLog.ts`'s existing `appendRun`/`updateLastRunForTarget` functions unchanged — no second run-record format. An editor-triggered launch still gets exactly one entry, not two: `swarmLauncher.ts`'s `buildLaunchEnv` (the one function both TS launch paths funnel through before ever spawning `./swarm`) unconditionally sets `SWARMFORGE_SKIP_SHELL_RUN_RECORD=1` on the process it spawns, and `swarmforge.sh` skips its own recording when that flag is present — a genuine shell-only launch never carries the flag, so it records by default. Both new calls degrade silently (best-effort, never blocking a real launch or stop) if the compiled CLI isn't present.

## Remote Access & Phone App (Optional Bridge)

The swarm cannot run on a phone — it's the orchestrator's agent processes, git worktrees, multiple model backends, and a filesystem clone, none of which exist on mobile. So the phone is a **remote control and observability client**, and the heavy lifting stays on the dev machine. This is the thin-client, fat-host pattern.

### Avoiding complexity: the filesystem is already the decoupling

Before reaching for a daemon, note how much the on-disk state already decouples for free. The swarm's *state* lives on disk: the message store (`.swarmforge/messages/`), heartbeats, worktrees/branches, and the run log. The VS Code extension is, for the most part, *reading those files and streaming each agent process's output*. So any client — the extension, a bridge, a phone — can reconstruct the full picture from disk without talking to any other client.

**Persistence across restarts: implemented via detached processes and re-discovery.** Agent processes run under the SwarmForge tmux server, detached from the VS Code extension host. When you close or reload the editor:
- The swarm and its agents keep running in tmux, unaffected by the extension's lifecycle
- On relaunch with a live swarm: the extension re-discovers it via `isSwarmReady()` and tiles automatically reconnect to the agents' output streams — no agent restarts, no in-flight work lost
- On cold relaunch (no live tmux session but prior `.swarmforge/` state on disk): the extension offers "Resume?" — resume from the last per-stage checkpoint rather than starting over

This is **no different from the tmux design** — the swarm lives independently of any UI frontend. The extension is purely an observer and control surface reading the same on-disk state. What's always free is observational decoupling: any client reads the same `.swarmforge/` files without coordination overhead.

The discipline that keeps complexity flat: **the filesystem stays the single source of truth.** No component (extension, bridge, or phone) holds authoritative state; they all read `.swarmforge/` and issue commands through the same orchestrator/helper calls the agents already use.

### Two tiers, one architecture

| Tier | When | What it is | Added complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1 — desktop only (v1)** | Default | Extension reads `.swarmforge/` files + streams tmux panes headlessly (`SWARMFORGE_TERMINAL=none`). Handoff phase 1 uses direct tmux injection (`SWARMFORGE_SKIP_DAEMON=1`); phase 2 adds `handoffd`. | ~none — filesystem is source of truth |
| **2 — remote (later)** | Opt-in, for phone | A thin bridge that *projects* the same on-disk state over an authenticated tunnel, plus a few control endpoints | a process + a wire protocol + auth — but no new state model |

The phone case is the *only* thing that actually needs a network service, because a phone can't read your laptop's filesystem or reach the host's orchestrator remotely — something must expose that. The bridge does exactly that and nothing more: it reads the same files the extension reads and forwards commands as the same orchestrator/helper calls. Tier 1 and Tier 2 are therefore the *same* architecture with an optional projection bolted on — not two designs, and crucially **no state-sync problem**, since there's only ever one source of truth on disk.

### Backlog Dashboard PWA (implemented — no dev machine, bridge, or tunnel needed)

A third, already-built option sidesteps Tier 2's tunnel/auth requirement entirely for read-only backlog visibility: `.github/workflows/backlog-dashboard.yml` runs on every push to `main` that touches `backlog/`, `docs/`, `specs/features/`, or the metrics/backlog-parsing/docs-generation code, generates two versioned JSON artifacts — `backlog.json` (schema: `docs/reference/backlog-dashboard-schema.md`) and `docs-tree.json` (schema: `docs/reference/docs-tree-schema.md`) — via `node out/tools/generate-backlog-dashboard.js` and `generate-docs-tree.js`, and publishes both to GitHub Pages alongside a small installable PWA (`pwa/`). Because it's static and served from Pages, it's reachable from any browser — including a phone, from anywhere — with **no dev machine running, no bridge started, no tunnel or token**. The dashboard shows the active/paused backlog board, done tickets grouped by milestone, and the same velocity/burndown/cycle-time/forecast numbers the `swarm-metrics` CLI and the bridge's `GET /metrics` report at that commit (never re-derived, so the three surfaces always agree). The burndown renders as a **classic sprint burndown line chart** (BL-287) — a solid "Remaining" polyline through each milestone's daily remaining-ticket count plus a dotted "Ideal" line from the first observed count straight down to zero at the latest observed date (the projection carries no milestone deadline, so the observed span stands in for a target end date), with date/count axis labels, light gridlines, and a legend — replacing the bar chart the burndown previously shared with the velocity chart (which is unchanged); still dependency-free inline SVG, no charting library. A client-side **filter/search bar** (BL-257 slice 1) over the already-fetched `backlog.json` combines a text query, status, and priority filter with AND; a filter matching nothing shows a localized empty state. A read-only **"needs human approval" list** (BL-251) shows every live (active + paused) ticket whose structured `human_approval` backlog field (`swarmforge/backlog-schema.md`) is `pending` — id and title only, no approve/reject control from the phone; approving still happens as it does today. The same daily briefing email carries an equivalent section. Both surfaces derive the list from the ONE `human_approval` field, never by re-parsing the free-text `# HUMAN APPROVAL: ...` comment some tickets still also carry, so they can't disagree; with nothing pending, both show an explicit empty state rather than blank or erroring. A one-time, idempotent backfill seeded the field on pre-existing live items from their legacy approval comments. Tapping a needs-approval entry drills into that ticket's **description and acceptance scenarios** (BL-266) — read-only, no approve/reject affordance — cross-referenced by ticket id from the same `docs-tree.json` the documentation drill-down explorer below already fetches (BL-117 already carries every ticket's description and resolved Gherkin scenarios there for every status), so the phone never shows a version of the ticket different from what the swarm actually builds against; no new store or second Gherkin parser. A **Listen** control speaks the description + scenarios aloud via the browser's on-device `window.speechSynthesis` (no network, no server, no storage — stays inside the static-PWA boundary), toggling between a "Start listening"/"Stop listening" label and matching `aria-label`. The PWA also has a read-only **documentation drill-down explorer**: vision docs (Specification, Roadmap, GettingStarted, both diagrams) → milestone → ticket → Gherkin scenario, with breadcrumb navigation and no *edit* surface anywhere — a ticket's full-detail view carries the same **Listen** control (BL-293), reused as-is: activating it reads the ticket's description followed by every one of its scenarios aloud on-device, covering the whole spec at the ticket level (not a separate per-scenario control) — resolving each ticket's acceptance criteria whether it's the pre-BL-111 inline-Gherkin form or the post-BL-111 `specs/features/*.feature` reference form transparently. Each ticket carries a whole-ticket **implemented vs not-yet** flag (BL-253) derived once from its backlog folder (`done/` → implemented; `active/`/`paused/` → not-yet) so the tree data and every consumer agree, with no duplicated status-derivation logic on the PWA side; not-yet tickets grey visually (a `.not-yet-implemented` CSS class) but stay fully expandable, and their Gherkin remains refinable through the existing BL-150 recertification flow (which was already structurally status-blind, confirmed rather than changed). Each ticket's docs-explorer view also shows a **timeline** (BL-257 slice 2) of its `specDateIso`/`closeDateIso` stages in order, sourced from the same git-derived ticket lifecycle events `docs-tree.json` generation already computes elsewhere — fully git-reproducible, unlike a richer per-role holding-window breakdown that would need live `.swarmforge/` mailbox state this static artifact's generation pipeline doesn't have. (BL-257's other two candidate slices — a changed-since-last-visit highlight, and live briefing-metric trends in the PWA — are parked as a `.feature.draft`: both need live, bridge-connected data the static, zero-connectivity PWA cannot reach, and BL-252 already settled that machine-local live metrics belong on the holistic UI/briefing, not `backlog.json`/the PWA; flagged back to the specifier rather than built onto the wrong surface.) A **full-text search box** (BL-254) filters the drill-down tree client-side by any ticket's title, description, or Gherkin scenario text (case-insensitive substring match) — no new search endpoint or index, it filters the same `docs-tree.json` the PWA already fetched. `filterDocsTree` (`extension/src/docs/docsTree.ts`) is the pure filter: matching a ticket keeps it (and prunes its milestone down to matching tickets only), and a blank/whitespace-only query returns the tree unchanged. `pwa/app.js` hand-mirrors this same filter logic in the browser (the PWA is an unbundled script with no access to the compiled TS module — kept in sync by hand, the same posture as BL-249's `PREFERENCES_CACHE_NAME`) and wires it to a single, statically-placed search input so typing never loses focus across re-renders. Both artifacts are offline-capable (the service worker caches the static shell cache-first and each JSON artifact network-first-with-cache-fallback, so an offline open still renders the last-fetched data with its own "as of `<generatedAtIso>`" honesty indicator) and installable as a home-screen PWA. The generating Action is not a required check — a failure is visible in GitHub Actions but never gates the pipeline.

The shell cache's name (`CACHE_NAME` in `pwa/sw.js`) is a content hash of the shell assets (`SHELL_ASSETS`), stamped into the served `sw.js` at deploy time by the "Stamp PWA cache name" step (`extension/src/tools/stamp-pwa-cache-name.ts`, run over `_site/` after the PWA static assets are copied in) — BL-249. A deploy that changes any shell asset yields a different `CACHE_NAME`, so the activate handler's existing purge-old-cache-on-change logic actually fires and returning users get the update; a byte-identical shell yields the same `CACHE_NAME`, so an unchanged shell is never force-re-downloaded. `pwa/sw.js` itself keeps a placeholder constant — only the served, stamped copy under `_site/` differs per deploy.

The dashboard also has a **Cost & Health card**, shown whenever a `docs/briefings/<date>.json` sidecar has been committed (hidden entirely otherwise). The daily briefing flow (BL-099: a once-a-day nudge into the coordinator's pane, whose composed `docs/briefings/<date>.md` gets emailed) now also emits this machine-readable JSON sidecar alongside it — per-agent token/cost totals, the top-5 most expensive tickets, spec-vs-close flow balance, reliability event counts, and resource anomalies, each carrying a trend. `backlog.json` folds in the most recently committed sidecar verbatim (see `costHealth` in `docs/reference/backlog-dashboard-schema.md`) — every figure on the card traces to that sidecar; the PWA never computes or invents a number.

**Headless morning generation trigger (BL-258):** BL-099's nudge above depends on the VS Code host's own once-a-day timer — a swarm running fully headless (no VS Code host) never gets the briefing GENERATED, so BL-214's daemon send path has nothing to send. `swarmforge/scripts/briefing_generation_schedule_lib.bb` adds a host-independent morning trigger in the same daemon that already handles the send: at/after a configured UTC time (`swarmforge.conf`'s `briefing_morning_time_utc`, default `08:00`) on any day whose `docs/briefings/<date>.md` doesn't yet exist, it sends the coordinator the identical BL-099 nudge prose. The file's own presence is the idempotency gate (the same signal BL-214's send path already keys off), so this composes safely with the VS Code host timer if both are present — whichever writes the file first silences every later check from either trigger. This only adds the generation trigger; BL-099's content and BL-214's send path are unchanged.

**Headless cost & health sidecar emission (BL-272):** the Cost & Health card above was previously populated only by the VS Code host's own `onBriefingDue` handler calling BL-213's `computeCostHealthSidecar -> writeCostHealthSidecar -> commitCostHealthSidecar` in-process — a swarm running fully headless never emitted `docs/briefings/<date>.json`, so the briefing's Cost & Health section and the phone card were silently absent on every headless day. `extension/src/tools/emit-cost-health-sidecar.ts` is a thin headless CLI (`out/tools/emit-cost-health-sidecar.js`) that runs the identical compute → write → commit path outside the extension host; `briefing_generation_schedule_lib.bb`'s `generate-briefing-if-due!` (the BL-258 trigger above) now invokes it via an injected `:emit-sidecar!` adapter — `handoffd.bb`'s `emit-cost-health-sidecar!` shells the CLI out — wrapped in a `try/catch` that mirrors the host's own best-effort posture, so a sidecar emission failure never suppresses the briefing-generation nudge. Idempotency is unchanged: `commitCostHealthSidecar` already fails closed on a no-op `git commit`, so re-running the emitter for an already-committed day makes no duplicate commit.

**Average cost per ticket, and its trend — the number the human intends to reduce (BL-338).** He asked for it explicitly: cost was visible per-role and per-hour, but never per unit of delivered work, so every efficiency decision on the project (parking idle roles, clearing context, cheaper per-role models) was argued from intuition rather than measurement. `costPerTicket.ts`'s `computeCostPerTicketSeries` buckets each DELIVERED (closed) ticket's total cost — summed across every role that held it, using BL-312's already-corrected, non-double-counted role-group totals — into weekly averages; an empty week is omitted, never filled with a fabricated $0. **Rework rides the figure for free, by construction, not by a separate accounting step**: a bounced ticket is re-held more than once, and `attributeUsageToTickets` already buckets every hold's usage under the same ticket id regardless of which round produced it, so summing a ticket's total already includes every bounce — the measured ~58% bounce rate is not quietly excluded. A delivered ticket with no priced usage anywhere is EXCLUDED from the average and tallied in a separate `excludedCount`, never silently treated as free. The accounting basis (`COST_PER_TICKET_BASIS`) is a single string carried on the sidecar data itself — rendered verbatim on every surface that shows the figure, so the PWA and the briefing email can never disagree about what is and isn't counted. Purely additive to the existing committed cost-health sidecar (`buildCostHealthSidecar`'s new optional `costPerTicketSeries` parameter) — it inherits that sidecar's already-reviewed committed-carrier compliance (`docs/briefings/<date>.json`, git-reproducible, never a live `.swarmforge/` read) rather than opening a new data path, so it renders in the SAME pre-existing "Cost & Health" section of both the static PWA (`pwa/app.js`, with a trend chart via the existing `barChart` helper) and the daily briefing email, hidden entirely (not shown as $0) whenever no delivered ticket has a priced cost yet.

**Briefing enrichment (BL-256):** the briefing composes optional sections, each an independent, droppable slice reusing existing telemetry rather than re-deriving it — `briefing_email_lib.bb`'s `send-unsent-briefings!` threads content through a `:suite-duration-line` (BL-252), `:needs-approval-section` (BL-251), `:merged-blocked-digest`, `:stage-dwell-section`, and `:chase-trend-section` in order, each independently appending its own block or leaving content untouched if unavailable — a missing section never breaks or silently drops the rest. Landed sections: a **what-merged/what's-blocked digest** (`extension/src/metrics/briefingDigest.ts`) listing tickets closed since the last briefing and tickets a role has held open past a threshold (12h default) with no existing stall flag reused or invented beyond this explicit one; a **per-stage dwell/throughput** line reusing BL-102's existing `stage-dwell-report.ts`; and a **QA-bounce/chase trend** line (`extension/src/tools/chase-trend-line.ts`) reporting chase/nudge/dead-letter counts and their trend direction over two adjacent 7-day windows, reusing BL-098's chaser telemetry and the same `computeTrend` every other briefing trend uses. **PWA deep links** (`extension/src/metrics/pwaDeepLinks.ts`) turn a briefing item into a one-tap link into its PWA view (`#ticket=<id>` / `#approval=<id>` hash routes) when the optional `swarmforge.conf` key `pwa_base_url` is configured — absent config degrades to no link, never a broken or fabricated URL. The "generous extras" slice (per-role resource use, cost-per-stage, forecast-ETA change call-outs) has not landed yet.

**Fixed: a long lede paragraph no longer swallows the whole subject line (BL-392).** The briefing email's subject keeps its BL-099 positional contract — the first non-empty line of the briefing is the headline — but appended it verbatim, and this project's briefing style opens with a multi-sentence markdown-laden lede rather than a short title, so a real subject once ran to a screen and a half. `build-briefing-subject` (`briefing_email_lib.bb`) now strips markdown emphasis/heading markers (`**`, `*`, `_`, backticks, a leading `#`) from the headline before bounding it to 80 characters, truncating at a word boundary with a single-character ellipsis (falling back to a hard cut only when one unbroken token has no word boundary within budget). A headline already within the limit passes through unchanged; a headline that strips down to nothing, or an empty briefing, still yields a date-only subject with no dangling separator, exactly as before.

**Fixed: the briefing body now sends as rendered HTML, not a plain-text markdown wall (BL-393).** The email body carried only the plain-text markdown, so on a phone mail client its `##` headings, `|` table pipes, and `**bold**` collapsed into an undifferentiated wall — the metrics were present but unreadable. `markdown_to_html_lib.bb`'s `render-markdown-to-html` is a minimal, pure, exported renderer (headings to `<h1>`-`<h6>`, GFM-style pipe tables to `<table>`/`<tr>`/`<th|td>`, `**bold**` to `<strong>`, every other non-blank line its own `<p>`, HTML-escaped before any markup is generated) applied to the exact same assembled `content` that already rides the plain-text part — including every appended optional section (suite-duration, needs-approval, stage-dwell, chase-trend, etc.) — so the HTML body is byte-complete by construction, never a lede-only variant. `:html` is now ALWAYS passed to `:send-email!` (previously nil whenever no diagrams were available, which was exactly the run that read as "thin"); when diagrams are available, their own `<div>`/`<img cid:...>` html is appended after the rendered body rather than replacing it, so both coexist. This changed a shipped invariant: BL-286's diagram-cid-05 scenario, which asserted the no-diagram send has no `:html` field, no longer holds — updated in the same parcel to assert the rendered body's `:html` is present with no `:attachments`. The plain-text part is unchanged, so a plaintext-only client still gets the full markdown.

**Not-done ticket count (BL-263):** both the PWA backlog dashboard and the daily briefing show a single "not done" total — every live ticket (`board.active.length + board.paused.length`), excluding `done`. `computeNotDoneCount` (`extension/src/metrics/backlogDashboard.ts`) is the one pure derivation; `buildBacklogDashboard` emits it as `backlog.json`'s `notDoneCount` field (schema: `docs/reference/backlog-dashboard-schema.md`), which `pwa/app.js` renders verbatim (localized label via `pwa/locales.js`) and which `extension/src/tools/not-done-count-line.ts` — a CLI `briefing_email_lib.bb` shells out to, wired as the `:not-done-count-line` optional adapter alongside BL-256/BL-258/BL-260's — composes into the briefing as the same number, so the two surfaces can never disagree. Zero (every ticket done) renders like any other count, never a blank/error state.

**Telegram front-desk bridge cost line, front-desk only (BL-511, amended 2026-07-18 in flight to narrow scope).** The human asked how much extra he's paying for the Telegram front-desk bridge; the daily briefing now shows one line with the exact answer for the front-desk operator only, never an estimate. Each front-desk `claude -p --output-format json` invocation already reports its own exact `total_cost_usd` before `operator_runtime.bb`'s `reap-finished-front-desk-operator!` deletes that result file — `operator_lib.bb`'s `front-desk-cost-record` captures it there and `append-bridge-cost-record!` appends one JSONL record per invocation to a durable, machine-local, gitignored log (`.swarmforge/operator/bridge-cost.jsonl`, per the local-engineering live-data-stays-off-the-static-PWA rule — never committed or folded into `backlog.json`). `telegramBridgeCost.ts`'s pure `computeTelegramBridgeCostForDay` sums a day's records, EXCLUDING any record with a null/unpriced cost from the total (tallied separately as `unknownCount`) rather than counting it as $0 — the same honest-null discipline `estimateCostUsd` already applies; `formatTelegramBridgeCostLine` renders `Telegram bridge cost: $X.XX today (N front-desk calls[, M unpriced excluded])`, or an empty string on a no-activity day. `extension/src/tools/telegram-bridge-cost-line.ts` is the thin CLI wrapper (log path and day-key injected, no hidden clock read); `briefing_email_lib.bb`'s `:telegram-bridge-cost-line` optional adapter shells it the same way every other optional section works, omitting the line without error on an absent or unreadable log. **Scope note:** the ticket originally also covered the always-on Operator's Telegram-attributable share (prorated by its wakeup batch's telegram/total event ratio), but the Operator runs as an interactive `claude --remote-control` session (`launch_operator.sh`), never a headless `-p` call, so it emits no per-wakeup `total_cost_usd` anywhere on disk — its cost lives only server-side on claude.ai, unreachable at reap time. Estimating it (count × average) would have broken both the human's exact-cost basis and the honest-null discipline, so per his 2026-07-18 decision the Operator's share is measured and reported nowhere; `telegramBridgeCost.ts` documents this in a header comment rather than shipping a silently-zero "Operator $0.00 attributed" term.

**Rendered architecture diagrams inline (BL-260):** the morning briefing email now shows the project's architecture diagrams as viewable images in the body, not just a link to their Mermaid source. `extension/src/diagrams/mermaidRender.ts` renders `docs/diagrams/architecture.mmd` and `docs/diagrams/swarm-flow.mmd` to PNG entirely locally and deterministically — `beautiful-mermaid` (a pure-JS/TS Mermaid renderer, elkjs layout, no DOM/browser) lays out the SVG and `@resvg/resvg-js` rasterizes it, chosen over `@mermaid-js/mermaid-cli` specifically because `mmdc` needs a downloaded, spawned headless Chromium that this project's own build/CI environment can't support. Both packages are pinned in `extension/package.json`. Because `beautiful-mermaid`'s SVG paints via CSS `var()`/`color-mix()` custom properties meant for a live browser cascade, `flattenMermaidThemeVars` resolves every variable to a literal color and strips the generated `<style>` block (which otherwise pulls a Google Fonts `@import` — an external network reference the reproducibility/privacy constraint (BL-252 spirit) forbids) before handing the SVG to the static rasterizer; identical source and theme produce byte-identical PNG bytes across separate process runs, verified empirically, so no diagram is ever rendered by or shipped to an external service. `extension/src/tools/render-briefing-diagrams.ts` is the CLI Babashka shells out to (it has no way to import compiled TS/npm packages): it prints `[{name, base64}, ...]` for the two maintained diagrams, and any failure — a missing dependency, an unparseable `.mmd`, a not-yet-compiled checkout — degrades to nil rather than throwing. On the Babashka side, `briefing_email_lib.bb`'s `build-diagram-section` turns that payload into an optional `:diagram-section` adapter for `send-unsent-briefings!`: when diagrams rendered, it supplies an HTML body plus a plaintext note pointing a non-HTML client at `docs/diagrams/` in the repo; when rendering is unavailable, the email still sends with a clear no-diagram plaintext note instead of failing. `daemon_alarm_lib.bb`'s `send-alarm-email!`/`send-configured-email!` and `handoffd.bb`'s `send-configured-briefing-email!` each grew a new optional-html arity (the html-less arity is unchanged, so every pre-BL-260 caller/test keeps its exact prior behavior).

**Not-done ticket burndown chart in the morning briefing (2026-08-15):** the same cid-PNG diagram path now also carries a 30-day remaining-open (not-yet-closed) ticket line chart alongside the architecture diagrams. `notDoneBurndown.ts` derives the daily series purely from `deriveTicketLifecycles` (git history of `backlog/`), builds an SVG in the style of the earlier hand-made `docs/briefings/burndown-*.svg` charts, and rasterizes it via `@resvg/resvg-js` at `BURNDOWN_RENDER_WIDTH` (1920). `render-briefing-burndown.ts` is the CLI Babashka shells out to (same `[{name, base64}]` contract as `render-briefing-diagrams.ts`, name `not-done-burndown`); `handoffd.bb`'s `briefing-diagram-section` concatenates architecture + burndown payloads so either source can fail open without suppressing the other. `build-diagram-section` titles the chart "Not-done ticket burndown" and mentions it in the plaintext note when present. A blank/failed burndown never blocks the briefing send.

**The morning briefing leads with a token-burn exhaustion warning (BL-619).** The account-level usage percentage the human watches on his phone is not programmatically readable — no endpoint in this repo or documented in the Anthropic API surfaces it — so the projection anchors on a number the human transcribes himself: `node extension/out/tools/usage-anchor.js record <pct>` appends `{atMs, pct, scope}` to `.swarmforge/operator/usage-anchors.jsonl` (machine-local, gitignored). `burnProjection.ts`'s pure `decideProjection` derives a burn rate from the latest two anchors in the current weekly window (falling back to the average since the window opened at 0% when only one anchor exists), projects when the anchored percentage would reach 100 at that rate, and warns iff that projected exhaustion instant falls before the next configured reset (`config usage_week_reset_day thu` / `usage_week_reset_local 07:00` in `swarmforge.conf`, defaulting to the incident's own Thursday-07:00 schedule). Local transcript burn (tokens/hr, reusing `extension/src/metrics/burnRate.ts`) rides alongside as corroborating rate context, never as the projection's own basis. Surfaced via the established three-step briefing-section pattern (compiled TS CLI + `handoffd.bb` adapter + `briefing_email_lib.bb` key) with two deliberate deviations, because the human's directive says the briefing should *lead* with the warning: an active warning is prepended above the coordinator-authored body rather than appended like every other section, and the email subject gains a token-burn marker. The ok-path (no exhaustion projected) is a single appended status line; the no-anchor path reports local tokens/hr only, states the account projection is unavailable, and names the anchor command — `burnSectionText.ts` never fabricates a percentage it cannot back with a recorded anchor. A malformed reset-schedule config degrades to the same local-burn-only rendering with a loud log line rather than crashing the send, and any section failure degrades to sending the briefing without it (the same BL-260 failure posture every briefing section already follows). Out of scope for this slice: an immediate Telegram alert when the projection first flips (briefing-only, per the human's own "at least" wording), a Telegram command to record anchors, automatic throttling (the section names the levers — pause usage, the BL-617 nightly cooldown, or a lowered `active_backlog_max_depth` (Article 3.5 circuit breaker) — it pulls none of them), and per-model projection scope. Runbook: [Token-Burn Exhaustion Warning in the Morning Briefing](../how-to/BL-619-token-burn-briefing-warning.md).

**Higher-resolution briefing diagram PNGs (BL-402).** The human reported the inline architecture/swarm-flow diagrams looked blurry on a high-DPI screen. The fix stays on the existing cid-PNG pipeline rather than switching to SVG — Gmail (the human's client) strips/blocks SVG in every embedding form (inline `<svg>`, `data:image/svg+xml`, or a cid-referenced `image/svg+xml`), which is exactly the defect class BL-286 moved to cid-PNG to avoid. `mermaidRender.ts` now rasterizes through a named `DIAGRAM_RENDER_WIDTH` constant (3200, up from a bare `1600` literal) passed to `Resvg`'s `fitTo: { mode: 'width', value: ... }` — resvg rasterizes the vector at the requested width, so this is a genuinely higher-resolution render, not an upscaled bitmap. Rendering stays local and deterministic (BL-260's byte-identical-output guarantee holds at the new width), and the composed `<img>` keeps `style="max-width:100%;height:auto"` (`briefing_email_lib.bb`'s `build-diagram-section`), so the higher-res PNG displays at the email column width rather than blowing out the layout.

**Fixed: cid inline attachments, not data-URI images (BL-286).** BL-260 originally embedded each diagram as an inline `<img src="data:image/png;base64,...">` — Gmail and most webmail clients block data-URI image sources, so every diagram rendered broken/blank in the human's actual client. `build-diagram-section` now emits `<img src="cid:<content-id>">` per diagram and returns the image bytes as attachment descriptors (`{:filename :content-id :base64}`) alongside the HTML, rather than inlining them into the markup; `send-unsent-briefings!` threads those through to `:send-email!`, and `daemon_alarm_lib.bb`'s `default-post!`/`send-alarm-email!` include them in the Resend JSON body as `:attachments` (`{:filename :content :content_id}`, the RFC 2392 inline-attachment shape Gmail actually renders) — each `content_id` matches exactly one `cid:` reference in the HTML. Fully backward compatible: absent diagrams (or any pre-BL-260 caller) produce the identical prior payload with no `:attachments` key. (As of BL-813 below, the BL-144 death alarm is no longer one of those no-attachment callers — it now always supplies its own failure-log attachment through this same `:attachments` path.)

**Bilingual French/English, N-language design (board titles):** The dashboard has a visible locale toggle cycling through whatever locales are configured (`window.LOCALES`' own keys). English is always the first-launch default regardless of browser locale; switching re-renders every already-fetched section instantly from cached data — no reload, no re-fetch — and the choice persists across visits via the Cache Storage API (never `localStorage`), in a dedicated `PREFERENCES_CACHE_NAME` cache kept permanently static and distinct from the shell's per-deploy `CACHE_NAME` — sw.js's activate handler explicitly exempts it from the shell-invalidation purge above, so a shell-changing deploy never wipes a returning user's saved locale (BL-249 hardener bounce; before this exemption, the purge deleted any cache key that wasn't the current `CACHE_NAME`, which would have wiped preferences the moment `CACHE_NAME` started actually changing). Board ticket titles carry a per-configured-target-locale `titleTranslations` map on `backlog.json` (BL-230, schema doc above), keyed by locale code against `extension/src/i18n/targetLocales.ts`'s `TARGET_LOCALES` (French (`fr`) is the first delivered target) — adding a target locale is a config-and-rebuild operation, no per-language code change. Vision doc markdown, ticket description, and Gherkin scenario text (`docs-tree.json`) still carry BL-118's original fixed additive `*Fr`/`*FrUntranslated` sibling pair; generalizing them to the same N-locale map is a planned follow-on slice. Both mechanisms share the same build-time translation pass: a CI-run pass (a DeepL adapter, with a null/pass-through fallback — publishing never fails or blocks on translation) whose content-hash-and-locale-keyed cache is committed to `docs/i18n/translation-cache.json` so an unchanged string is never re-translated and builds stay reproducible. Jargon tokens (ticket ids, pipeline role names, the product name — the reviewable preserve-list in `extension/src/i18n/jargonPreserve.ts`) are wrapped before each engine call and unwrapped after, so they survive translation verbatim rather than being machine-translated themselves. An `*Untranslated: true` flag (or, for board titles, an entry's own `untranslated: true`) marks a field that's still showing English because translation was unavailable or failed for it. The PWA itself now surfaces this: whenever a rendered `*Fr` field's paired `*Untranslated` flag is true — ticket title, vision-doc content, ticket description, or Gherkin scenario text (BL-261) — a localized "translation unavailable" notice renders alongside the English fallback, so it is never presented as a genuine French translation; a genuine translation shows no indicator. (Before BL-261, `pwa/app.js` read the `*Fr` fields unconditionally and never checked the paired flag, so a failed translation silently looked like a real one — the flags existed and were correctly published on `docs-tree.json` the whole time, this was a rendering-layer gap only.) A locale with no entry at all falls back to the source text. Gherkin scenario text always shows the canonical English by default in either locale (the binding acceptance contract), with the translated rendering one tap away. Operationally: the Action needs an `MT_API_KEY` secret (DeepL) to actually translate — configured as a GitHub Actions secret, never in the client bundle or the repo.

**Font size:** The dashboard defaults to a large 28px root font size (phone-readable out of the box, since every view sizes text in `rem` relative to it) with A-/A+ buttons in the chrome, alongside the locale toggle, stepping it by 2px within a 16-40px clamp — applied instantly with no reload. The choice persists the same way as the locale preference: the same dedicated, purge-exempt `PREFERENCES_CACHE_NAME` cache (never `localStorage`), falling back to the 28px default on a missing or out-of-range stored value.

**Collapsible sections (BL-291):** each top-level dashboard section (backlog board, velocity, burndown, cycle time, cost & health, documentation explorer, recertification, etc.) has a keyboard-operable header control that collapses/expands its body, `aria-expanded` kept in sync at creation and on every toggle. Each section's open/collapsed state persists independently across reloads on the same `PREFERENCES_CACHE_NAME` mechanism as the locale and font-size preferences — keyed by the section's stable `data-i18n` heading key, never DOM order (which drifts as sections like Cost & Health show/hide based on data availability) — so a returning visitor sees the layout they left, and a first-ever visit defaults every section open.

**Gherkin scenario recertification (receiver, inbound address, and serverless handler now built — the remaining routing is an operator go-live step):** A third published artifact, `recert-batch.json`, drip-feeds one oldest-reviewed-first Gherkin scenario at a time (only scenarios carrying a BL-111 stable `# TICKET-ID slug` tag are trackable; untagged ones are excluded, never mistracked under a position that could shift) into a "Recertify a scenario" section of the PWA. Reviewing from the phone offers three outcomes, each composing a `mailto:` link since the PWA is fully static with no live backend to call: **Confirm** (still accurate — just advances the scenario's last-reviewed timestamp), **Update** (propose new scenario text), and **Delete** (gated behind an explicit in-app confirmation screen before any send link exists). Confirm applies directly since it changes no content; Update/Delete are real contract changes and land as durable, one-per-change proposals for specifier review — the same pattern `rule_proposal` already uses — via a Resend Inbound webhook (BL-217). The shown scenario also carries the BL-266 **Listen** control (BL-271) — reused unchanged, not reimplemented — reading the scenario's name then its Gherkin text aloud via on-device `speechSynthesis`; it appears only while a scenario is present and is omitted once nothing needs recertification. Above the scenario, a **"BL-### — title"** line (BL-280) shows which backlog item the scenario belongs to — `recertifiableScenariosFrom` (`extension/src/docs/recertification.ts`) now carries the ticket's title (and French title, when set) alongside the existing `ticketId` on each `RecertifiableScenario`, an additive field so `recert-batch.json` stays git-SHA-reproducible. When a title is resolvable the line is a tap-through link into the ticket's full detail, reusing the docs explorer's own in-page navigation (`navButton` → `{level: 'ticket'}` → `renderDocsTicket`, the same mechanism BL-256's deep-link scheme already uses — no new routing) and its existing locale fallback (French title under the `fr` locale, else English); a scenario with no resolvable ticket shows the bare id with no link and no error.

The webhook's core (`extension/src/notify/recertInboundWebhook.ts`) is platform-agnostic: it verifies the Resend/Svix signature and rejects a stale/replayed timestamp (outside a 300-second freshness window), so neither an unauthenticated nor a captured-and-replayed request can ever create a proposal; it then checks the sender against a configured allowlist (BL-248 — see below) before parsing the phone-composed email with BL-150's existing `parseRecertEmail`, and commits exactly one proposal per change to `backlog/recert-inbox/<scenarioId>-<timestamp>.json` via GitHub's Contents API (`recertProposalRepoCommit.ts`) — the serverless function has no filesystem access to a running host's `.swarmforge/`. A host-side bridge (`extension/src/tools/bridge-recert-proposals.ts`) ingests those committed files into BL-150's existing durable review queue (`.swarmforge/recert_proposals/<month>.jsonl`), closing the loop into the specifier's normal recertification review. A malformed but validly-signed, allowlisted email produces no proposal and is logged rather than crashing. The signing secret and the repo-write credential live only in the function/host environment — never in the repo — and the repo-write credential is minimally scoped; proposals are never auto-applied, so specifier review remains the gate even for a malformed proposal.

**Sender allowlist (BL-248).** Signature verification only proves Resend delivered the request — it says nothing about *who* sent the original email. `HandleInboundEmailWebhookDeps` now carries a `senderAllowlist: string[]` (sourced from the serverless function's own environment, the same deployment-agnostic posture as the signing `secret` — the core cannot read this host's `.swarmforge/`), checked case-insensitively against the inbound `data.from` field, after signature/freshness auth and before the email is even parsed for a recert outcome. **Fail-closed by design:** an empty or missing allowlist rejects every sender (403 "sender not allowed") rather than accepting anything signed, since an allowlist that fails open is not a control. It is not mirrored into `swarmforge.conf` (left as an operator-set deployment env var, not built into the repo config).

**Serverless deployment handler (BL-288).** `api/recert-webhook.js` is a thin Vercel Node function (`vercel.json` at the repo root) that wraps `recertInboundWebhook.ts`'s core end to end: it extracts the `svix-id`/`svix-timestamp`/`svix-signature` headers and the RAW request body — with the platform's automatic JSON body parsing disabled, since Svix signature verification checks the exact bytes and a re-serialized body silently breaks it — assembles `HandleInboundEmailWebhookDeps` entirely from the deployment environment (signing secret, the BL-248 sender allowlist, GitHub owner/repo/branch/token for `commitProposal`), calls `handleInboundEmailWebhook`, and maps its `{status, body}` onto the platform HTTP response. The wrapper is intentionally thin and unit-tested for wiring only (raw-body correctness, header extraction, env-to-deps assembly, response mapping) — the core's own behavior stays covered by its existing BL-217/BL-248 tests. This closes the "code built, last-mile go-live never done" gap the same shape as the BL-272 cost-health sidecar: `backlog/recert-inbox/` never existed and zero proposals ever committed because the wrapper simply didn't exist yet, not because of a misconfiguration.

The PWA's inbound address (`recertEmailTo`, config-injected from `swarmforge.conf`'s `recert_email_to` — never a hardcoded placeholder) is now a real, Resend-managed receiving address (BL-223), replacing the old `.invalid`-TLD placeholder (RFC 2606 — guaranteed non-deliverable) that stood in before BL-217's receiver existed. Still open (operator go-live, not a build gap — see `docs/how-to/BL-223-recert-inbound-address-golive.md`): deploying `api/recert-webhook.js` to Vercel, setting its environment secrets, and routing the Resend Inbound webhook at the deployed endpoint. Applying an *accepted* update/delete proposal back into its `.feature` file also has no tool yet (out of scope for BL-217; tracked under BL-150 + the existing `rule_proposal` flow).

**Telegram announces a waiting recert batch and deep-links into the PWA (BL-339) — notify only, verdicts still given in the PWA.** The human asked whether recert feedback could be done via Telegram; the answer he chose was notify-and-deep-link, not in-thread verdicts: recert stays a batch review activity in the PWA (where the UI already works), and Telegram's job is only to tell him work is waiting and take him straight to it. A standalone CLI (`extension/src/tools/notify-recert-batch.ts`) computes the real waiting batch via the same `computeRecertBatch` the PWA itself renders (never a second derivation), decides whether to announce (`decideRecertAnnouncement`, `extension/src/notify/recertBatchNotifier.ts`), and sends one Telegram message naming the batch count plus a `#recert=1` deep link (`buildRecertDeepLink`, `extension/src/metrics/pwaDeepLinks.ts`) — reusing the same BL-256 deep-link scheme the docs explorer already uses, not a second link mechanism. `pwa/app.js` now parses that `#recert=1` hash route and scrolls the recert section into view on load, so the link actually lands on the work. Anti-spam tracks the waiting batch's own scenario-id set rather than a boolean: because `selectForRecertification` always returns up to the batch size from the whole recertifiable pool (marking one scenario reviewed just reorders the pool, it never empties), a same-outstanding-batch tick never re-announces, while a genuinely different batch — even the same size — does. The armed state is written only on confirmed Telegram delivery, never on a bare send attempt (the BL-333/BL-345 "arm on delivery" rule, reapplied). Wired into `handoffd.bb`'s existing chase-sweep cadence as its own `recert-notify-sweep!` adapter (same shape as the other `*-sweep!` Babashka-to-Node adapters in that file) — a disposable, independent CLI, deliberately not routed through the live, currently-running Telegram Front Desk Bot process, so it can never destabilize that connection. Out of scope, deliberately: no verdict can be typed into Telegram and accepted — `confirmScenario`'s only caller anywhere in `extension/src` remains the existing inbound-email path (BL-223); this CLI never references it.

### The remote bridge (Tier 2)

```
        ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
        │   agent processes + .swarmforge/  (on disk)   │  ← single source of truth
        └───────┬─────────────────────────┬────────┘
                │ reads files / streams    │ reads files
                │                          │
        ┌───────▼──────────┐      ┌────────▼─────────────┐
        │  VS Code extension│      │  Remote bridge (opt) │
        │   (Tier 1, always)│      │  projects state +    │
        └───────────────────┘      │  control endpoints   │
                                    └────────┬─────────────┘
                                             │ authenticated tunnel
                                    ┌────────▼─────────────┐
                                    │  Phone app           │
                                    │  (monitor + nudge)    │
                                    └──────────────────────┘
```

The bridge exposes:

- **A read projection** — pipeline stage, per-agent status/heartbeat, completion %, run log — all derived from the same on-disk state, pushed over an event stream (WebSocket/SSE)
- **A small control surface — narrower than originally scoped here, by deliberate operator posture (BL-240, 2026-07-10):** the ONLY write route the bridge exposes is answering a captured `to: human` gate (`POST /gate-answer {role, answer}`), authenticated, dispatched through the exact same tmux send-keys call the extension uses when the operator types into a tile locally, and refused for any role that isn't currently showing a captured gate. Respawn-an-agent, stop-the-swarm, and switch-a-model remain future work on this surface, not yet implemented — a client cannot do them remotely today.
