- **`GET /gates` — the pending-gate list (BL-265 slice 1).** A read-scoped route listing every role currently showing a captured `to: human` gate (role + question snippet); a role with no pending gate is simply absent, and nothing gated returns an empty list, never an error. `filterPendingGates` (`extension/src/bridge/gateSnapshot.ts`) narrows `computeRoleGateStatesLive`'s per-role snapshot (built for the Telegram narrator, BL-239, which needs the full gated/not-gated set to detect a resolved transition) down to only the gated entries. This closes gap #10's missing read half — the write half (`POST /gate-answer` above) already existed; a client still needs a UI to actually view and answer from, which is slice 2 (holistic UI, `extension/src/bridge/holisticUiHtml.ts`, parked as `specs/features/BL-265-holistic-gate-answer-view.slice-2-ui.feature.draft` until built) — deliberately NOT the static backlog-dashboard PWA, which has no live bridge connection, token, or write path (see the PWA-vs-holistic-UI boundary rule in `local-engineering.prompt`).
- **`GET /companion-manifest` + `GET /companion-package/<name>` — the companion-manifest and package catalog (BL-866, epic BL-865's foundation slice).** The contract every later offline slice of Bubble's offline-first sync reads: `/companion-manifest` lists each package the bridge can currently serve (`backlog`, sourced from the same `readBacklogFolders` the panel uses; `docs`, the vision-doc tree via `readVisionDocs`) with a **generation** — a `sha256` of the package's own content, truncated to 16 hex chars, computed fresh on every request from the exact content about to be served, so a served body and the generation it carries can never drift apart by separate bookkeeping — and a **format version** (`companionManifest.ts`, `COMPANION_PACKAGE_FORMAT = 'json'`). `/companion-package/<name>?generation=<g>` serves that package: omit `generation` (or name a stale one) and the current body comes back at `200` with the generation in both the JSON body and an `etag` header; name the generation already held and the answer is `304` with an `etag` header and **zero bytes on the wire** — the cheap-refresh path a phone needs to keep the BL-659 corpus (~2-3 MB compressed) current without re-downloading it unchanged. A package whose source cannot be read is left off the manifest rather than advertised (`docs` degrades this way if every vision-doc source is unreadable — `readVisionDocs` already tolerates individual missing docs; zero docs read back is what trips this), and one that was advertised but becomes unreadable by request time is refused `503` with a reason rather than served as an empty package; an unknown package name is refused `404`. Both routes sit behind the bridge's existing `isAuthorizedForRead` gate, same as every other read route. Bridge-side only, fully covered by the Node unit suite.
- **Bubble holds those packages on the device (BL-907, epic BL-865's phone-side slice).** `CompanionPackageSync` (pure Kotlin, no `android.*` type in any signature — the Bubble testability boundary) owns every sync/cache decision, proven by the JVM unit suite plus two BL-654 property tests: a held package's generation always comes from the same fetch as its data (never relabeled with a stale or a different fetch's generation), and no sync outcome — the successful fetch or any of the four failure kinds (unknown package, unreadable package, connection failure, interrupted transfer) — ever leaves the device holding less than it held before; only a successful fetch replaces what's held, every failure reports itself and leaves the existing copy untouched. `CompanionPackageStore` wires those decisions to one atomically-written JSON file per package under app-private storage (temp file, then rename, so a sync that dies mid-write can't corrupt the previous complete copy) and is the ticket's device-surface half, verified by a recorded manual procedure rather than the JVM suite. Before any package has ever synced, a read reports nothing held rather than an empty package. See the new [how-to](../how-to/BL-907-bubble-offline-package-sync.md).
- **Bubble browses those packages (BL-908, epic BL-865's browse-UI slice).** `KnowledgeReader` (pure Kotlin, no `android.*` type in any signature) holds every panel decision — what a folder lists, what a ticket's detail shows, what a document opens to, what generation a view states — reading only what BL-907 already holds on the device, never the network, so a `Ready` state is reached identically with the network on or off. A `Ready` state cannot be constructed without a generation, so "no view presents package content without stating the generation it was read at" holds structurally. `KnowledgeActivity` wires this against real views: two tabs (backlog, docs), four folder chips, and a detail dialog per ticket/document; reached from the expanded bubble's new `knowledgeBtn` with no re-pairing. An architect send-back (the only sync trigger lived inside the empty-state view, so it vanished for the rest of the app's life once both packages had synced once) was fixed by giving the sync action a permanent header home (`syncBtnHeader`) alongside the empty-state one. Read-only; a diagram document shows its source, labelled as a diagram, never a rendered image. See the new [how-to](../how-to/BL-908-bubble-knowledge-screen-backlog-docs-panels.md).
- **Auth + tunnel** — token-based; opt-in and encrypted (see the remote-access security gap)

It deliberately does *not* hold or cache authoritative state, run its own watchdog, or duplicate logic. If it dies, the swarm is unaffected and the desktop extension carries on — because neither depends on it.

### What the phone app is good for

The phone is not where you'd read full agent transcripts or resolve a merge — it's for **awareness and light steering** while away from the desk:

- **Glanceable status:** which stage the parcel is at, per-agent liveness dots, run completion %
- **Push notifications** (the mobile-native win): "PR ready for review," "agent dead-lettered," "agent is asking you a question," "run finished/failed"
- **Light controls:** approve/answer a `to: human` gate — the one control the bridge's write path supports today (BL-240); respawn a stuck agent, pause/stop the swarm, and switch a model are envisioned as future single-tap additions to this surface, not yet built
- **The Work Tree** in collapsed form: backlog → feature → scenario with the same red→green completion circles, so you can see what's done from anywhere
- **Tap a tile** to see that agent's recent output (tailed, not the full scrollback) and type a one-line nudge

### What stays desktop-only

- Full terminal interaction / long typing into an agent
- Merge-conflict resolution review
- Diff/PR review (better on desktop, though the phone can *open* the PR in GitHub's app)
- Tile layout / resizing

### How it reuses what's already specced

Everything the phone shows already exists as on-disk state: heartbeats, message store with statuses, completion %, pipeline stage, run log. The phone is a thin projection of that — no new backend concepts, just a second client surface reading the same files (via the bridge) plus an event stream.

### Human approval gates over mobile

This pairs naturally with the `to: human` gate (see Correctness & Failure Handling): when an agent blocks to ask a question, it writes the gate to the message store; the bridge sees it and pushes to whatever remote client is connected (the desktop extension sees it directly). Answering from your phone unblocks the pipeline without going back to the desk — arguably the single most valuable mobile feature, since a blocked swarm otherwise sits idle until you return.

### Chat adapter (Signal / Telegram / WhatsApp / Teams) — human channel only

**Interface vs incarnation (2026-07-30).** Architecture may name two interfaces:
**messaging** (the human chat channel / chat adapter) and **host agent** (the
IDE seat that drives Remote verbs, pairing, and future pack staffing). The
current everyday incarnations are **Telegram** (messaging) and **Cursor** (host
agent). The operator **phone app** product name is **Bubble** (native Android
under `android/`; BL-707). That duality / product lock is deliberate — not a
ubiquitous-language failure. Docs may say “host agent (today: Cursor)” when
teaching architecture; operators still say Telegram and Cursor when naming live
processes, env vars, and slash verbs, and say **Bubble** for the phone app. Do
**not** run a purity rename that erases those incarnation names from code or
how-tos; see `backlog/INTAKE-messaging-host-agent-interface-vs-incarnation.md`.

Instead of (or alongside) Bubble, the bridge can expose a **chat adapter**: a bot in a messaging app becomes the human's remote channel. This is attractive because the platform already solved delivery, identity, encryption, and a UI that's already on your phone — no push infra or custom app to build.

**Hard boundary: the chat app is a human-facing projection, never the agent coordination bus.** Agents continue to talk *only* through the on-disk message store (with its append-only log, leases, sequencing, chase, dead-letter). Routing agent-to-agent traffic through a consumer chat API would trade those hard-won guarantees for an unreliable network dependency in the core path — explicitly out of scope. The adapter holds no state; it projects store events outward and turns human replies into `human-input` / gate-answer messages.

```
message store  ──►  bridge  ──►  chat adapter  ──►  Signal/Telegram/etc.
   (truth)        (projects)     (human only)         (you, on your phone)
```

**Per-run thread as activity feed.** Each run gets one thread/conversation; the bot narrates stage transitions, gates, dead-letters, and the final PR link. A scrollable, human-readable log of the run on your phone — and the place gates are asked and answered.

**What the human can do from chat:** receive notifications, and answer a `to: human` gate by replying to its prompt message. That reply-to-a-gate-prompt is the adapter's *only* inbound surface, by construction, not by a command deny-list — there is no command parser at all, so a bare `/stop`, `/respawn coder`, an unprompted message, or a reply to anything other than a currently-pending gate prompt is never honored. Anything needing a real UI — diff review, merge resolution, tile layout, or a stop/respawn control — stays desktop (or the bridge's own gate-answer-only write path, BL-240).

**Platform trade-offs (pick per context):**

| Platform | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **Telegram** | Easiest real bot API — free, instant, unprompted messages fine. Best path of least resistance. **The BL-239 single-chat narrator described below was retired (BL-353)**; the headless Concierge front desk (below) is the live Telegram surface now. |
| **Signal** | Best privacy, but no official bot API (`signal-cli`, unofficial). Workable, gray-area. Not built. |
| **WhatsApp** | Official Cloud API exists but built for business→customer: approval, per-conversation cost, 24-hour-window rules make unprompted pings awkward. Heavier than it looks. Not built. |
| **Teams** | Right choice *only* in a corporate/Teams context; first-class bots but heavyweight setup (Azure app registration). Overkill for a solo dev. Not built. |

**Implementation (Telegram, BL-239) — RETIRED (BL-353), superseded by the Concierge front desk below.** The single-chat narrator + inbound relay described above (`vscode.*`-gated `setInterval` polling, started only from `activate()`) is gone: it never fired at all once the swarm moved to running fully headless, since nothing headless could reach a VS-Code-hosted timer. Before deleting it, BL-353 first established from code which of its four signals (stage-transition, gate-needs-you, dead-letter, PR-link) the headless Concierge front desk (below, and BL-274+/BL-295+) already carried, and ported the two that were not: **dead-letter** (a new `notify-dead-letters.js` CLI, wired into `handoffd.bb`'s chase-sweep cadence exactly like BL-339's recert notifier, announcing into BL-346's reserved Operator topic) and **PR-link** (announced synchronously from the `swarmforge.openPR` command's own success path, the only place a PR is ever actually created — reusing the existing credential resolvers, not a new poll). **gate-needs-you** was already covered by the Concierge's own `NeedsApproval` event + `bl-topic-approval-sweep!` gate-answer chain. **Stage-transition** was judged already covered in substance, not byte-for-byte: `TaskStarted`/`TaskCompleted`/`NeedsApproval` plus BL-349's headless stuck-escalation email together answer "is this ticket moving, and will I be told if it silently isn't" without a new per-role active/idle posting stream. Only once that per-signal accounting was done did `extension.ts` lose `startOrRestartTelegramAdapter`, `stopTelegramAdapter`, and every call site (8 total, confirmed by grep, not the ticket's own partial list). The four Telegram credential commands (`SwarmForge: Set/Clear Telegram Bot Token`/`Chat Id`) are **kept** — general credential management, still consumed by the ported PR-link announcement and, via environment variables rather than VS Code secrets, by the real headless front-desk bot process. A known, pre-existing, narrower limitation carried over unchanged at the time (not introduced by this ticket): a gate on a role holding no resolvable ticket was invisible to the Concierge's gate-needs-you path, where the legacy narrator had no such restriction — see BL-358 below, which closes it once the standing Operator topic gave the untagged case a real destination.

The adapter above is retired; see "Operator front desk: per-subject Telegram topics" and "Concierge: one Telegram topic per BL-### work item" below for the headless system that replaced it, plus BL-339 (recert notify), BL-346 (standing Operator topic), and BL-349 (stuck-role escalation email) for the notification surfaces layered on top of it this same session.

**Operator front desk: per-subject Telegram topics over the bridge (BL-281).** Beyond the per-run narration thread above, the **Operator** — a role that runs outside the swarm's build pipeline as the human-facing front desk, on its own tmux session/socket — can host each discussion subject as its own Telegram **forum topic**, mapped one-to-one to a `SUP-###` thread (reusing BL-275's thread store), so parallel discussions never bleed context: a disposable Operator wake for one `SUP-###` reloads only that subject's transcript, never another topic's. The path is asynchronous, mediated entirely by the bridge — never a direct or synchronous call between Telegram and the Operator runtime:

```
Telegram  ◄──►  Front Desk Bot (bridge client)  ──POST /telegram-inbound──►  bridgeServer  ──event──►  Operator runtime  ──►  disposable Operator LLM
                        ▲                                                         │
                        └──────────────────── SSE reply relay ◄────────────────────┘
```

`extension/src/tools/telegram-front-desk-bot.ts` is a thin adapter (its pure decision logic lives in `telegramFrontDeskBotCore.ts`, testable with fixture updates and no live Telegram) that owns Telegram entirely: it filters inbound updates to the one authorized principal, demuxes each by its `message_thread_id` against its own persisted `{topic: SUP-###}` map, and `POST`s an already-resolved `{subjectId, channel, text}` to the bridge's new `POST /telegram-inbound` route — the bridge itself never sees raw Telegram specifics. That route (control-auth-gated exactly like the existing `POST /gate-answer`) appends the message to the `SUP-###` thread and enqueues a per-subject Operator event, then responds immediately without waiting for a reply — ingestion and reply are decoupled, never a synchronous RPC. The disposable Operator, woken for that `SUP-###`, loads only that subject's transcript, and its reply is appended to `.swarmforge/operator/telegram-reply-outbox.jsonl` (`operator_reply.bb`); the bridge relays each new outbox entry over its existing SSE stream, and the bot posts it back into the same topic. A principal message with no subject mapped yet **auto-opens** one (BL-294) rather than being dropped: a private DM (no `message_thread_id`) opens/reuses a single default subject, and a message on a not-yet-mapped topic opens a subject for that topic and records the mapping — either way, only one subject ever opens per context, and every later message there reuses it; a non-principal message still opens nothing. This means the front desk works over a plain DM with no group setup at all — the one-time **Topics supergroup** setup below is required only for the full per-subject-topic experience, not to start talking to it at all. **One-time human setup (not automated, only needed for per-subject topics):** create a Telegram **supergroup with Topics enabled** and add the bot as an admin with the "Manage Topics" permission — creating a forum topic requires this; a regular chat or a group without Topics enabled cannot host per-subject threads.

**Thread lifecycle (BL-276).** Each `SUP-###` thread carries a status (open / resolved / closed). The Operator **never closes a thread of its own will** — only an explicit human confirmation resolves one (`resolve-thread` in `support_lib.bb`); there is no autonomous or 3-strike close. When a thread has gone idle for a day or more, counted from the human's own last message in it (never the Operator's own replies), the Operator may post one gentle nudge into that thread's topic over the same reply path BL-281 already uses — never a second nudge until the human replies again, and any reply resets the idle clock. No email path exists for this nudge; it is Telegram-topic only.

**Proactive notify (BL-284).** The Operator can also ping a subject's topic unsolicited — with no inbound message first — when something about that subject changes, over the same reply-outbox → SSE → bot egress the idle nudge above already proves out (`operator_notify.bb`'s decision is a pure, adapter-injected function mirroring the idle-nudge decision; the runtime appends via the existing `append-to-reply-outbox!`). A notice for one subject is routed only into that subject's own topic, never another's, and a status change that doesn't actually concern the human produces no notice — the desk stays quiet rather than spamming. This slice routes only to a subject's own existing topic; a general/ops topic for subject-less swarm-wide notices, and folding BL-239's run-narration into topics, are deferred (BL-239's per-run narration thread keeps working unchanged in the meantime).

**Long-term memory (BL-282).** Beyond a subject's own per-thread transcript, the Operator keeps a separate, runtime-owned long-term memory store of durable, generalizable facts distilled from past conversations (`operator_memory_lib.bb` over `operator_memory_store.bb`, modeled on BL-275's thread-store split) — proposed by the disposable Operator, appended and deduplicated idempotently. Every wake reloads these durable facts alongside that subject's own transcript, so the Operator's replies stay contextually consistent across separate runs and restarts. The no-cross-subject-bleed guarantee (BL-281) still holds: only distilled, generalizable facts ever enter this store — a subject's raw private transcript is never written into it, so waking for one subject never surfaces another subject's conversation detail. This MVP loads every durable fact on each wake; relevance-ranked retrieval is deferred.

**Decide + Status (BL-285).** From a subject's topic, the Operator can also answer a status question or relay a gate approval, replying into that same topic over the same egress. A status question is answered from the live projection it actually concerns — `backlog.json` for ticket/backlog state, the Operator's own `status.json` for swarm liveness, the BL-265 gate view for "what's gated" — never fabricated: an answer not present in a projection is reported as unknown, not guessed. An approval goes through the existing BL-240 gate-answer write path only (no second write surface): with exactly one currently-pending gate it answers that gate and confirms in the topic; with zero pending gates it answers nothing and says there's nothing to approve; with more than one pending gate it answers nothing and asks in-topic which gate is meant — the Operator never fabricates an approval or answers a gate that isn't actually pending.

**Clarifying questions with a bounded await (BL-306).** The disposable Operator is stateless across runs — it acts once and exits — so "ask a question, then wait for the answer" splits between the LLM and the always-alive runtime: when a decision only the human can make comes up, the Operator may (distinct from its existing fire-and-forget notify/escalate) post ONE specific clarifying question into the front-desk `SUP-###` thread over the same egress as any other Operator message, and the runtime records a runtime-owned awaiting-answer state (`.swarmforge/operator/awaiting-answer.json`: the question, the thread, when asked) so it is never re-posted while pending. A human reply in that same thread is delivered to the next woken Operator as the paired answer, and the awaiting state clears. If no reply arrives within a bounded window, the runtime escalates the question exactly once ("[still needed] ...") then drops the awaiting state — never an endless re-ask, and the Operator never fabricates an answer on timeout. A pending question gates only that one decision: emergencies (agent exits, the swarm going down, a provider event) are still handled normally while a question waits. This MVP supports one pending question at a time and asks only in the `SUP-###` thread, never a `BL-###` topic.

**The pending question follows the human across threads (BL-354).** Humans answer wherever they're looking, not necessarily the thread the Operator asked in — a live incident showed a reply typed into the wrong `SUP-###` thread being silently dropped, with the runtime then nagging the human for an answer he'd already given. The thread gate from BL-306 stays (only a reply in the await's *current* thread pairs as the answer), but a reply in a different thread is no longer silently lost. `resolve-pending-answer` (`swarmforge/scripts/operator_lib.bb`) now returns one of three outcomes: **pair** (inbound thread matches the await's thread — today's behavior, unchanged: the reply is the answer, the await clears); **re-home** (a question is pending, but the inbound thread differs — the message is delivered to the woken Operator with the pending question attached but no answer, the question is re-posted into the thread the human is actually in over the same reply-outbox egress as the escalation sweep, and `awaiting-answer.json` is rewritten with that thread as its new `thread_id`, keeping the original `asked_at_ms` so the bounded-await deadline is never extended by thread-hopping); or **none** (no question pending — an ordinary message, unchanged). The human's next reply in the re-homed thread then pairs normally, and an unanswered question's single "[still needed]" escalation fires into whichever thread the await is currently homed to.


**Unanswered `role_ask` markers escalate once by GitHub mention past a threshold (GH-25).** `operator_runtime.bb`'s tick scans `.swarmforge/operator/role-awaiting/*.json`; when age since `asked_at_ms` exceeds `SWARMFORGE_ASK_ESCALATION_MINUTES` (default 30) and `escalated_at_ms` is absent, it posts one `@ldecorps` comment on the configured ops issue (`SWARMFORGE_ASK_ESCALATION_ISSUE` or `ask_escalation_issue` in conf) using cached GitHub creds — GitHub delivers the email — then stamps `escalated_at_ms` so later ticks never re-post. Fires even when the question never reached Telegram (safety net above GH-26). Missing/malformed ops issue degrades to a log warning and `ask_escalation.transport: unconfigured` in `status.json`, never a crash; pending/escalated state is published under `role_questions`. How-to: `docs/how-to/GH-25-email-escalation-for-unanswered-role-questions.md`.

**Pipeline role clarifying questions into per-role topics (BL-607).** BL-306 bounds the Operator's own asking and waiting within a single SUP thread. Pipeline roles — initially the specifier, generic-but-opt-in for others — now own the same capability for their own role-specific topics, solving the constraint-driven design gap where "ask the human to resolve ambiguity" was prose without infrastructure. A role invokes `swarmforge/scripts/role_ask.bb <repo-root> --role specifier --question "<query>" [--options '["opt1","opt2"]']` to raise a question carrying optional enumerated options (renders as tappable buttons via BL-483's existing button rendering) or free-text (omit `--options`); a human can always answer via either path, typed reply or button tap, never both enforced. The question posts into that role's *own* topic from `role-topic-map.json` (the existing BL-425 per-role steering channel), not the shared agent-questions topic, and the runtime records a per-role awaiting-answer state (`.swarmforge/operator/<role>-pending-question.json`: the question, the role, when asked) so it is never re-posted while pending — exactly one pending question per role at a time, and an attempt to ask a second while one is pending is refused with a `"asked": false, "reason": "already-pending"` report. **Two-leg answer delivery:** (1) If the asking role's pane is still live when the human responds (common while the role just asked; rare on a mono-router pack since the resident rotates away frequently), the existing BL-425 steering path delivers the chosen option's label (or typed reply text) as keystrokes directly into that pane; the pending marker clears, and the role resumes on the next loop. (2) If the pane is dormant when the human answers (the common case on mono-router packs), `redirectToRole` reports `no-pane`, and `decideQuestionAnswerForDormantRole` (`telegramFrontDeskBotCore.ts`) enqueues the answer as a `note` into that role's inbox instead, so `ready_for_next.sh` picks it up on the role's next rotation and returns it as a parcel — the mechanism that makes this usable when the resident is not currently that role. **Not polling, not fabricated:** The asking role does NOT spin or reschedule waiting (banned by every role prompt and would trip the endless-loop circuit breaker); it records its context and ends its turn. Recovery happens over tmux wake (leg 1) or `ready_for_next.sh` (leg 2). A role never fabricates a default answer on timeout; a pending question that goes unanswered indefinitely is simply pending, carrying no escalation or forced conclusion — separate tickets (BL-584) will add timeout-escalation semantics later, distinct from this round-trip. The Operator's existing SUP-thread ask path (BL-306) is completely unaffected: it stays byte-identical, asks into a different topic (`SUP-###`), and is keyed to the Operator's own lifecycle, not a role's.


**Coordinator handoff (BL-283) — the front desk's final slice.** When a subject's discussion becomes actionable, the Operator files an intake to the coordinator the same way any human-sourced intake arrives (`.swarmforge/operator/INTAKE-<slug>.md` referencing the `SUP-###`, plus a coordinator note) and the thread records the resulting `BL-###` link — but the Operator only *proposes*: it never specs, promotes, creates, or closes the ticket itself, and the resulting `BL-###` carries `source: SUP-###` so the two stay connected. Thereafter, whenever the linked ticket's backlog status changes, the Operator posts the new status into that subject's topic over the same BL-284 proactive-notice pipe (no second notice path) — quiet when nothing changed, and a status notice for one subject never reaches another's topic. This closes the loop the BL-274 front-desk epic was built for: Talk (BL-281) + Lifecycle (BL-276) + Memory (BL-282) + Notify (BL-284) + Decide/Status (BL-285) + Coordinator handoff (BL-283).

**BL-607's relay transport was dark until BL-708 (2026-08-04).** The `role_ask.bb` → Telegram path described above never actually delivered: the bridge's `readNewReplyOutboxEntries` (`extension/src/bridge/operatorEventQueue.ts`) narrowed every reply-outbox entry to `{id, threadId, text, retractsPendingQuestion}` before it reached the SSE wire, so `roleQuestion`, `agentQuestion`, and `options` never reached `telegramFrontDeskBotCore.ts`'s `relayOneRecord` — every role-ask fell through to the ordinary-reply branch for a synthetic `role-ask-<role>` thread id that resolves to no topic, and the record was acked and dropped as if delivered. The relay now carries those three fields through unchanged, and a `roleQuestion` for a role absent from `role-topic-map.json` surfaces a `console.error` naming the role before its record is acked, so an undeliverable question no longer reads as a silent success.

**Concierge: one Telegram topic per BL-### work item (BL-295/BL-296/BL-297).** Additive to the `SUP-###` subject topics above, not a replacement: a `SUP-###` thread stays for open-ended pre-ticket discussion, and separately, each `BL-###` work item now gets its own Telegram topic for its own progress updates. The swarm itself stays completely Telegram-unaware — it emits a typed, Telegram-agnostic event stream (`extension/src/events/swarmEventStream.ts`: `TaskStarted`, `NeedsApproval`, `TaskCompleted`, extensible; every event carries `{type, backlogId, payload}` and nothing Telegram-shaped, generalizing BL-239's per-role narration diff into a per-ticket one) — and a separate **Concierge** (`extension/src/concierge/topicRouter.ts`) consumes that stream and routes each event into the item's own topic: the first event for a `BL-###` with no topic yet creates one named "BL-### - \<title\>" and persists the `backlog_id → telegram_topic_id` mapping (machine-local, gitignored); every later event for that item reuses the same topic. Every send carries a topic id — a hard contract, never the main group chat — and if a topic can't be created (no Topics-enabled supergroup, or a plain DM), the event is skipped and logged rather than falling back to the main chat. This reuses the same one-time supergroup-with-Topics setup as the `SUP-###` topics above; no second setup step. A completion summary + close are a later slice.

**Fixed: a new topic opened with a bare "TaskStarted: BL-XXX" line (BL-322).** `diffTaskStarted` minted its event with an empty payload, so — since the topic title already carries the ticket title — the message body added nothing at all. Rather than add a new schema field, the summary is derived from what every ticket YAML already has on disk: title → what it is, the first paragraph of `notes` → what it solves, the first `acceptance.steps` entry → how it works (`backlogReader.ts` now reads `notes` as a known field and the first entry of the modern nested `acceptance: {steps: [...]}` schema, in both its strict and lenient-fallback parse paths). `topicRouter.ts` composes and truncates the rendered message — each field capped at 300 characters, the whole message capped at 1000, well under Telegram's real 4096-character limit — verified against a real ~40-line ticket notes block (BL-316's own) rendering at 583 characters, truncated safely. A ticket missing `notes` or `acceptance.steps` still opens cleanly, falling back to the bare title line rather than an empty or malformed message; `TaskCompleted` and `NeedsApproval` rendering are unchanged.

Inbound is symmetric (BL-298): the Front Desk Bot's inbound decision now also resolves a reply's topic against `topicRouter.ts`'s inverse `backlogForTopic` lookup — a principal's reply in a `BL-###` topic routes to the Operator as context tagged with that backlog id and touches no `SUP-###` thread at all, while a reply in a `SUP-###` subject topic keeps behaving exactly as before (appended to that subject's thread, no regression); a non-principal reply still reaches neither.

On completion (BL-299), a `TaskCompleted` event posts a completion summary naming the item into its still-open topic, then **closes** the topic (Telegram's `closeForumTopic`, net-new on `telegramClient.ts`, mirroring `createForumTopic`) — read-only, history preserved, never deleted, since deleting would destroy the summary just posted; order matters, since a closed topic can no longer receive a post. A non-completion (progress) event still just posts and leaves the topic open; a completion event for an item with no topic is a no-op (posts nothing, closes nothing).

**Runtime wiring (BL-300) — the Concierge is now live.** BL-296 through BL-299 were pure, tested-but-dark modules with no live caller; BL-300 turns them on. The Front Desk Bot process (`telegram-front-desk-bot.ts`, which already runs the inbound long-poll and the bridge-SSE reply relay under one `Promise.all`) gains a third, outbound tick loop: on a configurable interval it builds a live snapshot, runs it through `deriveSwarmEvents` → `routeEvent` per derived event (looking up each item's title from the same snapshot), and persists the `backlogId → topicId` mapping to `.swarmforge/operator/backlog-topic-map.json` via a new writer (`recordTopicId`) — the missing piece that also unblocks BL-298's inbound BL-### reply routing, which reads that same file. Dedup is now durable, not just in-memory: the prior snapshot and already-emitted event set persist under `.swarmforge/operator/`, so an event routed before a restart is never routed again after one.

`TaskStarted`/`TaskCompleted` come from backlog folders alone (BL-300); `NeedsApproval` (BL-301) extends the same tick's snapshot with live tmux-pane gate state (`computeRoleGateStatesLive`, gracefully all-not-gated when no tmux socket exists) and an inverted role→ticket map (each role's currently-held ticket, from its open holding window), so a role newly awaiting a human decision posts into the `BL-###` topic of whatever it's currently holding — a gated role holding nothing is dropped, never mis-routed to the wrong ticket. A failed send holds that role's gate transition back in the persisted snapshot rather than dropping it, so the next tick retries rather than permanently losing the notice (the same retry symmetry BL-300 already applies to `TaskStarted`/`TaskCompleted`). This completes the BL-295 Concierge epic's full event set.

**Fixed: the human-in-the-loop was decorative in a `BL-###` topic (BL-325).** A real failure: a `NeedsApproval` notice landed, the human asked "what do I need to approve?", got no answer, and the ticket completed anyway — unblocked by an external Operator working blind, not by the human's reply. Three independent gaps, all shipped together as one loop (fixing any one alone would have left it open): (1) the gate's question snippet was captured by `computeRoleGateStatesLive` but discarded by `readGates` before it ever reached the Telegram message — the human saw only a ticket id, never what was being asked; the snippet now survives the whole path (`readGates` → `GateSignal` → `diffNeedsApproval` → `messageTextForEvent`) into the actual notice. (2) A reply typed into a `BL-###` topic was already resolving correctly (`backlogForTopic` → `TELEGRAM_BL_TOPIC_MESSAGE`) but the event had exactly one producer and zero consumers — recorded, never read. `operator_runtime.bb`'s new `bl-topic-approval-sweep!` now consumes it every tick, shelling straight into BL-285's existing `operator-decide.js approve` relay (reused, not duplicated) *before* that tick's pending-count is even read, so the answer reaches the gated pane in the same tick it arrives, never deferred behind an LLM Operator launch. (3) The reply/notify egress accepted only a `SUP-###` thread target, so even the Operator had no supported way to post into a `BL-###` topic; `resolveReplyTopicId` now falls back to the backlog→topic map so a reply keyed by `backlogId` routes into that item's own topic, while `SUP-###` resolution keeps its exact prior priority and behavior unchanged. **Bounce fix:** the first build reused BL-285's original count-based gate selector (0/1/2+ pending → nothing/answer/ask-which) for in-topic replies too — safe (never answers the wrong gate) but degraded exactly when it mattered: with two or more gates pending anywhere in the roster, a reply typed into ticket A's own topic got "which gate do you mean?" instead of directly answering A's, since the selector discarded the topic's own `backlogId` and just counted. `selectGateDecisionForTicket` (`operatorDecideStatus.ts`) now resolves the gate via that `backlogId` through the same role→ticket mapping BL-301's outbound routing already uses, applied in reverse — falling back to the original count-based selector only when the reply's thread doesn't resolve to a currently-gated role (a `SUP-###` thread, which never carries a `backlogId`, or a ticket with no pending gate of its own), so `SUP-###` behavior is completely unchanged.

**A `BL-###` topic's content is now serialised into the repo — the topic becomes a disposable projection, not the source of truth (BL-329).** Before this, a `BL-###` topic's messages existed only inside Telegram: the swarm's own outbound messages (task-started, needs-approval, completion) were never recorded anywhere, and the human's inbound messages landed only in `.swarmforge/operator/events.jsonl` — gitignored local runtime state, not a per-topic record. Deleting a topic destroyed its content outright. `extension/src/concierge/blTopicStore.ts` now keeps a durable, ordered, per-ticket record at `backlog/topics/<ticketId>.json`: `{seq, ts, author, type: 'inbound'|'outbound', text}` per message, mirroring `support_thread_store.bb`'s own shape rather than inventing a second mechanism. `appendMessage` writes atomically (tmp+rename, via the existing `atomicWrite`) and then git-commits just that one file (`commitTopicRecord`, built on the new shared `gitCommitScopedFile.ts#commitScopedFile` also used by the cost-health sidecar) — scoped so no other in-flight uncommitted work in the worktree is swept in, and fail-open so a commit error (including "nothing to commit") never blocks the write itself. `telegram-front-desk-bot.ts` calls `appendMessage` on every inbound human message and every outbound swarm send into a `BL-###` topic, so the record grows live. Past history is not abandoned: `extension/src/tools/backfill-bl-topic-store.ts` (run as `node backfill-bl-topic-store.js <project-root>`) replays `events.jsonl`'s `TELEGRAM_BL_TOPIC_MESSAGE` records into each ticket's store. Recreating a topic from its record (BL-332) is a later slice and not yet built; safe deletion (BL-331) is documented below.

**Records are actually reaching the repo now, and a missing opener is repairable (BL-348).** BL-329's fail-open commit had a silent gap: a failed `git commit` was swallowed with no trace, and 31 of 34 real records were found untracked on disk with no signal anything had gone wrong; separately, 26 records — every one whose store file was born at BL-330's reconciliation sweep rather than at a live `TaskStarted` — had no opening summary at all, just a bare completion message. Fail-open is unchanged (a commit failure still never blocks the write or throws), but it is no longer silent: `appendMessage` now reports a failed commit through an injectable `CommitFailureReporter` (`reportCommitFailureToStderr` by default), so an untracked record surfaces instead of hiding until someone happens to `git status` `backlog/topics/`. `node repair-bl-topic-records.js <project-root>` (`extension/src/tools/repair-bl-topic-records.ts`) fixes the other half: for every done ticket whose record is missing its opener, it regenerates the summary through the same exported `messageTextForEvent` the live path uses (never a second formatter), inserts it before the existing completion, and commits the result — idempotent by content, so re-running it a second time changes nothing, and a record with no matching done ticket or an opener already present is left untouched. A repaired record gains an opener and a completion, not a full transcript — the messages in between were never captured and stay lost.

**A missed completion is reconciled from current state, not lost forever (BL-330).** `diffTaskCompleted` (`swarmEventStream.ts`) only ever emits a transition the bot was alive to witness — comparing the previous snapshot's done-set against the current one — so a ticket that flips to done while the bot is down, crash-looping, or running a stale build (BL-328's own proven failure mode: a 25-hour-stale build) has its completion missed permanently, with no catch-up pass. For close-only that just leaves a stray open topic; for the archive-then-delete path this epic is building toward it is a data-loss trap, since a missed completion means a topic that was never archived, and a later retention sweep could delete it and destroy an un-archived transcript. `topicReconciliation.ts`'s `reconcileTopicLifecycle` is the safety net beneath the diff path, never a replacement for it: for every DONE ticket with a mapped topic, it checks whether that ticket's completion summary is already in BL-329's own durable record (`isAlreadyReconciled`) and, if not, brings the topic to its completed state by calling `routeEvent`'s existing `TaskCompleted` path directly — reusing `routeCompletionEvent`'s post-then-close behavior rather than building a second notify mechanism. A ticket with no topic ever mapped is skipped (reconciliation never creates a topic just to close it), and an in-flight ticket's topic is never touched. Idempotency is structural: an active/paused ticket is never even offered to this function (callers pass only `folders.done`), and an already-reconciled done ticket is detected via the same durable record BL-329 already maintains, not a second marker file. Wired into `telegram-front-desk-bot.ts`'s tick loop right after the existing Concierge tick, so it runs on every tick as a genuine safety net, not a separate manually-invoked sweep.

**Running headless (BL-292).** All six slices above were built, but nothing actually ran them outside a manually-started VS Code host — `startBridge` (`bridgeServer.ts`) was only invoked by the `swarmforge.startBridge` command, and the Front Desk Bot poller had no launcher at all, so the human's exported Telegram credentials reached nothing. A supervised headless launcher (`swarmforge/scripts/launch_front_desk.sh` + `front_desk_supervisor.bb`, mirroring `handoffd_supervisor.bb`'s bounded-restart-with-backoff and `launch_operator.sh`'s idempotent pid-guard) now brings up both: a thin CLI entrypoint (`extension/src/tools/start-bridge-headless.ts`) starts the bridge headless on a fixed port with a provisioned control token, and the Front Desk Bot is launched against it with the same token — the bridge comes up first, since the bot authenticates against it. No tunnel is needed for the front desk itself: the bot polls Telegram outbound and talks to the bridge over localhost; the front desk is now fully headless-capable. (Making the holistic UI itself reachable from a phone still needs an external tunnel — a separate, not-yet-built follow-on; this launcher serves the holistic UI headless only as a byproduct.)

**Reply egress is at-least-once, not at-most-once (BL-320).** The SSE reply relay in the diagram above (`bridgeServer.ts`'s `relayNewReplyOutboxEntries`) previously advanced its cursor the moment an outbox entry was *written* to the SSE socket, not when the bot actually received it — a dropped connection mid-relay (the real, observed undici `"terminated"` failure, same class as BL-302's inbound-poll crash) silently ate the reply, and the cursor lived only in memory, so a bridge restart forgot everything already relayed. This is the human's primary channel to the swarm when everything else is parked, so a silently dropped reply looked exactly like "the swarm ignored me" — the failure the whole front-desk epic (BL-274) exists to eliminate. The cursor is now ack-driven and persisted (`replyRelayCursor.ts`, `.swarmforge/operator/telegram-reply-relay-cursor.json`): `operator_reply.bb` stamps each outbox line with a UUID id, the bridge exposes `POST /reply-ack`, and `ackedIndex` only advances when the ack matches the entry actually sitting at the cursor — a stale or out-of-order ack leaves it unchanged rather than corrupting it forward. Every `/events` connection (fresh or reconnected) replays every still-unacked entry against a fresh read of the persisted cursor, so a bridge restart resumes from genuinely-delivered position; the bot tracks `seenId`s across its own reconnects so a redelivered-but-already-sent entry is re-acked, never re-posted to Telegram. `telegram-front-desk-bot.ts`'s `subscribeReplies` now wraps the SSE connection in its own retry-forever, capped-backoff reconnect loop (reusing BL-302's backoff helpers) so a dropped socket or failed ack triggers a real replay, not just the outer whole-process restart net.

**A restricted front-desk Operator answers the human even mid-attended-session (BL-334, fixes BL-333's alarm).** The single-Operator guard (`operator-running?`, keyed on one tmux session) was built to stop two Operators taking conflicting actions on the swarm — but an attended (interactive) Operator, told never to exit while the human is mid-conversation, permanently holds that one slot, so no disposable Operator was ever spawned to read the front desk: inbound Telegram messages queued unread for as long as the attended session ran (two days, once). The fix admits a SECOND Operator (`should-launch-front-desk-operator?`) that exists only to serve the front desk, eligible exactly when the full Operator is running (mutually exclusive with the full Operator's own launch decision by construction, both reading the same `full-operator-running?` fact within one tick) and gated by its own liveness guard (`front-desk-operator-running?`, its own tmux socket/pid file — never the full Operator's) so it never double-launches while one run is still in flight. It claims only `TELEGRAM_TOPIC_MESSAGE` events, into its own inflight file, never the events the full Operator has authority over, and both Operators' liveness is reported in one atomic `status.json` write (the front-desk Operator's state nested under `:front_desk`) so neither can overwrite the other's report. The restriction is structural, not a prompt instruction: the front-desk Operator launches headless as `claude -p --tools ""` — every tool removed from the session, no `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, no `--remote-control` — with all context it could need inlined into one self-contained one-shot prompt, and only its captured text completion (never a tool call it makes itself) reaches the trusted runtime, which alone performs the actual reply-outbox/thread-transcript write. This does not change attended mode's longevity — the human's interactive session is not cut short to serve the front desk — and BL-333's own front-desk-starvation alarm (an internal `status.json` signal, not user-facing) stays in place as the safety net for whatever this misses.

**A standing Operator topic — one always-there front door to the restricted Operator (BL-346).** The human's own request during a 2026-07-13 swarm-recovery incident: a persistent, pinned Telegram topic that IS the Operator's home, so he never has to hunt for the right `SUP-###` thread or wait for one to exist. `decideEnsureOperatorTopicAction` (`extension/src/tools/telegramFrontDeskBotCore.ts`) is the reserved-subject twin of the existing BL-topic router's `decideTopicAction`: reuse the topic already bound to a stable, reserved `OPERATOR_SUBJECT_ID` constant, or `create` if no binding exists yet. `ensureOperatorTopic` (`telegram-front-desk-bot.ts`) calls the existing `createForumTopic` once if that binding is absent and writes it into the same `telegram-topic-map.json` the `SUP-###` routing already reads — called once in `main()`, **before** any of the bot's polling loops start, so no inbound message can ever reach the loop before the binding exists. This closes the auto-adopt trap the ticket exists to prevent: without a pre-bound reservation, the first message into a freshly-created "Operator" topic would silently be adopted as just another disposable `SUP-N` issue thread by the existing `open-for-topic` branch, exactly as happened to three earlier hand-made topics. A message in the reserved topic reaches the restricted, `--tools ""` front-desk Operator (BL-334's boundary, completely untouched — this ticket's diff touches zero `.bb` files) as a standing conversation, reusing BL-281's transcript + long-term-memory prompt seam unchanged; the reply lands back in the same topic via the existing reply-outbox → SSE → `resolveReplyTopicId` egress. A failed topic create degrades quietly (logged, never thrown) and never blocks ordinary `SUP-###`/`BL-###` routing; the next restart retries, since the map still lacks the binding. Out of scope, deliberately: detecting that a *recorded* topic id was deleted in Telegram (no send-failure detector for that exists yet — the same missing machinery BL-332's recreate-topic-from-record will need) and mirroring `operator.log` activity into the topic (the human confirmed conversation-only scope).

**An untagged gate now reaches the human instead of being dropped (BL-358).** `diffNeedsApproval` (`swarmEventStream.ts`) used to key a gate transition by the ticket the gated role currently holds and drop the gate entirely when the role held none — there was nowhere untagged to send it when that rule was written. Observed live: the specifier sat blocked on a question while draining an INTAKE file (holding no `BL-###` ticket), and that question reached the human nowhere — parked in a tmux pane until an operator happened to look, the exact BL-325 failure mode reappearing through the one seam BL-325 didn't cover. The standing Operator topic (BL-346, just above) now gives the untagged case a real destination, so the drop is no longer honest. `SwarmEvent.backlogId` becomes `string | null`: `null` identifies an untagged `NeedsApproval`, carrying the gated role instead (`swarmEventKey` dedups by role in that case, so a role that stays blocked across ticks is still asked only once). `topicRouter.ts`'s `routeUntaggedGateEvent` sends a null-`backlogId` event to the standing Operator topic (via a new `RouteAdapters.ensureOperatorTopic`, wired to the front-desk bot's existing `decideEnsureOperatorTopicAction`/`OPERATOR_SUBJECT_ID` binding) instead of the per-ticket reuse-or-create path, reusing `messageTextForEvent` unchanged rather than a second formatter. `conciergeTick.ts`'s retry-hold-back logic now reverts a failed untagged transition the same way it already reverts a tagged one, so a failed post to the Operator topic is retried on the next tick, not dropped for good. The answer path needed no new code: `handleApprovalDecisionForTicket`'s existing count-based fallback already answers correctly when a reply's thread (the Operator topic's reserved subject id) matches no role's held ticket — BL-325's loop, unmodified, now proven for the untagged case too. A role gated *while holding* a ticket is unaffected and still asks in that ticket's own topic.

**A reply now reaches the thread the human actually asked in, General included (BL-355).** Any message posted in a forum supergroup's General topic carries no `message_thread_id`, so `telegramFrontDeskBotCore.ts` filed it under the single default support subject (`DEFAULT_SUBJECT_KEY`) and the reply relay routed the answer to that subject's mapped SUP topic — never back to General. The human hit this for real: five questions asked in General across one day, each answered, none visibly, so the swarm looked dead when it was not. `resolveReplyDelivery` (`telegramFrontDeskBotCore.ts`) replaces the old bare-topic-id resolution with an explicit three-way outcome (`ReplyDelivery`): a subject with a real topic binding (SUP or, via the backlog map, `BL-###`) keeps going to that topic exactly as before, preserving its conversation history; a subject whose *only* binding is the default (General) now delivers the full reply with no `message_thread_id`, which Telegram routes straight back to General — previously this case resolved to `undefined` and `relayOneRecord`'s existing guard silently dropped it; and a subject bound to both a real topic *and* the default (the human's exact symptom: asked in General, answered only in a topic he never opens) delivers the full answer to its real topic but also posts a short, fixed pointer (`REPLY_POINTER_TEXT`) into General via `deliverReply`, so asking from General can never again look like silence even when the canonical answer lives elsewhere. `hasDefaultBinding` detects that dual-binding case by checking whether `DEFAULT_SUBJECT_KEY` itself resolves to the same subject. Subject filing and transcript storage are unchanged — this only changes where the reply is *delivered*.

**Role benchmarking, slice 1 — the coder role, several models, one real end-to-end report (BL-340).** The human's own hand-written framework spec: existing benchmarks (HumanEval, SWE-Bench, LiveCodeBench) measure models as generic programmers, but SwarmForge assigns *specialised* roles, each wanting a different model, and he wants an evidence base for "best", "best value", and "cheapest acceptable" per role. This slice proves the harness on the narrowest useful case — the coder role, because it is the most objectively measurable (tests pass / compile) — against 2-3 configured models, end to end, producing a real report; the other seven roles, every provider, and historical trends are later slices, and the leaderboard itself (BL-347) is documented in its own entry below. `extension/src/benchmark/runBenchmark.ts` runs every configured model sequentially (never fanned out — repeated real CLI calls against the same provider account stay bounded) against the same pinned task fixture (`taskFixture.ts#loadTaskSpec`, `extension/test/fixtures/benchmark/coder-task-01`), each model repeated `repetitions` times via `runTrial.ts` so run-to-run variance is measurable rather than hidden; `aggregate.ts` reduces each model's runs to mean/stddev quality, cost, duration and token usage. A provider that cannot execute shell actions autonomously (`providerCapability.ts` — today just `aider`, mirroring its existing simulate-not-act limitation elsewhere in the swarm) is excluded structurally before any trial runs, rather than being scored as though it completed the task. `rank.ts#rankModels` produces the three answers the spec asked for — highest mean quality, highest quality-per-dollar, and the cheapest model whose mean quality still clears an explicit, stated `qualityThreshold` — with `noAcceptableModelReason` naming why when nothing clears it, never a silently empty field. Production wires a real `claudeCliExecutor.ts` (actually invoking the Claude CLI) and a real `nodeTestQualityEvaluator.ts` (actually running the fixture's test suite) — the harness is built around one fakeable `ModelExecutor`/`QualityEvaluator` port pair, the same shape `recruiter/candidate.ts` already uses, so tests substitute fakes without a second harness. The report is not just produced but *committed*: `reportArtifact.ts#writeBenchmarkReport`/`commitBenchmarkReport` write `docs/benchmarks/<date>.json` and git-commit only that file, mirroring `costHealthSidecar.ts`'s own committed-sidecar pattern exactly — the one sanctioned way a live, machine-local benchmark run's numbers cross into git-derivable state, since BL-347's leaderboard can only ever read git-derivable state. `run-role-benchmark.ts` is the CLI entry point (`node run-role-benchmark.js <fixture-dir> <models-file> <repetitions> <quality-threshold> <target-repo-path>`), its `main()` a thin dispatcher over the exported, in-process-testable `parseArgs`, per this codebase's CLI convention. A real run against real models is committed at `docs/benchmarks/2026-07-13.json`.

**Role benchmarking, slice 2 — the Role Leaderboard reaches the human on the backlog dashboard (BL-347).** The human, asked which of three readings of "think of the presentation layer" he meant, picked benchmark results only — cost-per-ticket (BL-338) and burn rate (BL-273) stay deliberately unmerged — and, on the separate question of destination, chose the static backlog-dashboard PWA: reference data that changes only when a benchmark runs wants an always-available home, not a daily re-send that would become briefing-email noise. Because a benchmark run is inherently machine-local and live, its numbers can only cross into the PWA (a pure, git-SHA-reproducible projection with no bridge/host connectivity per `local-engineering.prompt`) the same sanctioned way `costHealth` already does: `computeBacklogDashboard` folds in the latest COMMITTED `docs/benchmarks/<date>.json` (BL-340) verbatim as a new optional `roleLeaderboard` field, mirroring `readLatestCostHealthSidecar` — null on missing/malformed, never thrown, absent (not empty) when nothing has ever been committed. The PWA renders it as its first-ever `<table>` (every other section is a list or inline SVG chart, so this adds table markup and CSS to `pwa/index.html`, and with it a service-worker shell-hash bump), a collapsible "Role Leaderboard" section (`renderAll`, `pwa/app.js`) naming BEST / BEST VALUE / CHEAPEST ACCEPTABLE per role alongside the stated quality threshold, the run date, and the reported variance, hidden entirely rather than rendered empty when no report has been committed — collapse state persists via the PWA's existing Cache Storage mechanism, never localStorage. `docs/reference/backlog-dashboard-schema.md` documents the new field in the same parcel, additive within `schemaVersion` 1.

**A quality tie is reported as a tie, never resolved into a false winner by array order (BL-385).** The committed benchmark run (`docs/benchmarks/2026-07-13.json`) has haiku, sonnet and opus all landing at `meanQuality: 1`, `qualityStdDev: 0` — a perfect three-way tie — but `rank.ts`'s original `maxBy` reduced with a strict `>`, so a tie silently kept whichever model happened to be first in the config array, and the leaderboard (BL-347) told the human "Best: Claude Haiku" on the strength of array ordering, not a measurement; `bestByValue` and `cheapestAcceptable` inherited the same false confidence, since with quality identical across the board both reduce to plain cheapest. `rank.ts` now derives a tie honestly: `topScorers` collects every candidate sharing the top score (never fewer or more, regardless of array order) and `bestByQualityOf` reports `{ modelId: null, tied: true }` whenever two or more candidates share it — a genuine single winner among otherwise-tied runners-up is still named (the tie path must never swallow a real winner). `BenchmarkRanking` gains two fields: `couldNotDiscriminateReason` (non-null exactly when `bestByQuality` is null because of a real tie, distinct from `noAcceptableModelReason`'s separate "no candidates at all" case) and `bestByValueRankedByCostAlone` (true when best-value was computed under a quality tie — cheapest is still a defensible answer, but it must be labelled a ranking on cost alone, never presented as a quality-cost judgement). The leaderboard (`pwa/app.js#renderRoleLeaderboard`) renders a full-width reason row in place of a "Best" row when tied, and relabels "Best value" to "Best value (ranked by cost alone — quality tied)" via a new locale string in `pwa/locales.js`, in both English and French. The reported result does not depend on model array order — the property a `>`-vs-`>=` mutant would most easily restore — verified directly against the real committed three-way-tied fixture, shuffled.

**The battery can actually separate models (BL-386).** BL-385 stopped the leaderboard *reporting* a false winner; this is what gives it something true to report. The harness previously ran exactly one hardcoded task — `coder-task-01-word-frequency`, one exported function in one file, no dependencies — which every model one-shot for a perfect `meanQuality: 1`, `qualityStdDev: 0` three-way tie: the task was too easy to discriminate on, not the metric too coarse (quality is already fractional, `testsPassed / testsTotal`). `RunBenchmarkParams.task` became `tasks: TaskSpec[]`; `runBenchmark.ts` now loops every task × every model, `TrialOutcome` carries its own `taskId`, and `ModelAggregate` gains a per-task `taskScores` breakdown alongside `meanQuality`/`qualityStdDev`, which now reflect a model's showing across the whole battery rather than one task. `BenchmarkReport.taskId` (a single string) became `taskIds: string[]`. The battery gains a second, deliberately harder fixture, `coder-task-02-inventory-reservation`: a solution spanning two files (`inventory.js` + `reservations.js`) that holds an invariant — stock must never go negative — which only the hidden test suite enforces, never stated in the prompt; verified discriminating for real against three reference solutions (correct: 5/5, a naive one skipping the bounds check: 2/5, the raw stub: 0/5). `taskSoundness.ts` refuses a task whose own reference solution (a `reference/` overlay on the materialized fixture, never shown to a model) fails its own tests, before scoring any real model against it — the mirror-image bug (flooring every score instead of saturating them) this ticket's own mechanism could otherwise introduce; a fixture with no `reference/` directory is left unvalidated (sound by default), so the original `coder-task-01` fixture is unaffected. A hardener bounce closed one remaining edge: `roleForReport` (`pwa/app.js`) crashed when a battery root held zero tasks at all (`taskIds` *and* `refusedTasks` both empty — `loadTaskBattery` has no minimum-count guard) — it now returns `null` in that case and `renderRoleLeaderboard` hides the section, the same "hidden entirely, never rendered empty" contract the section already had for a wholly-absent report. `docs/reference/backlog-dashboard-schema.md` documents the `taskIds` shape change.

**A model's diff is scored by what survives the pipeline, not by what it first produces (BL-387).** The human's own framing driving this epic: "a coder's value isn't its first diff, it's the diff that survives cleaner -> architect -> hardener -> QA." Until now `runTrial.ts` scored a model's diff the instant the executor produced it — nothing routed it through the real review chain, so the harness was structurally blind to rework, plausibly where the real cost difference between models lives (BL-338's ~58% bounce rate). `runTrial` now judges the diff via a new `deps.oracle.review()` seam before ever scoring it; a stage that revises the diff edits the scratch directory directly, so the evaluator — reading from that same directory unconditionally, after review — scores whatever the pipeline actually accepted, never the model's raw output. A diff the oracle never accepts (`survived: false`) records zero quality credit but keeps its rework count, and `ran` stays true (the model DID execute; it's the review that failed it). `TrialOutcome` gains `survived`/`reworkRounds`; `PipelineOracle`/`PipelineReviewResult` (`types.ts`) are the new port. Production ships a real oracle, `pipelineReviewOracle.ts`: one-shot `claude` CLI calls per review stage (cleaner, architect, hardener, QA, in that order), each grounded in that role's own `swarmforge/roles/<role>.prompt` file and given real file-write access to the scratch diff to fix what it finds — mirroring `claudeCliExecutor.ts`'s pattern and `--dangerously-skip-permissions` posture exactly. The chain stops immediately on a `REJECT` verdict (or an unparseable/errored CLI response, treated identically — this boundary must never report a diff as having survived review when the review itself could not be read); each `REVISED` verdict counts one round of rework; the chain is bounded by construction, one pass per named stage, never an open-ended retry loop. That failure boundary covers the whole per-stage setup, not just the CLI call: a QA bounce found the stage's role-prompt read (`fs.readFileSync`) sat *outside* the `try`/`catch`, so a missing/unreadable `swarmforge/roles/<stage>.prompt` (e.g. a target repo not yet onboarded) threw uncaught through `runReviewChain` -> `runTrial` -> `runModel` -> `runBenchmark` and aborted the entire benchmark run — every model/task/repetition already completed — instead of degrading just that one trial to `{ survived: false, ... }`. Fixed by moving the role-prompt read inside the same `try`/`catch` as the CLI invocation, mirroring the `ModelExecutor` sibling boundary in `runTrial.ts` that already turns an execution failure into `ran: false` rather than throwing. `run-role-benchmark.ts` wires the oracle keyed off the *target* repo's own role prompts (the same repo the CLI's `--target-repo-path` already writes the report into — a benchmark measures a model against that target's actual pipeline, not the extension's own), defaulting the review model to `sonnet`, and gains its own `RUN_ROLE_BENCHMARK_ORACLE_FORCE_RESULT` E2E test seam mirroring the executor's existing one. This slice records the signal; it does not yet rank on it — the report and leaderboard consuming survival and rework is BL-388, so the benchmark measures rework while still ranking on first-pass test counts, an expected and deliberate gap.

**The epic's mandatory wiring slice — the ranking and the leaderboard now actually CONSUME survival and rework, closing BL-384 (BL-388).** BL-386 (a battery with a real ceiling) and BL-387 (an oracle that measures survival and rework) could both land fully green while `rank.ts` still ranked on first-pass test counts and the leaderboard still showed a first-pass answer — this is the slice that stops that from staying true. `aggregateModelTrials` (`aggregate.ts`) gains `survivalRate` (the fraction of a model's runs whose diff survived the pipeline's review chain, 0 for a model with no runs), `meanReworkRounds`, and `meanReworkAdjustedCostUsd` — each run priced at `costUsd * (1 + reworkRounds)`, so a run that bounced through N rounds of review costs as if it took N+1 passes, not just its first-pass invocation. `rank.ts`'s `bestByValueOf` and `cheapestAcceptableOf` now rank on `meanReworkAdjustedCostUsd` rather than raw `meanCostUsd`, so a model with a cheap first diff that caused heavy rework can no longer be named best-value or cheapest-acceptable on the strength of that first diff alone. BL-385's tie handling (`bestByQualityOf`, `topScorers`) is untouched by this change and still holds under the richer signal — a genuinely tied run is still reported as a tie, never resolved by the new metric. `report.ts`/`reportArtifact.ts` needed no changes: they pass `ModelAggregate` through wholesale, so the new fields already flow into the committed report. The leaderboard (`pwa/app.js#renderRoleLeaderboard`) gains two new columns, **Survived** (`survivalRate` as a rounded percentage) and **Rework** (`meanReworkRounds` to one decimal, suffixed "rounds"); a report committed before these fields existed renders "no data" for both, never a crash or a bare `NaN`. New human-facing surface: the Role Leaderboard's benchmark table now shows Survived/Rework alongside Quality/Cost/Duration for every category row.

**The starvation alarm now arms on delivery, not on attempt (BL-345).** BL-333's alarm previously persisted `:armed?` — and so suppressed every further alarm for the whole starvation episode — *before* the alarm email was even sent, discarding `send-configured-email!`'s own success/failure result; a transient send failure at the exact tick starvation crossed the threshold silently swallowed the alarm for days (the second occurrence of this defect class in this library, after BL-215). `operator_lib.bb` replaces the old attempt-based decision with three pure functions: `classify-delivery-result` (delivered / terminal-misconfig / transient-failure, folding a test fixture's forced result into terminal so it is never mistaken for a real failure), `starvation-alarm-should-attempt?` (gates each tick on armed?/starving?/backoff-due), and `next-starvation-alarm-state` (arms on delivered or terminal-misconfig, retries a transient failure with a bounded, backed-off attempt count, and arms *and* logs loudly once the cap is reached). `operator_runtime.bb`'s `starvation-alarm-sweep!` now actually consults the send's result through those functions, configurable via `OPERATOR_ALARM_MAX_ATTEMPTS` (default 5), `OPERATOR_ALARM_BACKOFF_BASE_MS` (default 60000) and `OPERATOR_ALARM_BACKOFF_MAX_MS` (default 1800000). On exhausting the retry cap the escalation channel *is* the broken email, so the loud log line and `status.json` are the only remaining signals — accepted rather than worked around with a second notifier. A misconfigured channel (no recipient, no API key) is warned about once and never retried, since retrying a misconfiguration can never succeed.

**A stuck role's escalation now emails the human on a headless box too (BL-349).** BL-336's dark-emitter audit found a real gap of the same shape as BL-215/BL-333/BL-345: when a role sits stuck/gated past grace+cooldown, the live `handoffd.bb`'s `:on-stuck-escalation!` adapter only wrote `.swarmforge/daemon/chase-escalations.json` — the code that actually emails the human, `NeedsHumanEmailNotifier`, exists only in the VS Code extension host, so on a headless box (how this swarm actually runs) a role could sit stuck indefinitely with the file written and nobody reading it. `stuck_escalation_email_lib.bb` (new) adds the missing email leg, reusing the same shared `daemon_alarm_lib.bb/send-configured-email!` sender the daemon-death and starvation alarms already use — no second email path — and reapplies BL-345's exact delivery-based arming rule, this time per-role (multiple roles can be independently stuck at once, each with its own retry/backoff state): a transient send failure never arms and is retried with bounded, backed-off attempts; a terminal misconfiguration warns once and arms; exhausting the retry cap arms and logs loudly rather than retrying forever. Wired into `handoffd.bb`'s existing `:on-stuck-escalation!` adapter alongside the unchanged `write-escalation!` call — the file record still exists exactly as before, the email is additive. Edge-triggered per-role: a role that stays stuck is not re-emailed on every sweep, and a role that recovers and later re-sticks starts from fresh (never-attempted) state and emails again. Out of scope, deliberately: retiring the extension-host `NeedsHumanEmailNotifier` (left as-is), and the other four findings from the same BL-336 audit (BL-350 through BL-353).

**The swarm now pushes its own work to origin, so it never looks dead from outside (BL-356).** Nothing in the swarm ever ran `git push`: publication depended entirely on an LLM role remembering to, and twice in one day it silently didn't — six commits sat local overnight until 04:00, then three more hours of closed/specced tickets sat local while `origin/main` stayed frozen, both times indistinguishable from a dead swarm until a human noticed and pushed by hand. `push_sweep_lib.bb` (new) is the pure decision/state logic for a periodic "does main need publishing?" sweep, wired into `handoffd.bb`'s existing sweep cadence the same way `recert-notify-sweep!`/`dead-letter-notify-sweep!` are — no new scheduling mechanism. Each tick compares local `main` against `origin/main`'s ahead/behind counts and takes one of three paths: **should-push** (local ahead, origin not ahead) pushes with a bounded, backed-off retry budget, raising a push-failure alarm only once that budget is exhausted; **diverged** (origin carries commits local doesn't) never force-pushes — it raises a divergence alarm and leaves reconciliation to a human; **nothing-to-push** clears all persisted state. Both alarms reuse `daemon_alarm_lib.bb/send-configured-email!` and reapply the BL-345/BL-349 delivery-based arming rule: a transient send failure never arms and retries bounded; a terminal misconfiguration warns once and arms. An architect bounce (2026-07-14) caught a cross-episode gap the first cut missed: the push-failure and divergence alarms each kept their own `armed?` flag, but only the two terminal transitions (`:nothing-to-push`, `:pushed`) cleared them — entering `:diverged` never cleared a stale `:should-push` alarm, and returning from `:diverged` to `:should-push` never cleared a stale divergence alarm, so a second, unrelated episode of either kind could be silently swallowed by a prior episode's leftover armed flag. Fixed by clearing the *other* transition's stale flag on entry to each branch, so every episode — not just the first — gets its own alarm.

**Push-sweep refuses to publish a `main` tip that is not QA-approved (BL-630).** The BL-590 post-mortem found the sweep above had no notion of an unreviewed `main` tip at all — every non-QA-approved commit reached `origin/main` within 15-140 seconds of being made, which is what made that landing unrecoverable; a local mistake is a `git reset`, a published one needs a force-push over a shared remote and is ruled out by policy. Before pushing, `push-sweep!` now checks whether the tip it would publish is an ancestor of `swarmforge-QA` (`git merge-base --is-ancestor <main-tip> swarmforge-QA`); when it is, the sweep pushes with no added latency and no per-commit enumeration. When it is not, each commit ahead of `origin/main` is checked individually and the push is refused unless every one of them is either already a QA ancestor or **bookkeeping-only** — its changed paths entirely under `backlog/`, `docs/`, or `swarmforge/`, the allowlist that keeps the coordinator's and specifier's routine bookkeeping reaching origin instead of a total refusal stalling it for most of the day whenever any pipeline work sits un-QA'd on `main`. A refusal is its own alarm class (`:non-qa-ancestor`), never absorbed into the push-failure/divergence retry-and-backoff state above, because retrying can never fix it and the existing "main is not reaching origin" alarm language would mislead a human into pushing by hand over it. **Architect bounce #2, same ticket:** the first cut exempted every merge commit outright by parent count alone; a merge that hand-resolves a real conflict carries content that exists in *neither* parent's tree, was never independently reviewed, and is invisible to every other commit's own single-parent diff, so that blanket exemption let exactly that content reach origin unchecked. Fixed by scrutinizing a merge's own *combined* diff (`git diff-tree -c`) instead of its parent count: an empty combined diff is a trivial merge (its content is already covered by its parents' own entries in the same ahead-commit set, exempt as before), a non-empty one means the merge itself carries independent content and is checked exactly like a non-merge commit's changed paths — proven with a real `git merge --no-ff` fixture forcing a hand-resolved conflict, a shape invisible to every test layer in both earlier rounds of this parcel. Three companion gates complete the BL-590 containment set: BL-629 mirrors this check at the deploy boundary (`build_freshness_cli.bb sync`), BL-631 adds detection/alerting on a `main` that already went bad, and BL-632 is the commit-time guard one layer earlier still. None of the four rewrites or force-pushes the non-QA commits the original incident already put on `origin/main` — fix-forward only, by operator ruling.

**Push-sweep also refuses a merge that took none of what it merged — authorization is not effect (BL-855).** BL-630 above checks WHO approved a commit; nothing checked whether a merge actually took anything from the parent it claimed to merge. `f28a84ad` — QA's own landing merge of an approved BL-848 commit — recorded correct ancestry, a correct commit message, and a closed ticket, yet its tree was byte-identical to its first parent's: 108 approved files across `swarmforge/scripts/`, `extension/src/`, `extension/test/`, and `android/app/` never reached `main`, and every audit trail said they had. Root cause is unconfirmed (the shape matches a `git merge -s ours` or a conflict resolution that took `main`'s side on every path) and deliberately left unaddressed — this check is command-agnostic by design, since it tests the merge's *result*, not the command that produced it. `push_sweep_lib.bb` gains `noop-landing-merge?`, consulted by `noop-merge-decision` at the same per-commit chokepoint `qa-gate-decision` (BL-630) already occupies before a commit reaches `origin`: a merge is flagged only when its second parent's tree differs from its first parent's (it had something to offer) AND the merge's own tree equals its first parent's (it took none of it) — sharpened past the naive "tree equals parent1" predicate, which a 400-merge scan showed over-flags 2x by also catching two harmless `--no-ff` merges-with-nothing-to-take. The refusal names the offending commit, its second parent, and how many paths were dropped, rather than a bare "push held" — the same completeness discipline the incident's own days-long silent trail argued for. Deliberately out of scope: partial-drop detection (a merge that legitimately took some paths and dropped others on purpose), repairing or re-landing already-dropped content, and a retro-audit of older history — all left as separate, non-blocking follow-ups. `swarmforge/roles/QA.prompt`'s landing step is expected to gain a pointer to this check in a later prompt-only parcel (the specifier's to write, not this ticket's deliverable).

**Push-sweep also refuses a path whose tip holds content no commit authored the change back to — the silent revert (BL-1098).** BL-855 above pins the merge that takes *nothing*. Its harder sibling is the merge that takes *most* of what it merges and quietly puts a handful of paths back to a superseded blob: BL-973's landed fix was reverted that way three times in twenty-four hours and restored by hand twice inside one landing, because `git log -- <path>` shows only merges and BL-855's noop-merge gate never fired (those merges differed from parent1 on dozens of other paths). The signature is always the same: for the affected path the tip holds a blob some *earlier* commit authored, while a *later* non-merge commit authored different content and no commit records the change back — or the path is simply absent with no delete commit. `push_sweep_lib.bb` gains `silent-revert-path?` / `silent-revert-decision`, wired through `handoffd.bb`'s `:silent-revert-gate-facts!` adapter as a sibling of the BL-855 noop-merge gate on the same `push-sweep!` decision path (reason keyword `:silent-revert`, deliberately distinct from `:noop-landing-merge`). The verdict is computed from git objects alone — commits, parents, trees, blobs — never from the working tree, so a dirty master checkout cannot change the answer. A path whose tip matches its newest authoring non-merge commit is never flagged (measured: all 27 recent pipeline stage merge-ups stay clean under this rule; a naive "one-sided change was discarded" rule would have flagged 22 of the last 60 merges, including the deliberate reconcile that was repairing this defect). Cost is bounded to paths merges in the pushed range touched — one authoring-commit lookup per candidate path, not a full-tree walk. A refusal names the path, the commit that authored the content the tip is missing, and the merge at which the path stopped matching that commit, so a restore has what it needs rather than a bare status. Human ruling: refuse (same posture as BL-855), not alarm-only.
